Muḥammad bin Isḥāq reported Ibn ʿAbbās's comment on the first half: "**Because they abandoned the truth after they had knowledge in it.**" On the second half, Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Allah is able to punish or pardon His servants as He wills." And Ibn Jarīr commented that Allah described Himself with the ability to do everything in this ayah "as a warning to the hypocrites of His control over everything, and to inform them that His ability completely encompasses them and that He is able to take away their hearing and sight."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads both parables as carrying that same warning: the hypocrites have been warned that they are **not beyond the power of Allah**, and that He can, as and when He likes, take away their sight and hearing, and even destroy them.

Notice that Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss on the closing clause holds two things open at once — that Allah is able to punish, and able to pardon, as He wills.

## Living it

The passage does not hand the reader a comfortable seat in the audience. Ibn Kathir's reading makes that difficult: the fire in ayah 17 was genuinely lit, and the person benefited from it and felt safe, before it was taken; and the hadith of the four hearts describes a heart containing both belief and hypocrisy, each sustained by its own supply, with the outcome going to whichever of the two gains the upper hand.

So the honest questions are the ones the ayat themselves raise. When Islam brings me a share of ease or standing, am I content with that share in the way Ibn ʿAbbās described — walking while the flash lasts? And when Islam costs me something, do I stand still? Are there truths I *recognise and speak about* while quietly reverting when the pressure comes?

And the prayer the sources put in the believers' mouths is not an argument but a request for light — the same words they cry when they see a lamp near them go dark: **"Our Lord! Keep perfect our light for us, and grant us forgiveness. Verily, You are Able to do all things"** (66:8).

passages.title: Worship your Lord and the challenge of the Qur'an
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat are the Qur'an's address to the whole human race: a call to worship Allah alone, backed by an argument any thinking person can follow, then a challenge to anyone who doubts the Book came from Allah. What binds them is the pair of principles on which, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the guidance of the Qur'an rests — Tawḥīd (the Oneness of Allah) in ayat 21–22 and Risālah (prophethood) in ayat 23–24 — with ayah 25 adding the reward for those who accept both.

## "Worship your Lord"

Maʿārif notes the setting: the first twenty ayat divided men into three groups by their response to the guidance — the true and God-fearing Muslims, the disbelievers who oppose it openly, and the hypocrites — indicating that the proper criterion for dividing men into groups is neither race nor colour, nor language nor geography, but religion. Now in ayah 21 all three are addressed at once, with the word *an-nās*: man in general, man as such. No one is left outside the summons.

Two words carry the command.

**ʿIbādah (worship)** — Maʿārif, citing Rūḥ al-Bayān, explains it as expending all the energies one has in total obedience to somebody, and shunning all disobedience out of one's awe and reverence. Not a slot in the day; the direction of a life.

**Rabb (Lord, Nurturer)** — of all Allah's beautiful names this one is chosen, and Maʿārif says the choice is itself meaningful, combining the affirmation with its argument in a very short sentence. *Rabb* is the One who nurtures: who changes man through gradual stages of development from a drop of water into a healthy, sentient and rational being, and who provides the means of his sustenance and growth. Maʿārif presses it with a question: what can a creature do for man, when it owes its very existence to the Creator? Can a needy one come to the help of another? So who else but the *Rabb* can be worthy of adoration and worship?

Because all three groups are addressed, Maʿārif (again on Rūḥ al-Bayān) reads the one command four ways at once: it calls the disbelievers to give up worshipping created beings and turn to the Creator; it asks the hypocrites to be sincere and true in their faith; it commands the sinning Muslims to change their ways and try to be perfect in their obedience; and it encourages the God-fearing Muslims to be steadfast and to make a greater effort in the way of Allah.

Then come qualities no created being could claim: **"Who created you and those before you."** This is the quality of giving existence to what did not exist before. Maʿārif draws an inference from the wording — the ayah mentions "those before you" and not "those who will come after you," and through this omission suggests that no *Ummah* (the community formed by all the followers of a prophet) will succeed the Ummah of the Prophet ﷺ, since no prophet will be sent after the Last Prophet ﷺ.

## The evidence spread out around you (ayah 22)

Maʿārif notes a division of labour: ayah 21 speaks of Allah's bounties pertaining to the human self (*anfus*), ayah 22 of those pertaining to man's physical environment (*āfāq*) — between them, in summary, all the kinds of blessings that descend on man.

**The earth as a *firāsh*** — a word that literally means "something spread out," a bed. Maʿārif notes its fitness: neither soft and fluid like water, on which one cannot settle, nor hard like stone or steel, which would make it difficult to harness, but given a middle state between the two so that man can use it conveniently. Nor does "spread out" necessarily imply the earth is not round: the great globe of the earth, in spite of being round, appears flat to the onlooker, and the usual way of the Qur'an is to describe things in an aspect familiar to an average man.

**The sky as a *binā'*** — Ibn Kathir glosses it simply as "a ceiling," comparing "And We have made the heaven a roof, safe and well-guarded" (21:32). Maʿārif describes it as an ornamented and beautiful ceiling.

**Water sent down** — Ibn Kathir: through the clouds, when they need the rain; and by it Allah caused the various types of vegetation and fruits to grow as sustenance for people and their cattle. Maʿārif adds that even in everyday idiom a thing coming down from above is said to come from the sky, and the Qur'an itself names the clouds: "Did you send it down from the clouds, or did We send it?" (56:69).

**Fruits as provision** — here Maʿārif meets the obvious objection: surely the farmer grows the crop? Human activity, it answers, accomplishes nothing more than removing the hindrances to the birth and growth of a plant, or protecting it from being destroyed; and even the water that feeds the plant is not the farmer's creation. The actual birth and growth of the tree, and the putting forth of leaves, branches and fruits, is the work of Divine Power, and of no one else: "Have you considered the soil you till? Is it you that give them growth or We?" (56:63).

Ibn Kathir sums the case: Allah is the Creator, the Sustainer, the Owner and Provider of this life and all that is in and on it; hence He alone deserves to be worshipped. Several scholars of tafsir, he notes — Ar-Rāzī among them — used these ayat as an argument for the existence of the Creator, and it is a most worthy method of argument.

## "Do not set up rivals to Allah — while you know"

The command lands on that last clause: *while you know*. Having seen who creates and who provides, the mind already knows.

Ibn Kathir cites the Two Ṣaḥīḥs: Ibn Masʿūd said, "I said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, 'Which evil deed is the worst with Allah?' He said, 'To take an equal with Allah, while He alone created you.'" Muʿādh also narrated the Prophet's statement: "Do you know Allah's right on His servants? They must worship Him alone and refrain from associating anything with Him in worship."

This reaches into speech itself. Another hadith, which Ibn Kathir cites without naming a collection, teaches: none of you should say, "What Allah and so-and-so person wills"; rather, let him say, "What Allah wills, and then what so-and-so person wills." A conjunction that sets a creature beside the Creator is corrected into a sequence that keeps Him first.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Al-Ḥārith Al-Ashʿarī — a report Ibn Kathir calls a *Ḥasan* hadith — the Prophet's ﷺ account of five commands Allah gave to Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā (peace be upon him) to implement and to order the Children of Israel to implement. The first was to worship Allah alone and not associate any with Him, with this parable: a man buys a servant with his own money, in silver or gold; the servant starts to work for the master but pays the profits to another person. Who among you would like his servant to do that? "Allah created you and sustains you. Therefore, worship Him alone and do not associate anything with Him."

## Why the ayah ends in hope, not guarantee

Ayah 21 closes with *laʿallakum tattaqūn* — "so that you may become God-fearing," which Maʿārif notes may also be rendered "so that you may save yourselves from hell" or "so that you may guard yourselves against evil." Maʿārif flags a doctrinal point in the particle *laʿalla*, which indicates an expectation or hope and is used where it is not definite that an action or event will necessarily be actualized. Now, if one really possesses *Īmān* (faith) and really believes in Tawḥīd, one will definitely attain salvation, as Allah Himself has promised. So why the language of expectation? To make man realize that no human action, by itself and in itself, can bring salvation as a necessary reward. One attains salvation only by the grace of Allah alone; the ability to perform good deeds, and *Īmān* itself, are only a sign of divine grace, not its cause.

And it is not enough, Maʿārif warns, to affirm Allah's Oneness orally; one must have complete certitude and keep that truth always present close to one's heart — for Tawḥīd, as Maʿārif puts it, is to *see* Him as one, and not merely to say that He is one.

## The challenge (ayat 23–24)

The argument now shifts from Allah's acts to Allah's speech, and Maʿārif notes that in both places the mode of argument is the same. Ayat 21–22 mention things no one except Allah can do, so no one else can be worthy of being worshipped. Ayat 23–24 refer to a kind of speech which cannot possibly come from anyone except Allah, and the like of which no human being can ever produce — so the helplessness of all created beings in producing something equal to it demonstrates that this is the Word of Allah alone, and that the one who brought it is His Messenger ﷺ.

**"If you are in *rayb*."** Maʿārif, following Imam Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, explains *rayb* as a kind of hesitation or indecision or suspicion which has no basis, and can therefore be easily overcome with the help of a little reflection. It is the word used at the sūrah's opening, of the Book "in which there is no *rayb*": the implication being that the truths the Qur'an sets out are so clear and evident that no such hesitation can arise except for those who do not possess knowledge.

**"Produce a sūrah the like of it."** Ibn Kathir reports this as the tafsir of Mujāhid, Qatādah, Ibn Jarīr aṭ-Ṭabarī, az-Zamakhsharī and ar-Rāzī, and notes that ar-Rāzī said it is also the tafsir of ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and the majority of the scholars. Ar-Rāzī preferred this view and observed that Allah has challenged the disbelievers as individuals and as groups, whether literate or illiterate, thus making the challenge truly complete.

Maʿārif adds a point from the wording: a *sūrah* is a passage of the Qur'an set apart from the others by revelation — there are 114, some long and some very short — and the ayah uses the word *sūrah* without the definite article, and hence includes the shortest of the sūrahs in the challenge. Ibn Kathir arrives at the same ground by his own route: the wording here and in 10:38 includes the short and the long sūrahs alike, so the challenge to creation stands with regard to both — and on this, he says, he knows of no disagreement between the scholars of old and new.

**"Call your witnesses besides Allah."** This closes the escape route that one man's failure proves nothing about another's. Ibn ʿAbbās said *shuhadā'* means "aids"; As-Suddī reported from Abū Mālik that it means "your partners" — go and seek the help of your deities to support and aid you; Mujāhid said it means people, that is, wise and eloquent men who will provide the testimony you seek. Maʿārif adds that *shahīd* signifies "one who is present," as a witness must be present in a court of law, and reads the word as referring either to men in general — the doubters may call to their aid any men whatsoever from anywhere in the world — or specifically to the idols of the disbelievers of Makkah, who thought those blocks of stone would appear on the Day of Judgment as witnesses in their favour. Maʿārif remarks that they were even allowed to hold an international "workshop" for the purpose.

**"And you will never do it."** Ibn Kathir points out that this is itself another miracle: Allah clearly stated without doubt that the Qur'an will never be opposed or challenged by anything similar to it, for eternity — a true statement that has not been changed until the present and shall never change. "How can anyone be able to produce something like the Qur'an, when the Qur'an is the Word of Allah Who created everything? How can the words of the created ever be similar to the Words of the Creator?"

## The men best placed to answer it

Those first challenged were, in Ibn Kathir's words, the most eloquent among all nations, and they had tremendous hatred and enmity for the Prophet ﷺ and his religion. Maʿārif adds that the infidels of Makkah were ready to give up their very lives for the purpose of obliterating Islam — and in throwing out this challenge, the Qur'an gave them an easy chance of accomplishing that very purpose, and even hurt their tribal sense of honour by predicting that they would never be able to take it up. Some of them, Maʿārif says, were so mad in their hostility that if they could see a chance of hurting him ﷺ by doing so, they would readily have slit their own throats out of sheer spite. And yet not a single contender came up for the trial.

Maʿārif, drawing on Suyūṭī's *Al-Khaṣā'iṣ al-Kubrā*, tells the episode of Walīd ibn Mughīrah. Worried that the crowds coming to Makkah for the annual pilgrimage would fall under the Prophet's ﷺ spell, the tribal chiefs referred the problem to Walīd, the eldest and wisest among them. Tell the pilgrims he is a madman? Walīd foresaw that when they heard him ﷺ speaking with such lucidity and eloquence they would know at once the allegation was untrue. Dismiss him as a poet? An understanding of the arts of poetry being innate in most Arabs, they would easily see he was no poet. Put him down as a soothsayer? They would discover how false that was and only turn against the accusers. Summing up his own impression, Walīd swore that there was not a single man among them who knew more about Arabic poetry than he did, and that he found in this speech a kind of sweetness and grace he had never found in the speech of any poet or of any eloquent man. After much thought his advice was to accuse the Prophet ﷺ of being a sorcerer who used his art to separate sons from fathers and wives from husbands — an accusation that quietly conceded the power of what he had heard.

Maʿārif reports that even the vilest enemies of the Prophet ﷺ — Akhnas ibn Sharīq, Abū Sufyān, and Abū Jahl himself — are reported to have crept out in the darkness of night to hear him ﷺ reciting, and to have been so entranced that they could not tear themselves away till dawn. Yet they stayed stubborn in their denial: as Abū Jahl confessed in so many words, his clan had been successfully vying with Banū ʿAbd Manāf in all possible virtues, but now that their rivals had produced a prophet, they could not come up with something to match the claim.

The one man who tried is recorded by Ibn Kathir. Before he became Muslim, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ met Musaylimah the Liar, who asked what had recently been revealed to his fellow in Makkah. ʿAmr said, "A short, yet eloquent Surah," and recited: "By al-ʿAṣr. Verily, man is in loss" (103:1–2). Musaylimah thought for a while and claimed a similar sūrah had been revealed to him: "O Wabr, O Wabr, you are but two ears and a chest, and the rest of you is unworthy and thin." ʿAmr answered, "By Allah! You know that I know that you are lying."

## Why this counts as a miracle

To the objection that poets like Shakespeare or Ḥāfiẓ have never been successfully imitated either, Maʿārif answers that a miracle is by definition something which occurs without the like means having been employed. Every poet or writer in the world, even the greatest, is known to have undergone a process of education and training in his art. But the Book came at a time and place offering no facilities for such an education — the Arabs were then known as the *ummiyyūn*, "the illiterates" — and through a Prophet ﷺ who could not even read or write, and who had not tried to learn even the arts of poetry and rhetoric on which the Arabs prided themselves. And it is not merely a question of literary style: Maʿārif insists we must above all take into account the spiritual efficacy and transforming power the Qur'an has shown these fourteen hundred years.

Ibn Kathir cites the Two Ṣaḥīḥs — the wording, he notes, is Muslim's — that Abū Hurayrah said the Prophet ﷺ said: "Every Prophet was given a miracle, the type of which brings mankind to faith. What I was given is a revelation that Allah sent down to me. Yet, I hope that I will have the most following on the Day of Resurrection." Maʿārif draws the distinction: it has been the way of Allah to manifest some miracle through each prophet, but each miracle appears with a certain prophet and ends with him; the Qur'an, by contrast, is a miracle which is to survive till the end of time. Since the challenge still stands, the miracle too lives on.

## The Fire (ayah 24)

"Then fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones." Ibn Kathir explains that *fuel* is wood, or similar substances, used to start and feed a fire. On the stones he reports two views: that they are the giant, rotten, black, sulfuric stones that become hottest when heated; and it was also reported that they are the idols and rivals worshipped instead of Allah, as in "Certainly you and that which you are worshipping now besides Allah, are but fuel for Hell" (21:98).

"**Prepared** for the disbelievers." Ibn Kathir says it appears most obvious that this refers to the Fire fuelled by men and stones, and it may also refer to the stones themselves — with no contradiction between the two views, since they depend upon each other. *Prepared* means kept, and it will surely touch those who disbelieve in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. From this word many of the Imams of the Sunnah argued that the Fire exists now; among the reports he cites is one from Ibn Masʿūd — a hadith, he says, that is in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim — that the Companions heard the sound of a falling object, and when they asked about it the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "This is a stone that was thrown from the top of Jahannam seventy years ago, but only now reached its bottom."

## The good news (ayah 25)

Ibn Kathir explains the pattern: after mentioning the torment prepared for His enemies who disbelieve, Allah mentions the condition of His happy, loyal friends who believe, adhere to the faith and perform good deeds. This alternation — faith and then disbelief, or the miserable and then the happy — is the reason, on the correct opinion of the scholars, that the Qur'an is called *al-Mathānī*.

**Gardens beneath which rivers flow.** Ibn Kathir says the rivers run beneath its trees and rooms, and that from hadiths it is learned that the sand of Paradise is scented musk while its stones are pearls and jewels. Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported that Abū Hurayrah said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "The rivers of Paradise spring from beneath hills, or mountains of musk."

**"This is what we were provided with before."** The fruit looks familiar; the taste is not. Ibn Kathir gathers the reports: Abū al-ʿĀliyah — they look like each other, but the taste is different; ʿIkrimah — they are similar to the fruits of this life, but the fruits of Paradise taste better; Ibn ʿAbbās — nothing in Paradise resembles anything in the life of this world, except in name. Maʿārif notes both readings — that the resemblance may be among the fruits of Paradise themselves, alike in shape but each time different in taste, or between them and the fruits of the earth — and says the point either way is a kind of joy the believers had never known before, a joy that keeps renewing itself at every moment.

Maʿārif adds a caution against the claim that in speaking of the fruits of Paradise the Qur'an is merely using a figurative mode of expression for a bliss that is by nature intangible. It does not rule out analogical or symbolical interpretation: many authentic Muslim scholars, particularly the Sufis, have made such attempts, and they have proved illuminating in many ways. But no genuine Sufi, Maʿārif says, has ever claimed that symbolical interpretation (*Iʿtibār*) is the same thing as exegesis (*tafsir*), or that his own interpretation was the only valid one; its purpose has been to aid spiritual realization, not to oppose the regular mode of exegesis. And if a thing is used as a metaphor or symbol, that does not argue that it has no objective existence. Since the Qur'an has spoken of the fruits of Paradise and of similar things, Maʿārif concludes, they must have an objective existence — though not a physical one in the current sense of the word — and even though we have no knowledge as to their nature and state, all of which we can safely leave to Allah Himself.

**Purified spouses.** Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Purified from filth and impurity." Mujāhid said: from menstruation, relieving the call of nature, urine, spit, semen and pregnancies. Qatādah said: purified from impurity and sin. Maʿārif sums it as clean externally and pure internally — free of everything physically disgusting, and of everything morally disgusting, like bad temper or unfaithfulness.

**"They will abide therein forever."** Ibn Kathir reads this as ultimate happiness: the believers will enjoy everlasting delight, safe from death and disruption of their bliss, for it never ends or ceases. Maʿārif adds the contrast with everything we know here: the joys of Paradise will also be unlike the joys of the earth in that they will not be short-lived, nor will one have to be trembling with the fear of losing them, for the believers shall live in perpetual bliss forever.

## What the passage asks of us

Notice the condition attached to the glad tidings: those who believe **and do righteous deeds**. Maʿārif draws the balance carefully: *Īmān* itself can save a man from being consigned to the fires of hell for ever — every Muslim, even a great sinner, will finally be taken out of hell once he has undergone a period of punishment — but no one can altogether escape the fires of hell unless he has been doing the good deeds defined by the Sharīʿah.

So the passage runs in one arc from the ground under your feet to the Garden. Look honestly at what made you and what feeds you, and the conclusion about who deserves your worship follows — down to keeping your speech clear of setting creatures beside the Creator.

passages.title: Why Allah gives the parable of a mosquito
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat answer an objection. Allah had just described the hypocrites with two vivid images — a man who kindles a fire, and a rainstorm from the sky — and the complaint came back that a Book from Allah would not stoop to such lowly comparisons. Ayah 26 replies that Allah is not ashamed to draw a parable from a mosquito or anything above it, and then turns the objection itself into a sieve: the same parable guides many and leaves many further astray. Ayah 27 tells us who ends up on the losing side of that sieve — not the ignorant, but the covenant-breakers.

## The objection behind the revelation

Ibn Kathir reports from As-Suddi, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and some of the Companions, that when Allah gave those two examples of the hypocrites — *"Their likeness is as the likeness of one who kindled a fire"* and *"Or like a rainstorm from the sky"* — the hypocrites said: **"Allah is far more exalted than for Him to make such examples."** So Allah revealed 2:26–27, down to the words *"who are the losers."*

Sa'id reports a parallel complaint from Qatadah: when Allah mentioned the flies and the spider in His Book, the people of misguidance said, "Why did Allah mention these things?" — and this ayah came down.

Maarif ul Quran places the exchange in its argumentative flow. The preceding ayat had affirmed that the Qur'an admits of no kind of doubt, and that anyone suspicious of its being the Word of Allah should try to produce even a small surah comparable to it. These two verses, it says, refer to an objection the disbelievers raised about the Qur'an, and give the answer to it. Their objection was one of style: had the Qur'an been the Word of Allah, it would not have employed contemptible creatures like an ant or a gnat in its parables, since such a thing goes against the sublimity and majesty of Allah when it would embarrass even a man with some sense of dignity.

## "Allah is not ashamed"

The ayah opens by denying the very thing the objectors had appealed to. Their claim was about embarrassment — about what lies beneath a speaker's dignity — and the reply is framed in exactly those terms: Allah is not ashamed, He does not shy away. Qatadah put it plainly: "Allah does not shy away from the truth when He mentions a matter as a parable, whether this matter is significant or not." Ibn Kathir states the principle in his own words too: in this ayah Allah has told us that He does not shy away or hesitate in making an example or parable of anything, whether the example involves a significant or an insignificant matter.

Maarif ul Quran gives the reason from the side of eloquence: when one intends to speak of a detestable thing or person or situation in a parable, using a gnat or something even more contemptible neither transgresses the principles of eloquence or logic, nor does it go against the sense of dignity or modesty — and hence Allah does not feel shy in using such imagery. A mean thing described by a mean image is not a lapse in taste; it is accuracy. Such doubts, it concludes, arise only in the minds of those whom their disbelief has drained of all power to see things in a proper perspective; such empty misgivings never touch the minds and hearts of true believers.

## "Or so much more" — Fama fawqaha

Ayah 26 does not stop at the mosquito. Ibn Kathir glosses *Fama fawqaha* as something bigger than the mosquito, the mosquito being one of the most insignificant and tiniest of creatures; the rendering of the ayah his text carries also allows the alternative, "or less when it is smaller than it." Either way, Ibn Kathir's conclusion is that Allah has informed us there is no matter too small to be exempt from being used as an example, even something as insignificant as a mosquito or a spider.

He illustrates the phrase from the Sunnah: Muslim narrated that 'A'ishah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"No Muslim is harmed by a thorn, Fama fawqaha (or something larger), but a good deed will be written for him and an evil deed will be erased from his record."** The idiom is the same in both places — a smallest instance named, and everything above it swept in.

**And why a mosquito in particular?** Ibn Kathir preserves a striking reading from Ar-Rabi' bin Anas, reported by Abu Ja'far Ar-Razi: "This is an example that Allah has given for the life of this world. The mosquito lives as long as it needs food, but when it gets fat, it dies." That, he said, is also the example of people whom Allah mentioned in the Qur'an: when they acquire and collect the delights of this world, Allah then takes them away. He then recited, *"So, when they forgot the warning with which they had been reminded, We opened for them the gates of every pleasant thing"* (6:44). The creature dismissed as too trivial for the Qur'an turns out, on this reading, to be a portrait of the life men chase.

Ibn Kathir then shows how normal this method is across the Qur'an: the fly that false deities cannot create and cannot even reclaim what it snatches from them, "so weak are both the seeker and the sought" (22:73); the spider's house, "the frailest of houses" (29:41); the goodly word as a tree rooted firm with branches reaching the sky, against the evil word as a tree uprooted from the surface of the earth (14:24–27); the owned slave with no power of any sort, and the mute man who is a burden on his master, set against the man who commands justice (16:75–76); and a parable drawn from our own selves (30:28). Small things and great — the criterion is never the size of the image but the truth it carries.

## The same words, two destinations

The heart of ayah 26 is what happens next. Believers "know that it is the truth from their Lord"; the disbelievers ask, "What did Allah intend by this parable?" And then: *"By it He misleads many, and many He guides thereby. And He misleads thereby only the Fasiqin."*

Mujahid's comment goes to the believing side: "The believers believe in these parables, whether they involve large matters or small, because they know that they are the truth from their Lord, and Allah guides the believers by these parables."

As-Suddi, again from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and other Companions, explains the other side: "By it He misleads many" means the hypocrites, for "the straying of the hypocrites increases when they reject the parables that Allah mentioned for them which they know are true. This is how Allah misleads them." Notice the sequence: their misguidance is an increase upon a rejection they themselves made, of what they themselves knew to be true. Ibn Kathir gives the mirror image on the other side: Allah adds guidance to their guidance, and faith to their faith, because they firmly believe in what they know to be true.

Maarif ul Quran names this as the reason for the parables in the first place: they serve as a test for men. For those ready to think and to understand they become a source of guidance; for those who refuse to understand — out of indifference or out of a stubborn hostility and denial — they are a cause of greater confusion and misguidance. The parable, then, is put to the listener as a test, and the listener's response is what decides which way it works on him.

## Who is a fasiq?

The ayah names the ones misled: *Al-fasiqin*. Maarif ul Quran gives the root: *fasaqa*, meaning to go outside, or to stray beyond a limit. In the terminology of the Shari'ah, *fisq* signifies going beyond the circle of obedience to Allah — transgressing the commandments of Allah.

Ibn Kathir gives the same root sense through Arab usage: the Arabs say the date *Fasaqat* when it comes out of its skin, and they call the mouse a *Fuwaysiqah*, because it leaves its den to cause mischief. The image is exact — something that will not stay inside the boundary set for it. On the mouse, he cites that the Two Sahihs recorded 'A'ishah saying that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"Five animals are Fawasiq, and they must be killed during Ihram and otherwise: the crow, the kite, the scorpion, the mouse and the rabid dog."**

How wide is the word? Ibn Kathir says *Fasiq* includes both the disbeliever and the disobedient, but the *fisq* of the disbeliever is worse — and it is that severe kind the ayah is describing here, as we know from how Allah goes on to characterise them in ayah 27. Maarif ul Quran maps the same range from the side of the jurists: because transgression does not stop at being merely disobedient in one's actions but can sometimes lead to outright denial and disbelief, the word *fasiq* is applied to a disbeliever as well, a use frequent in the Qur'an; yet a Muslim who is a habitual sinner is also called a fasiq, and this is how the *Fuqaha'* (jurists) ordinarily use the word, making the fasiq the counterpart of the kafir on the opposite side — a man who commits a major sin and does not repent, or who insists on committing minor sins and makes it a habit. (Maarif ul Quran cites Mazhari for this discussion.)

## The three marks in ayah 27

Ayah 27 gives the fasiq three identifying features: a bond broken with Allah above, bonds severed with people around, and corruption spreading in the earth.

**They break Allah's covenant after ratifying it.** Ibn Kathir first gives the broad meaning: the covenant these deviant people broke is Allah's covenant with His creation — to obey Him and avoid the sins He prohibited — a covenant reiterated in Allah's Books and by the words of His Messengers. Simply ignoring it constitutes breaking it.

He then reports two more specific views without collapsing them into one. It was said the ayah concerns the disbelievers and hypocrites among the People of the Book; on that reading the covenant broken is the pledge Allah took from them in the Tawrah to follow Muhammad ﷺ when he is sent as a Prophet, and to believe in him and in what he was sent with. They broke it by rejecting the Prophet ﷺ after they knew the truth about him, and by hiding that truth from people though they had sworn to Allah they would do otherwise; Allah informed us that they threw the covenant behind their backs and sold it for a miserable price.

It was also reported — from Muqatil bin Hayyan, a view Ibn Kathir calls "very good," noting that Az-Zamakhshari held it too — that the ayah refers to all disbelievers, idol worshippers and hypocrites alike. Allah took their pledge to believe in His Oneness, showing them the signs that testify to His Lordship, and took a covenant from them to obey His commands and refrain from His prohibitions, knowing that His Messengers would bring proofs and miracles none among creation could ever produce. The covenant was broken when they denied what was proven to them to be authentic and rejected Allah's Prophets and Books, although they knew that they were the truth.

Maarif ul Quran traces the covenant further back still, to the one all men made with Allah before any of them came down to the earth: Allah brought together the spirits of all men and asked them, *"Am I not your Lord?"* and they replied with one voice, *"Yes"* (7:172). This acceptance and affirmation of Allah as their only Lord and Master requires that men should in no way be disobedient to Him; Allah's Books and His Prophets come to remind them of this covenant, to renew it, and to teach them in detail how to act upon it. Then comes the question that ties ayah 27 back to ayah 26: those who break this covenant — how can they ever be expected to learn from the Prophets and the Books of Allah?

**They sever what Allah has ordered to be joined.** Qatadah asserted that this refers to keeping relations with relatives, and Ibn Kathir notes that Ibn Jarir At-Tabari preferred this opinion, comparing: *"Would you then, if you were given the authority, do mischief in the land, and sever your ties of kinship?"* (47:22). But Ibn Kathir also records the broader reading: it has been said that the meaning here is more general, so that everything Allah has commanded to nurture, and which people severed, is included in it.

Maarif ul Quran takes that broader path: it includes the relationship between Allah and His servant, between a man and his parents and relatives, between him and his neighbours and friends, between one Muslim and another, between one man and another. Indeed, it says, Islam *means* fulfilling one's obligations with regard to all these relationships — religion itself signifying the divinely ordained laws that bind us to fulfil our obligations with regard to Allah (*Huququllah*) and with regard to His servants (*Huquq al-'Ibad*).

**And they spread corruption in the earth.** Maarif ul Quran treats this as the result rather than a separate crime: deficiency in fulfilling those obligations produces all kinds of disorder among men, so that the transgressors end up being destructive for others and for themselves. The fundamental cause of disorder in human society, it says, is the sundering of these relationships.

Ibn Kathir notes that these traits are the characteristics of the disbelievers and contradict the qualities of the believers, quoting Surat Ar-Ra'd, where those who fulfil the covenant of Allah, join what Allah has commanded to be joined, and dread the terrible reckoning stand opposite those who break, sever and work mischief — "on them is the curse" (13:19–21, 25).

## What the loss actually is

The passage ends: *"it is they who are the losers."* Muqatil bin Hayyan's comment is a single phrase — "In the Hereafter." Ibn Jarir At-Tabari draws out the metaphor buried in the word: "losers" refers to whoever decreased his own share of Allah's mercy by disobeying Him, "just as the merchant loses in his trade by sustaining capital loss." Such is the case with the hypocrite and the disbeliever, who lose their share of the mercy Allah has in store for His servants on the Day of Resurrection — "and that is when the disbeliever and the hypocrite most desperately need Allah's mercy." The bankruptcy is declared at the moment nothing else can help.

Ad-Dahhak reported from Ibn 'Abbas a rule worth holding on to: every characteristic Allah uses to describe those other than the people of Islam — such as being losers — refers to disbelief; but when the same terms are attributed to the people of Islam, they refer to sin. Maarif ul Quran adds that such transgressors are the losers in this world as in the other, and that there is a suggestion here that the real loss pertains to the other world, the loss of this world being too small a thing to be worthy of serious consideration.

## Living it

**Do not despise a small sign.** Ibn Kathir's conclusion from this ayah is that no matter is too small to be used as an example — not even a mosquito or a spider. If Allah is not ashamed to teach through so slight a creature, no believer should treat a small verse or a small reminder as beneath serious attention.

**Speak plainly when the truth requires it.** Maarif ul Quran derives a rule from ayah 26: if one intends to explain something useful or essential for the spiritual guidance of one's readers or listeners, it is neither sinful nor reprehensible to refer to something generally supposed to be contemptible or dirty, nor does it go against the dignity of the writer or the speaker. Examples of such imagery, it notes, occur in the Qur'an, in the Hadith, and in the writings of the Sufis and other great Muslim scholars, all of whom set aside the habitual idea of modesty or seriousness in the interest of the real object to be attained.

**Watch how you respond to what you do not yet understand.** "What did Allah intend by this parable?" is quoted in the ayah as the disbelievers' response, not a student's question. Meeting the Qur'an with the believer's posture — that it is the truth from my Lord — is, on Ibn Kathir's reading, precisely how Allah adds guidance to a person's guidance and faith to his faith.

**Keep your agreements.** Maarif ul Quran draws from the mention of covenant-breaking that infringing a contract or agreement made with one's fellow men is a grave sin, which may have the consequence of depriving a man of the ability to do good deeds. It pairs this with ayah 27's demand that we maintain the relationships the Shari'ah has commanded us to keep intact and never break them — beginning, as Qatadah and Ibn Jarir read the ayah, with our own relatives.

passages.title: From lifelessness to life: proof against denial
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat make an argument from gratitude. Having already established Allah's existence, His Oneness, and prophethood by direct proofs, the Qur'an now turns to something no honest person can dispute: you did not give yourself life, and you did not make the world you live off. Ayah 28 points to the blessing that belongs to your own being; ayah 29 widens the lens to the blessings you share with every creature — the earth beneath you and the heavens above. Together they say: if you will not follow an argument, at least be grateful to your Benefactor, for even gratitude will lead you to obedience.

## Why the tone changes here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the connection carefully. The earlier verses affirmed Allah's existence and Oneness and the truth of prophethood, offering self-evident proofs and refuting the whimsical and false notions of the doubters and the disbelievers. Yet there are still men who do not recognise the bounty of Allah and persist in their denial. So the address shifts. The suggestion, as Maʿārif puts it, is that if these people will not take the trouble of considering the arguments the Qur'an has already advanced, then at the very least — as every man with an undistorted nature must — they should be grateful to their benefactor, for even this would be a way of realising why they should be obedient to Allah.

## "How can you deny Allah?"

Ayah 28 does not begin with a proof but with surprise: *How can you deny Allah?* Ibn Kathir reads the verse as Allah testifying to the fact that He exists and that He is the Creator and the Sustainer who has full authority over His servants — and then asking how anyone could deny His existence, or worship others alongside Him, given what follows.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notices something easy to miss. On the face of it, the disbelievers being addressed had never denied Allah at all; what they denied was the Holy Prophet ﷺ. All the same, the Qur'an equates that denial with the denial of Allah Himself. The point is stated plainly: a man who does not apparently deny Allah, but refuses to accept the Holy Prophet ﷺ as the Messenger of Allah and the Qur'an as the Book of Allah, would still be counted among those who do not believe in Allah.

## *Amwāt* — "you were lifeless"

The Arabic word is **أموات (amwāt)**, the plural of "dead". English "dead" suggests someone who lived and then stopped; here it means the opposite end of the arc — the state before life ever began.

Ibn Jarir reported from ʿAṭāʼ that Ibn ʿAbbas explained the phrase this way: "You did not exist beforehand. You were nothing until Allah created you; He will bring death to you and then bring you back to life during Resurrection." Ibn Kathir gives the meaning as Allah bringing them from the state of non-existence to life, and gathers the Qur'an's own commentary on itself: *"Were they created by nothing? Or were they themselves the creators? Or did they create the heavens and the earth? Nay, but they have no firm belief"* (52:35–36), and *"Has there not been over man a period of time, when he was not a thing worth mentioning?"* (76:1). There are, he notes, many other ayat on this subject.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the picture a physical texture: man existed, if at all, in the shape of billions of lifeless particles aimlessly floating; Allah brought them together, made them into a man, and gave them life. Hold that image beside the arrogance of denial and you feel the force of the question.

## Two deaths and two lives

Ayah 28 lays out a sequence: you were lifeless — He gave you life — He will cause you to die — then He will bring you to life again — then to Him you return. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān numbers the stages: the first "death", or state of lifelessness, was at the beginning, before man received life from Allah; the second death comes when a man completes the life-span allotted to him; and the second life will be given on the Day of Judgment, when Allah collects the lifeless and scattered particles of each and every man again and gives him a new life.

Ibn ʿAbbas, in the report Ibn Kathir cites, connected this directly to the words the Qur'an records from people in the Hereafter: *"Our Lord! You have made us to die twice and You have given us life twice"* (40:11). The pattern in ayah 28 is not a rhetorical flourish; it is the shape of every human existence.

And the verse ends where all of it ends — *unto Him you will return*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this refers to the Resurrection, when all men will rise from their graves, will be assembled for giving an account of their deeds, and be finally punished or rewarded according to what they had been doing in the world.

## Death counted as a blessing

Here is the subtle turn. These verses are recounting blessings, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the chief blessing of Allah for man is life, for without life he cannot profit from any other blessing — obvious enough. But the verse counts *death* too as a blessing. Why? Because physical death is the door to the perpetual life of the other world, after which there is no death. What terrifies people is, in this accounting, part of the generosity.

## What about life in the grave?

A thoughtful reader will ask: ayah 28 mentions only one kind of life following physical death — the one that begins on the Day of Resurrection — but says nothing about the life in the grave, although the Qur'an and Hadith speak explicitly of how people will be questioned about their faith in their graves, and will also receive some reward or punishment.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that this life in the grave is something intermediary — **Barzakh (برزخ)**, the period between death and resurrection — between the life man has in this world and the one he will have in the other. It is a state in between the two, resembling the life one has while dreaming; it can be called a supplement to the life of this world as also a prelude to the life hereafter. In short, this intermediary life is not in itself a distinct entity, and hence need not be mentioned separately.

## Ayah 29: the blessing widens

Ayah 28 spoke of the blessings particular to the very being of man. Ayah 29 turns to the general blessings man shares with other creatures: firstly the earth and all that it contains, on which man's life immediately depends, and secondly the skies, with which life on earth is directly related.

Ibn Kathir frames it as a second body of evidence. After Allah mentioned the proofs of His creating them, and what they can witness in themselves as proof of that, He mentioned another proof they can witness: the creation of the heavens and the earth.

**"Created for you all that is on earth."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes how much this small phrase comprehends: all kinds of benefits which accrue to man from the earth and its produce. It means there is nothing in the universe from which man does not derive some benefit in one way or another, directly or indirectly. There are things man uses physically as food or medicine; other things are useful for him without his knowing it; even poisonous or dangerous things do him some good; even things forbidden for him in one of their aspects may in some other aspect be quite beneficial; and finally, almost everything can serve to teach him a lesson or illuminate him in the interest of his life in the Hereafter.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes the great Sufi Ibn ʿAṭāʼ on precisely this verse: "Allah has created the universe for you so that it should serve you and you should serve Allah. A wise man should thus know that he will certainly get what has been created for him, and should not, in worrying about it, forget the Being for whom he himself has been created" (*Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*).

## *Istawā*

The verse then says Allah *istawā ilā al-samāʼ* — and fashioned it into seven heavens. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word: **إستوى (istawā)** initially means "to stand upright, to climb", and thence signifies "to turn or pay attention to something", and, in a wider sense, "to take a straight and firm decision which nothing can hinder." The implication here is that Allah being Omniscient and Omnipotent, it was not at all difficult for Him to create the universe, once He had decided to do so. Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase in the same direction — *He turned towards the heaven* — and explains *fa-sawwāhunna* as His making the heaven into seven heavens.

## Which came first — the earth or the heavens?

Here the classical commentary goes deep, and the sources preserve a real discussion among the scholars.

Ibn Kathir says that ayah 2:29 is explained in detail in Sūrat as-Sajdah (citing 41:9–12), where Allah describes creating the earth in two Days, placing firm mountains upon it, blessing it and measuring out its sustenance in four Days, then turning to the heaven when it was smoke and saying to it and to the earth, *"Come both of you willingly or unwillingly"* — and they both said, *"We come willingly"* — after which He finished them as seven heavens in two Days. These ayat, Ibn Kathir observes, indicate that Allah started creation by creating earth, then made heaven into seven heavens. This is how building usually starts, with the lower floors first and then the top floors, as the scholars of Tafsir reiterated.

But another passage seems to point the other way. Ibn Kathir cites it: *"Are you more difficult to create or is the heaven that He constructed? He raised its height, and has perfected it... And the earth, after that, He spread it out"* (79:27–33).

Before resolving that, Ibn Kathir records a second reading of the word **ثُمَّ (thumma)**, "then", in ayah 29: it is said that "then" here relates only to the order of reciting the information being given, not to the order in which the events being mentioned took place — reported from Ibn ʿAbbas by ʿAli bin Abi Talhah.

**Mujahid**, commenting on *"He it is Who created for you all that is on earth"*, said: Allah created the earth before heaven, and when He created the earth, smoke burst out of it — which is why Allah said, *"Then He turned towards the heaven when it was smoke"* (41:11). And *"made them seven heavens"*, Mujahid added, means one above the other, while the seven earths means one below the other. Ibn Kathir notes that this ayah testifies to the earth having been created before heaven, as Allah indicated in the ayat of Sūrat as-Sajdah.

As for the apparent counter-evidence in 79:30, Ibn Kathir resolves it. **Sahih Al-Bukhari** records that when Ibn ʿAbbas was questioned about this matter, he said the earth was created before heaven, and the earth was spread out only after the creation of the heaven. Several Tafsir scholars of old and recent times also said similarly. The key is the word **daḥā** (translated "spread out"): it means the earth's treasures were brought to its surface after the job of creating whatever will reside on earth and heaven was finished. When the earth became *daḥā*, the water burst out to its surface and the various types, colours, shapes and kinds of plants grew, and the stars started rotating along with the planets that rotate around them. Ibn Kathir closes as the scholars do: *and Allah knows best*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reaches the same settlement: ayah 29 shows the earth was created before the skies, as indicated by the word *thumma*, "then"; and 79:30 does not necessarily mean the earth was created after the skies. What it actually implies is that although the earth had already been created when the skies came into being, a final shape was given to it after the creation of the skies (*Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ* and others).

## A point of law that arises here

Because ayah 29 says everything in the world was created *for man*, some scholars concluded that it is essentially legitimate (**ḥalāl حلال**) and permissible (**mubāḥ مباح**) for man to make use of everything, except the things forbidden by the Sharīʿah — so the use of a thing is to be regarded as lawful so long as the Qur'an or the Hadith does not forbid it. Other scholars say the contrary: the mere fact of a thing having been created for the benefit of man does not argue that it automatically becomes lawful to use, so the use of everything is essentially unlawful unless an explicit statement in the Qur'an or the Hadith, or an argument based on them, establishes the use of a thing as legitimate.

There are still other authentic scholars who have not taken sides in this controversy. **Ibn Hayyan**, in his commentary *Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*, points out that this verse does not provide a valid basis for either view: the letter *lām* in the phrase *khalaqa lakum* indicates causation, signifying that the universe has been "created for your sake", so one cannot draw any conclusion from the phrase as to the use of everything being essentially legitimate or illegitimate. The injunctions regarding the legitimacy or illegitimacy of particular things have been provided elsewhere in the Qur'an and the Hadith, and it is obligatory to follow those injunctions.

## Seven heavens, and "Knower of everything"

According to ayah 29, the skies are seven in number. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān remarks that this shows the opinion of the ancient Greek astronomers and some Muslim philosophers, who used to speak of nine heavens, was no more than a conjecture.

The ayah closes with *"and He is the Knower of everything."* Ibn Kathir explains this to mean that His knowledge encompasses all His creation, just as He said in another ayah: *"Should not He Who has created know?"* (67:14).

## Living it

The passage asks for something very simple and very demanding. Look honestly at where you came from — nothing — and at what you are living off: an earth stocked for you, a sky ordered above you. Let that recognition settle into gratitude, and let gratitude settle into obedience, because in this passage the two are the same road.

And keep Ibn ʿAṭāʼ's measure close: the universe was created for you so that it should serve you and you should serve Allah — so do not, in worrying about what was made for you, forget the Being for whom you yourself were made.

passages.title: Adam's appointment and the teaching of the names
passages.tafsir:
Before Adam was ever placed on the earth, he was announced in the highest assembly. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah reiterated His favour on the Children of Adam by mentioning them in the highest of heights before He created them. These four ayat record a conversation between Allah and the angels: an announcement (ayah 30), a question, a brief answer, then a demonstration in which Adam is taught the names of all things while the angels are shown why this creature — and not they — was chosen (ayat 31–33). One argument holds the passage together: the qualification for viceregency on earth is not innocence but knowledge, and all knowledge is a gift.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the context. The preceding verses had been recounting Allah's blessings and asking man to recognise them and not to be ungrateful to his Benefactor. Blessings are of two kinds — tangible (food, water, money, houses, land) and intangible (honour, happiness, knowledge). The earlier verses spoke of the first; from ayah 30 onward, ten verses tell the story of Adam (ʿalayhi as-salām), and these concern blessings of the second kind: how Allah bestowed the gift of knowledge on him, made the angels prostrate before him to show their respect, and gave men the honour of being his sons.

## "I am going to place a khalīfah on earth"

Ibn Kathir reads this as an announcement of a species rather than a naming of one man: "people reproducing generation after generation, century after century." He supports this from the Qurʼān's own usage of the word's root, where it consistently carries succession and replacement — Allah "has made you (*khalāʼif*) generations coming after generations, replacing each other on the earth" (6:165), "makes you (*khulafāʼ*) inheritors of the earth" (27:62), and if He willed He would have "made angels to replace you (*yakhlufūn*) on the earth" (43:60). The argument is contextual too: it appears Allah was not referring to Adam specifically as khalīfah, otherwise He would not have allowed the angels' statement about mischief and bloodshed to stand.

Al-Qurtubi, as Ibn Kathir reports him, draws out a second sense the word carries: a *khalīfah* is also the person who judges the disputes that occur between people, forbidding them from injustice and sin. On that reading, Ibn Kathir says, the angels may have understood what they said from the word *khalīfah* itself.

From this ayah Al-Qurtubi and other scholars also derived the obligation of appointing a khalīfah — to pass judgement on matters of dispute, to aid the oppressed against the oppressor, to implement the penal code and to forbid evil — since there are many tasks that can only be fulfilled by appointing the imām, and what is necessary in performing an obligation is an obligation itself. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the chain of divinely appointed viceregents from Adam (ʿalayhi as-salām) to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and cites a hadith reported by al-Bukhari and Muslim: *"The Israelites were governed by their prophets. When a prophet died, another would come to take his place. And beware, no prophet is to come after me. Of course, there will be my deputies (khulafāʼ), and there will be many of them."*

## The angels' question

Everything turns on how you hear the angels, and both commentaries insist it was not objection. Ibn Kathir writes that their statement "was not a form of disputing with Allah, nor out of envy for the Children of Adam, as some mistakenly thought" — Allah has described them as those who do not precede Him in speaking, meaning they do not ask Allah anything without His permission. Their words were "only a question for the sake of learning about the wisdom of that": our Lord, what is the wisdom of creating such creatures, since they will cause trouble in the earth and spill blood? If the wisdom behind this is that You be worshipped, we praise and glorify You and never indulge in mischief. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān agrees: they were neither raising an objection, nor being vain and proud, nor asserting a right; it was a humble submission and an offer of their services, and they were "only being curious," speaking "according to their own lights."

**How did they know man would shed blood?** Ibn Kathir says the angels knew this according to their understanding of human nature, since Allah had stated He would create man from clay — or they understood it from the word *khalīfah* in Al-Qurtubi's sense — and he cites Qatādah for the point that they had knowledge this creation would commit mischief on the earth. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, citing Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, that most authoritative scholars hold — on the basis of *āthār*, reports available about the blessed Companions — that it was Allah Himself who informed the angels on this occasion how man would behave on the earth, and only then did they become curious about the wisdom of choosing him in spite of that propensity.

**Why did Allah tell them at all?** Not to seek advice, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: one turns for advice only when one cannot see every aspect of a problem clearly, or when the rights of others are equal to one's own. Neither situation obtains here — Allah knows everything about the smallest particle of dust, and every creature, man or angel, is His slave: *"He cannot be questioned as to what He does, while they are to be questioned"* (21:23). Rather, quoting Rūḥ al-Bayān, it says Allah in His wisdom gave a mere statement the form of a consultation in order to teach men the advisability of mutual consultation — after all, the Prophet ﷺ could have received by revelation all he needed for the affairs of the world, and yet the Qurʼān asks him to seek the advice of his Companions, so that the community would learn this lesson from him and the way of mutual consultation be established through him.

A second reason follows, from a narration coming down from the blessed Companion Ibn ʿAbbās (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) and cited by Ibn Jarir: before man appeared, the angels had taken it for granted that Allah would not create a being superior to them and greater in knowledge. Allah mentioned the matter in their assembly so that they might disclose what they had been thinking.

## "I know what you do not know"

Ibn Kathir's primary reading: "I know that the benefit of creating this type of creature outweighs the harm that you mentioned, that which you have no knowledge of." He then fills in that benefit — "I will create among them Prophets and send Messengers. I will also create among them truthful ones, martyrs, righteous believers, worshippers, the modest, the pious, the scholars who implement their knowledge, humble people and those who love Allah and follow His Messengers."

He reports other views too: "I have a specific wisdom in creating them, which you do not have knowledge of"; or, as a reply to their words *"while we glorify You with praises and thanks and sanctify You"* — "I know that Iblīs is not as you are, although he is among you"; or, on a view of Ar-Rāzī and others, that the angels' words were in effect a request that they be allowed to inhabit the earth, so the answer means "I know whether your inhabiting the heavens is better, or worse, for you." Ibn Kathir closes the list as scholars do where certainty is unavailable: *Allah knows best.*

He then cites a report in the Ṣaḥīḥ. When the angels ascend to Allah with the records of the servants' deeds, Allah asks them — while having better knowledge — "How did you leave My servants?" They say, "We came to them while they were praying and left them while they were praying." This is because the angels work in shifts with mankind and change over during the Fajr and ʿAṣr prayers; and Ibn Kathir quotes the Messenger of Allah ﷺ here: *"The deeds of the night are elevated to Allah before the morning, and the deeds of the morning before the night falls."* The angels' answer, Ibn Kathir says, is itself an explanation of "I know that which you do not know."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the response as two answers: first in the mode of authority — the angels knew nothing about the nature and the requirements of divine viceregency — then in the mode of wisdom, the demonstration of the names. And it names the key subtlety: **the very peculiarity that made man look unfit in the angels' eyes is what makes him fit.** A deputy is needed on the earth precisely for the purpose of preventing bloodshed and disorder; if there is no possibility of disorder in a place, where is the need to send an administrator there? Just as Allah created beings as innocent and sinless as the angels, beings as totally evil as Satan and his progeny, and beings like the jinn in whom evil dominated over good, His will and wisdom was also to create beings in whom good and evil should be equally mixed — who should try to conquer the evil in themselves and grow in goodness so as to seek and attain the pleasure of their Creator.

## The names (ayah 31)

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah "stated the virtue of Adam above the angels, because He taught Adam, rather than them, the names of everything." This occurred after the angels prostrated to him; the discussion precedes that event here only to show the importance of his position, and the absence of the angels' knowledge about the creation of the khalīfah when they asked about it.

**What were "the names"?** Ad-Daḥḥāk reports Ibn ʿAbbās saying they are "the names that people use, such as human, animal, sky, earth, land, sea, horse, donkey, and so forth, including the names of the other species." Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir report, through ʿĀṣim bin Kulayb from Saʿīd bin Maʿbad, that Ibn ʿAbbās was asked whether Allah taught him even the names of the plate and the pot — and he answered, "Yes, and even the terms for breaking wind!" These are names down to the smallest and most ordinary thing, including, as Ibn Kathir sums up, "their proper names, the names of their characteristics, and what they do."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pushes deeper: the names refer not merely to the chemical, biological or psychological properties of things and men, but to their essential qualities and aptitudes. It adds two positions with attribution. Maulānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānawī, in *Bayān al-Qurʼān*, adds that this knowledge even includes a knowledge of the injunctions of the Sharīʿah as to the distinction between the lawful and the unlawful. And many great Sufis maintain that Adam (ʿalayhi as-salām) was given the knowledge of the names of Allah — not of all the divine names in detail, of course, since it is not possible for a created being to comprehend the Infinite, but of divine names in a summary form; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this interpretation was advanced by as authentic a commentator as Qāḍī Thanāʼullāh of Panipat in *Tafsīr al-Maẓharī*, on the reasoning that everything that exists reflects some divine attribute, which in its turn is a manifestation of a divine name. These are scholars' views, offered as such, not one settled reading. The same commentary also condemns rendering the name "Adam" simply as "Man," which denies his existence and his prophethood.

**Why not the angels?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes there is no indication in the Qurʼān that Adam was taught in privacy, apart from the angels; it may well be that the teaching was open to them as well, his nature allowing him to receive what theirs did not. Or the teaching may not have taken an external form at all, the Adamic nature being made to carry this knowledge within itself with no formal education — just as an infant does not have to be taught how to suck the mother's milk, or a duckling how to swim. Angelic nature is not capable of such awareness: an angel cannot really experience the pain of hunger and thirst, the tumult of the passions, or the torment from the bite of a scorpion or a snake. And to the question "could Allah, being omnipotent, not have changed the angels' nature?", the answer given is that the question boils down to: why did Allah not change the angels into men? For if their nature had been altered, they would no longer have remained angels.

From the episode a general principle follows: a ruler must know fully the nature, temperament and peculiarities of those over whom he rules, or he cannot enforce justice and order. "If one does not know the pain of being hungry, how can one deal justice to the man who has unjustly been kept hungry?"

The same commentary records that Imām al-Ashʿarī understood this episode to show that language as such was created by Allah Himself and not invented by man — its use by different kinds of men later producing the many forms of language.

## The angels' reply (ayah 32)

*"Glory is to You, we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Verily, You are the Knower, the Wise."*

Ibn Kathir reads this as the angels praising Allah's holiness and His perfection above every kind of deficiency, and affirming that no creature could ever acquire any part of Allah's knowledge except by His permission, nor could anyone know anything except what Allah teaches them. Allah "is knowledgeable of everything, Most Wise about His creation, and He makes the wisest decisions, and He teaches and deprives whom He wills from knowledge. Verily, Allah's wisdom and justice in all matters is perfect."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān catches a further nuance in *subḥānaka* — "To You belongs all purity." In this context it also implies that Allah is free from the charge of having withheld from the angels the knowledge He gave to Adam (ʿalayhi as-salām); being the all-knowing and the all-wise, He gives to each creature the kind and degree of knowledge and understanding which He alone knows to be in consonance with that creature's specific nature. And it notes the beauty of their conduct: when they found that there was another being more suitable for the function, they as humbly acknowledged the fact and withdrew their earlier opinion.

## "O Adam, inform them" (ayah 33)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to a subtle suggestion in the use of two words. In asking the angels for the names, Allah said *anbiʼūnī* — "Tell **Me**." In commanding Adam (ʿalayhi as-salām), He said *anbiʼhum* — "Tell **them**." The difference in the mode of expression shows that Adam was given the rank of a teacher and the angels that of pupils; it is thus an indication of his superiority over them. The episode also indicates that an increase or decrease is possible in the degree of knowledge the angels possess, since through Adam they were given at least a primary knowledge about a thing they had not known before.

Ibn Kathir preserves early descriptions of the scene. Zayd bin Aslam said, "You are Jibrīl, you are Mīkāʼīl, you are Isrāfīl" — until he mentioned the name of the crow. Mujāhid glossed it as "the name of the pigeon, the crow and everything," and statements of similar meaning were reported from Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah.

**"What you reveal and what you have been concealing."** Ibn Kathir's plain reading is that Allah is stating that He knows the seen and the unseen alike, and he brings in *"He knows the secret and that which is yet more hidden"* (20:7), and the hoopoe's words to Sulaymān about the One "Who brings to light what is hidden in the heavens and the earth, and knows what you conceal and what you reveal" (27:25–26). He also transmits two more specific readings. Ad-Daḥḥāk reports Ibn ʿAbbās: "I know the secrets, just as I know the apparent things, such as what Iblīs concealed in his heart of arrogance and pride." And Abū Jaʿfar Ar-Rāzī narrates from Ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas that the apparent part of what the angels said was their question about mischief and bloodshed, while the hidden meaning was "We have more knowledge and honour than any creation our Lord would create" — but they came to know that Allah favoured Adam above them regarding knowledge and honour.

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir notes that Al-Bukhari, in his Ṣaḥīḥ, explained this ayah in the Book of Tafsīr with a report from Anas bin Mālik: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ described the believers gathering on the Day of Resurrection and saying, "We should seek a means of intercession with our Lord." They go to Adam and say, *"O Adam! You are the father of all mankind, Allah created you with His Own Hand, ordered the angels to prostrate for you and taught you the names of everything."* He answers, "I cannot do what you have asked," remembering his error and feeling embarrassed, and sends them on to Nūḥ, and then in turn to Ibrāhīm, Mūsā and ʿĪsā, each declining, until they reach the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who is told: "Raise your head; ask, for you will be given what you ask, and intercede, for your intercession will be accepted." Ibn Kathir records that this hadith was also collected by Muslim, An-Nasāʼī and Ibn Mājah.

His reason for quoting it is precise, and he states it himself: that part of the hadith — the address to Adam — testifies to the fact that Allah taught Adam the names of all creatures. What this passage records is thus what the believers will still be recalling of him on the Day of Resurrection.

## Living it

**Knowledge is a trust, not a possession.** Ibn Kathir's note that Allah "teaches and deprives whom He wills from knowledge" should make the learned grateful rather than proud, and the unlearned hopeful rather than resentful.

**Ask as the angels asked** — for the sake of learning the wisdom, not to object — and accept the answer when it comes; and remember that if what the angels kept hidden in themselves was known, so is what we keep hidden.

**Your capacity for wrong is not a disqualification.** The very peculiarity that made man look unfit, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is what makes him fit. The struggle against the evil in yourself is not evidence that you were a mistake; it is the arena in which a mixed creature seeks and attains his Creator's pleasure.

passages.title: Iblis's refusal, the fall, and Adam's repentance
passages.tafsir:
# Ayat 34–39: The refusal, the fall, and the return

**What this passage is about.** The previous ayat showed the angels learning that Adam possessed the knowledge needed for the office of vicegerency, and that they did not. Now, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, Allah willed to manifest that superiority in a visible and concrete form — so He commanded the angels to prostrate before Adam in his honour. What follows is a single unbroken story told in six ayat: an honour given, a refusal that ends in ruin, a home granted, a boundary crossed, a repentance accepted, and finally a rule laid down for every one of Adam's children. Two creatures fail in this passage, and they fail in opposite ways. Watch how each one answers for his failure — the whole passage turns on that.

## Ayah 34: the honour made visible, and the first sin ever committed

Ibn Kathir opens by saying that this ayah mentions the great honour Allah granted Adam, and that Allah reminded Adam's offspring of this fact. He notes the report of Musa's supplication — "O my Lord! Show me Adam who caused us and himself to be thrown out of Paradise" — and that when Musa met Adam he said to him, "Are you Adam whom Allah created with His Own Hands, blew life into and commanded the angels to prostrate before?"

**Was the command only to the angels?** The wording addresses the angels. But, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out, the fact that Iblis is the one excepted also suggests the command was given to all the created beings then in existence that possessed understanding, jinn as well as angels. The Qur'an mentions the angels alone because when superior beings like the angels were required to show respect for Adam, it goes without saying that lesser creatures were ordered to do the same.

**Iblis was not an angel.** Ibn Kathir is clear that Iblis was included in the command although he was not an angel; he "was trying — and pretending — to imitate the angels' behavior and deeds," and this is why the command took him in. Ibn Kathir points to Allah's words, *"Except Iblis. He was one of the Jinn; he disobeyed the command of his Lord"* (18:50). Muhammad bin Ishaq reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Before he undertook the path of sin, Iblis was with the angels and was called ʿAzazil. He was among the residents of the earth and was one of the most active worshippers and knowledgeable persons among the angels. This fact caused him to be arrogant. Iblis was from a genus called Jinn." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that his attainment in knowledge earned him the title *Ṭāʾūs al-Malāʾikah*, "the Peacock among the angels."

Sit with that for a moment. The first being to be expelled from the mercy of Allah was not an ignorant one. He was among the most active worshippers and the most knowledgeable — and, as Ibn ʿAbbas says, that is exactly the fact that made him arrogant.

**Prostration to Adam, obedience to Allah.** Qatadah's comment settles what might otherwise trouble a reader: "The obedience was for Allah and the prostration was before Adam. Allah honored Adam and commanded the angels to prostrate before him." Ibn Kathir also reports that some said this prostration was just a prostration of greeting, peace and honour, citing Yusuf's story, *"And he raised his parents to the throne and they fell down before him prostrate"* (12:100). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān argues the same point from the other side: such a prostration evidently cannot have been intended as an act of worship, since worshipping anyone other than Allah is *shirk* (associating partners with Allah) and *kufr* (disbelief), and no Sharīʿah could possibly permit it. In the days of the ancient prophets, then, prostrating before someone appears to have been an act of courtesy or respect, holding roughly the value that a greeting, a handshake or standing up in someone's honour holds for us.

**And is such a prostration allowed now? No.** Ibn Kathir notes the practice was allowed for previous nations but repealed for ours. Muʿadh said to the Prophet ﷺ that he had visited Ash-Sham and found the people there prostrating before their priests and scholars, and that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was more deserving of prostration. The Prophet ﷺ answered: *"No. If I was to command any human to prostrate before another human, I would command the wife to prostrate before her husband because of the enormity of his right on her."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that this narration has come down through twenty Companions, and notes that by the standard of *Tadrīb al-Rāwī* — a well-known work on the principles of hadith science — a report transmitted by as few as ten Companions is *mutawātir* (mass-transmitted), and enjoys the same authority in matters of ruling as the Qur'an itself.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the wisdom behind the repeal. Some acts are not shirk or disbelief in themselves, but may, through people's ignorance or thoughtlessness, become a prelude to them. The Sharīʿahs of the earlier prophets did not forbid such acts absolutely, but guarded them from being turned into instruments of shirk — and the practice of prostrating in respect did in time open that very door, causing distortions that later prophets had to rectify. Because the Prophet ﷺ is the last of the prophets and his Sharīʿah must remain valid until the end of time, Allah has stopped every chink through which idolatry could enter. Imam Al-Jassas states in *Aḥkām al-Qurʼān* that while it was permissible in the Sharīʿah of the earlier prophets to prostrate in honour of one's elders, our Sharīʿah has forbidden prostrating, bowing very low, or standing with one hand placed on the other in the manner of Salah before anyone — anything that might suggest worship — and has allowed only *salām* (greeting) and a handshake as a gesture of courtesy. The same principle explains other prohibitions: making pictures of living things, offering Salah at the hours the idolaters reserved for worshipping their gods, and — in a hadith reported by Muslim — a master calling his slave *ʿabd* or a slave calling his master *rabb*. The words themselves are harmless; they can be misconstrued. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that of Salah's four actions, standing and sitting are things one does habitually in daily life, while bowing and prostrating are not — which is why the Sharīʿah has identified those two with worship and reserved them for Allah alone.

**Why Iblis's refusal was disbelief.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious question: by the Sharīʿah, giving up an obligation in practice is a sin and a transgression, not infidelity — so why is Iblis described as an infidel? Because he did not merely fail to act; he *defied and challenged* a divine commandment, and in refusing to prostrate he virtually said that in his own opinion Adam was not worthy of it. Qatadah puts the same thing in terms of the heart behind it: "Iblis, the enemy of Allah, envied Adam because Allah honored Adam. He said, 'I was created from fire, and he was created from clay.' Therefore, the first error ever committed was arrogance, for the enemy of Allah was too arrogant to prostrate before Adam." Ibn Kathir follows this with a hadith he says is recorded in the Sahih: *"No person who has the weight of a mustard seed of arrogance in his heart shall enter Paradise."* Iblis had disbelief, arrogance and rebellion, says Ibn Kathir, all of which caused him to be expelled from the holy presence of Allah, and from His mercy.

How does a being of such learning fall so far? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the scholars' differing explanations: some say it was his pride and vanity that caused Allah to take back from him the wealth of knowledge and understanding, so that he came to act like an ignorant fool; others suggest his error was due to self-love and ambition.
