Ibn Kathir adds that the "horrible torment" here refers to the killing of the male infants, and that Sūrat Ibrāhīm makes this explicit: *"…and were slaughtering your sons and letting your women live"* (14:6). He notes that Allah mentions saving their children from being slaughtered precisely in order to remind them of the many favours He granted them.

**"And therein was a mighty trial from your Lord."** Ibn Jarir understood this to mean: *our saving your fathers from what they suffered at Pharaoh's hand is a great blessing from your Lord*. Ibn Kathir then draws out something easy to miss — **there is a test inside a blessing just as there is inside a hardship**, citing *"And We shall make a trial of you with evil and with good"* (21:35) and *"And We tried them with good and evil, that they might turn to Him"* (7:168). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays the two possibilities side by side: the "great trial" is either the slaughter of the sons — a calamity, and calamity tests **patience** — or the deliverance itself, a blessing, and blessing tests **gratitude**. Both readings leave the reader nowhere to hide. Whichever way life turns, something is being asked of you.

## The sea (ayah 50)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene: Musa (peace be upon him) laboured for a long time as a messenger to bring Pharaoh and his people to the truth, and when they persisted in their denial, Allah commanded him to take the Israelites and **leave Egypt secretly**. On the way they came up against a sea, with Pharaoh and his army in hot pursuit behind them. Allah commanded the sea to split and make a way; they went over smoothly. When Pharaoh and his men followed them into the sea, the water gathered back over them and they were drowned then and there.

Ibn Kathir's comment on **"and We saved you"** is worth pausing over: *"We saved you from them, drowning them while you watched, bringing relief to your hearts and humiliation to your enemy."* That phrase in the ayah — **"while you were watching"** — is the point. Rescue and judgement were not reported to them second-hand; in Ibn Kathir's wording, the drowning happened while they watched. It is worth holding that scene in mind while reading ayah 51.

**A doctrinal point.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Bayān al-Qurʼān) stops here to say plainly that the splitting of the sea in ayah 50 clearly proves that **miracles do occur at the hands of prophets** — against the attempts of some Westernised Muslims to deny them.

## From the Sunnah: the day of ʿĀshūrāʼ

Ibn Kathir reports that the day the Children of Israel were saved from Pharaoh was called the day of ʿĀshūrāʼ. Imam Ahmad reported that Ibn ʿAbbas said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to Al-Madinah and found the Jews fasting the day of ʿĀshūrāʼ. He asked them, "What is this day that you fast?" They said: this is a good day, on which Allah saved the Children of Israel from their enemy, and Musa used to fast this day. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> **"I have more right to Musa than you have."**

He ﷺ then fasted that day and ordered that it be fasted. Ibn Kathir states that this hadith was collected by **Al-Bukhari, Muslim, An-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah**.

So the Sunnah keeps the rescue described in ayah 50 alive in the Muslim calendar: the day of the deliverance is a day the Prophet ﷺ himself fasted and told his community to fast.

## Forty nights, and the calf (ayah 51)

Ibn Kathir explains that Musa went to the meeting place with his Lord at the end of a period of forty days, and that this period is broken down in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf: *"And We appointed for Musa thirty nights and added ten more"* (7:142). It was said that these were the days of Dhul-Qaʿdah plus the first ten of Dhul-Hijjah, after the Israelites had been delivered from Pharaoh and had safely crossed the sea.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the human story. With Pharaoh drowned and the Israelites finally at peace — according to one report back in Egypt, according to another settled somewhere else — they wished they could receive a *sharīʿah*, a religious code of laws from Allah to follow. Allah answered the supplication of Musa (peace be upon him) and promised that if he came to Mount Ṭūr (Sinai) and devoted himself to worship for a month, he would receive a Divine Book. He gladly obeyed and was granted the Torah. He was then ordered to worship ten days more: he had broken his fast at the end of the month and so lost **the special odour that rises from the mouth of a fasting person, which is very pleasant to Allah** — so he was commanded to fast ten additional days and regain it. In all, forty days of total fasting and devotion.

And while he was on Mount Sinai, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān continues, something very odious happened to the Israelites. A man among them called **Sāmiriyy** fashioned the figure of a calf out of gold or silver and put into it some of the dust he had picked up from under the hooves of the horse of Jibrāʼīl (peace be upon him), at the time when Pharaoh and his army had been drowned. The golden calf immediately acquired life, and **the ignorant among the Israelites** were so impressed that they started worshipping it.

**Why "you were wrongdoers" (ẓālimūn)?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that ayah 51 calls them "unjust" for this sin, because **injustice lies in putting things in improper places** — and idolatry is essentially just that. To take the created and set it where only the Creator belongs is precisely that misplacement.

## "Then We forgave you" (ayah 52)

The speed of this ayah is itself the mercy: after the sea, after the mountain, after the calf — *then We pardoned you*. But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to block a false conclusion: **the Israelites were forgiven only when they had offered tawbah (repentance)**, in the manner recounted in ayah 54. Pardon came, but through the door of repentance.

**"So that you might be grateful."** The Arabic word here is *laʿalla*, which indicates expectation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses the question a careful reader will feel: in this context it does **not** mean that Allah had, or could have, any doubt or misgiving about this or any other matter. What the word implies is that when a man receives a pardon, **the onlookers may expect him to feel grateful**. The expectation describes what the situation calls for, not any uncertainty in the knowledge of Allah.

## The Book and the Criterion (ayah 53)

Ibn Kathir: *"the Scripture"* means the Tawrāh, and *al-Furqān* is **that which differentiates between truth and falsehood, guidance and deviation** — *"so that you may be guided aright"*, after their escape from the sea. He points to the parallel in Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ: *"And indeed We gave Musa — after We had destroyed the generations of old — the Scripture as an enlightenment for mankind, and a guidance and a mercy, that they might remember"* (28:43).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Torah is the book which was given to Musa (peace be upon him), and explains that in the language of the Holy Qur'an *al-Furqān* is a term signifying something which separates truth from falsehood, or distinguishes the one from the other. Here it refers either to **(a)** the injunctions of the sharīʿah found in the Torah, since the sharīʿah resolves all the differences that may arise with regard to doctrine or to the practice of good deeds; or to **(b)** miracles, which decide between a true and a false claim in a palpable manner; or even to **(c)** the Torah itself, which has the twin qualities of being a Book of Allah and being an instrument for separating truth from falsehood.

## What repentance cost (ayah 54)

Musa (peace be upon him) says: *"O my people! Verily, you have wronged yourselves by worshipping the calf. So turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves…"* — which Ibn Kathir glosses as **the innocent killing the wrongdoers among them**. This, he says, was the repentance required from the Children of Israel for worshipping the calf.

**When did he say it?** Al-Hasan Al-Basri held that this came after their hearts had already turned — after *"And when they regretted and saw that they had gone astray, they said: If our Lord does not have mercy upon us and forgive us…"* (7:149). It was at that moment that Musa said to them, *"O my people! Verily, you have wronged yourselves by worshipping the calf."*

**"To your Bāriʼ."** Abu al-ʿĀliyah, Saʿīd bin Jubayr and Ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas explained *Bāriʼ* as **"your Creator."** Ibn Kathir draws out why this particular name is used: it **alerts the Children of Israel to the enormity of their error** — "Repent to He Who created you after you associated others with Him in worship." The word chosen puts their crime and its remedy in the same breath.

**How it was carried out.** An-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded Ibn ʿAbbas saying that Allah told the Children of Israel their repentance would be to slay by the sword every person they met, be he father or son, not caring whom they killed — and that those who were guilty, whose guilt Musa and Harun were not aware of, admitted their sin and did as they were ordered, **so Allah forgave both the killer and the one killed**. Ibn Jarir also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that Allah ordered Musa to command his people to kill each other: those who had worshipped the calf were ordered to sit down, and those who had not to stand holding knives in their hands. When the killing began, **a great darkness suddenly overcame them**; after the darkness lifted, seventy thousand had been killed — and those who were killed were forgiven, and those who remained alive were forgiven too.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this the **special mode of offering tawbah prescribed for the Israelites in that situation**: those who had not indulged in the worship of the golden calf were to execute those who had. It adds that similarly, in the Islamic sharīʿah too, certain major sins necessarily entail capital punishment even when the sinner has offered this tawbah — for example, a life in return for a life in the case of intentional homicide, or death by stoning in the case of adultery **established through proper evidence**. And when the Israelites acted upon this divine commandment, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, they became worthy of receiving the mercy and favour of Allah in the other world.

**"Truly, He is the One Who accepts repentance, the Most Merciful."** The passage that began with sons being slaughtered by a tyrant ends with a community surviving its own worst hour — not because the sin was small, but because *at-Tawwāb ar-Raḥīm* is who Allah is.

## Living it

**Remember specifically.** The whole passage is built on "remember when…" — not a vague gratitude but named events: this rescue, this crossing, this pardon. Do the same with your own life.

**Expect the test in the good times.** Ibn Kathir's point from 21:35 and 7:168 is the practical heart of ayah 49: there is a test in the blessing the same as there is in the hardship. Hardship asks for patience; blessing asks for thanks.

**Nothing is beyond pardon, and pardon has a door.** Ayah 52 announces forgiveness; ayah 54 shows what it cost. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's warning stands: they were forgiven *only when they repented*. Mercy is real, and it is entered through turning back.

**Hold to the criterion.** A people who had watched the sea split still fell for a calf — the ignorant among them, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, were *so impressed* that they began to worship it. What is impressive is not the same as what is true, and *al-Furqān* is precisely what separates the two.

passages.title: Demanding to see Allah; the clouds and the manna
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These three ayat continue Allah's roll-call of favours to the Children of Israel — but they do it by pairing each favour with the ingratitude that met it. In ayah 55 a group of them tells Musa (peace be upon him) that they will not believe him until they see Allah with their own eyes, and a thunderbolt seizes them. In ayah 56 Allah raises them after their death "so that you might be grateful." In ayah 57 the scene widens to the years of wandering: shade from cloud, food sent down from above, and the closing verdict that their rebellion harmed no one but themselves.

What holds the three together is a single rhythm: **demand → death → revival → provision → ingratitude.** Ibn Kathir frames ayat 55–56 as Allah saying, in effect, *Remember My favour on you for resurrecting you after you were seized with lightning when you asked to see Me directly* — a statement he reports from Ibn Jurayj. And he notes that after Allah mentions the calamities He saved them from, He goes on to mention the favours He granted them. The passage is one continuous argument: you were shown more than any people, and you still turned away.

## How they came to say it

The sources give us two complementary accounts of the moment.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** places it just after Musa (peace be upon him) brought the Torah down from Mount Tur (Sinai) and presented it to the Israelites as the Book of Allah. Some of them were insolent enough to say they could not believe it unless Allah Himself told them so in so many words. With the permission of Allah, Musa (peace be upon him) replied that even this condition would be fulfilled if they went with him to Mount Tur. The Israelites chose seventy men. Arriving there, **they heard the words of Allah with their own ears** — and then, in their perversity, invented a new ruse. It was not enough, they said, to hear the speech, for they could not be sure whether it was Allah Himself who had spoken or someone else. But they would be finally convinced if they could *see* Allah with their own eyes.

That detail is the heart of it, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's own word for what followed is *perversity*: the condition was met, and a new one was invented in its place.

*A reflection of my own, not something the sources say:* a condition that relocates every time it is satisfied was never really a request for evidence.

**Ibn Kathir** preserves a second telling, from ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam. Musa (peace be upon him) returned from meeting his Lord carrying the Tablets on which Allah had written the Tawrah, and found that they had worshipped the calf in his absence. He commanded them to kill themselves, they complied, and Allah forgave them. Then he said to them, "These Tablets have Allah's Book, containing what He commanded you and what He forbade for you." They answered: *Should we believe this statement because you said it? By Allah, we will not believe until we see Allah in the open, until He shows us Himself and says: This is My Book, therefore adhere to it. Why does He not talk to us as He talked to you, O Musa?*

Read that last line slowly. The narration records the question; it does not tell us what lay behind it.

*A reflection of my own:* underneath a demand for proof there can sit a quarrel with the channel — that revelation came through a man, and not to each of them directly.

## The words they chose

Two things in the Arabic of ayah 55 carry the weight.

**"We shall never believe *in you* (lan nuʼmina *laka*)."** The refusal is worded toward the messenger. ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd's narration has the same shape: *Should we believe this statement because you said it?* *A reflection of my own:* the Book was in front of them, and the objection fastened itself to the human being holding it.

**"*Jahratan*"** — rendered "plainly." Ibn ʿAbbas explains it as *"publicly"* and *"so that we gaze at Allah."* What they were asking for was open and public, not a quiet inner certainty.

Both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answer this the same way. Ibn Jurayj's words in Ibn Kathir are that they asked to see Allah directly, *"which neither you nor anyone else can bear or attain."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it as: it is beyond the power of a living being to see Allah in the physical world, and so they had to pay for their impertinence. The point is not a denial of Allah's greatness — it is a statement about what created eyes can bear in this world.

## The thunderbolt, and "while you were looking"

Ayah 55 ends with *fa-akhadhatkumu al-ṣāʿiqah wa antum tanẓurūn* — "you were seized with a bolt of lightning while you were looking on."

ʿUrwah bin Ruwaym reads "while you were looking" as meaning **some of them were struck with lightning while others were watching**; Allah then resurrected those who had been struck, and struck the ones who had been watching. The punishment moved through the group in full view.

As-Suddi supplies what happened next. They died, and Musa (peace be upon him) stood up crying and supplicating to Allah: *O Lord! What should I say to the Children of Israel when I go back to them after You destroyed the best of them* — and he prayed with the words the Qur'an preserves, "If it had been Your will, You could have destroyed them and me before; would You destroy us for the deeds of the foolish ones among us?" Allah then revealed to Musa that **these seventy men were among those who had worshipped the calf**. The demand to see Allah did not come from a group untouched by the calf; it came from among the very people who had bowed to it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a further dimension to Musa's fear. The Israelites had always been mistrustful of him, and he feared they would suspect him of having taken these men to a solitary place and had them slaughtered. So he prayed to Allah to save him from such a vile accusation — and Allah granted his prayer and gave them new life.

## Raised from the dead — ayah 56

Allah brought them back **one man at a time, while the rest of them were watching how Allah was bringing them back to life** (As-Suddi). The return was not merely granted; it was *watched*, one man after another. This is why the ayah closes with *laʿallakum tashkurūn* — "so that you might be grateful."

Ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas explains the shape of it: **death was their punishment, and they were resurrected after they died so they could finish out their lives** — Qatadah said similarly. The penalty was carried out in full; the return was a lifespan handed back.

**A point the scholars differed over.** Once a person has been dead and brought back, is he still religiously accountable? Ibn Kathir reports that Al-Mawardi records two opinions. The first: since the Children of Israel witnessed these miracles, they were *compelled* to believe, and so did not have to fulfil the commandments. The second: they were required to adhere to the commandments, so that no responsible adult is free of such responsibilities. **Al-Qurtubi said the second is what is correct** — although they witnessed these tremendous calamities and incidents, that did not mean they were no longer responsible for fulfilling the commandments; rather they are responsible, "and this is clear. Allah knows best."

The narration from ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd shows why the question is not academic. After they were revived, Musa (peace be upon him) said to them, "Take the Book of Allah." They said, "No." He said, "What is the matter with you?" They said, "The problem is that we died and came back to life." He said again, "Take the Book of Allah." They said, "No." So Allah sent some angels who made the mountain topple over them.

They had said: *we will not believe until we see*. They saw death, and they saw life given back — and still said no. *A reflection of my own:* a miracle can settle a question without softening a heart; that softening is asked of us, not done to us.

## Ayah 57: the wilderness of Tīh

To feel the mercy in this ayah you need the setting, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supplies. The Israelites belonged to Syria but had gone to Egypt in the time of Yusuf (peace be upon him) and settled there, while Syria itself had come under the domination of a people called the ʿAmāliqah. After Pharaoh was drowned and the Israelites could live in peace, Allah commanded them to go to war against the ʿAmāliqah and to free their homeland. They started on the expedition — but on approaching Syria, when they came to learn of the military strength of the foe, their courage failed them and they refused to engage in the fighting.

Allah punished them for their disobedience: for a full forty years they wandered in a wilderness and could not even go back to Egypt. The wilderness was not very vast — only a stretch of some ten miles, lying between Egypt and Syria. They would make a day-long march in the direction of Egypt and stop somewhere for the night, and on getting up the next morning would always find themselves just where they had started from. Forty years of that, in futile rage and exasperation. That is why the wilderness is called **Tīh**, which signifies *having lost one's way*.

It was barren space — without a tree or a building that could offer protection against heat or cold, no food to eat and no clothes to wear. And yet, in answer to the prayer of Musa (peace be upon him), Allah made a miraculous provision for all their needs.

**The shade.** When they could not bear the scorching sun, Allah sent them the shade of a thin, white cloud. In the hadith about the trials, An-Nasa'i recorded Ibn ʿAbbas saying that Allah shaded the Children of Israel with clouds during the years of wandering; Ibn Abi Hatim said that narrations similar to Ibn ʿAbbas's were reported from Ibn ʿUmar, Ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas, Abu Mijlaz, Ad-Dahhak and As-Suddi. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said this happened when they were in the desert and the clouds shielded them from the sun. Ibn Jarir said that several scholars said this type of cloud **"was cooler and better than the type we know."**

**Al-Mann.** Ibn ʿAbbas, in the report of ʿAli bin Abi Talhah, said the manna used to descend to them upon the trees, and they used to eat whatever they wished of it. Qatadah describes it as **whiter than milk and sweeter than honey**, raining down on them just as the snow falls, from dawn until sunrise. One of them would collect enough for that particular day, for if it remained more than that it would spoil. On the sixth day, Friday, one would collect enough for the sixth and the seventh day, the Sabbath, during which one would not leave home to seek a livelihood. Ibn Kathir adds that the type of manna we know provides sufficient food when eaten alone, being nutritious and sweet, and that when mixed with water it becomes a sweet drink.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the word itself: Allah produced honeydew in abundance which they could easily gather, and so it is designated **mann**, which signifies *a gift or favour*. The name of the food is the name of the kindness.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites the following as evidence that manna is not restricted to one type. **Al-Bukhari** narrated from Saʿd bin Zayd that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Kamʼah (truffles) is a type of manna, and its liquid is a remedy for the eyes."* Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith was also collected by Imam Ahmad, and by the group of hadith compilers with the exception of Abu Dawud, and that **At-Tirmidhi graded it Hasan Sahih**. At-Tirmidhi also recorded Abu Hurayrah saying that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"The ʿAjwah (pressed, dried date) is from Paradise and it cures poison; al-Kamʼah (truffles) is a form of manna, and its liquid heals the eye."* Ibn Kathir notes that At-Tirmidhi is the only one of them who recorded this second narration.

**As-Salwā.** ʿAli bin Abi Talhah reported that Ibn ʿAbbas said the salwā is a bird that looks like the quail — the same opinion is reported from Mujahid, Ash-Shaʿbi, Ad-Dahhak, Al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah and Ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas. ʿIkrimah said the salwā is a bird in Paradise about the size of a sparrow. Qatadah said it is a bird similar to a sparrow, and reports the same daily rule — an Israelite could catch as many quails as sufficed for that particular day, otherwise the meat would spoil, and on Friday he would collect enough for the sixth and the seventh day, the Sabbath. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pictures it vividly: the quails would not flee but came around them, so that they could catch the birds with little effort.

Note the verb Allah chooses: *anzalnā* — **We sent down**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that because both things were unusual, the Qur'an says Allah made them "descend" for the benefit of the Israelites.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, lists the rest of that provision: when they were thirsty, Allah commanded Musa (peace be upon him) to strike a rock with his staff, and twelve streams gushed forth; when they complained of the thick darkness of the night, Allah produced for them a constant pillar of light; and when their clothes began to wear out, their clothes would neither go dirty nor wear out, while the clothes of the children **grew with their growth**.

## "Eat of the good things"

Allah says *kulū min ṭayyibāti mā razaqnākum*. Ibn Kathir notes what kind of command this is: **a simple order of allowance, guiding to what is good.** That is the whole of his comment on it.

*A reflection of my own:* an allowance is not a weight laid on someone's shoulders. It is a table opened, and a hand pointed toward the best of what is on it.

## "And they did not wrong Us"

The passage closes: *wa mā ẓalamūnā wa lākin kānū anfusahum yaẓlimūn*. Ibn Kathir explains the meaning as: *We commanded them to eat from what We gave them, and to perform the acts of worship* — but they rebelled. He connects it to Allah's words elsewhere, "Eat of the provision of your Lord, and be grateful to Him" (34:15). And he states the outcome plainly: they rebelled, disbelieved and committed injustice against themselves, even though they saw the clear signs, tremendous miracles and extraordinary events.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the concrete instance. Allah had commanded them to take as much of the miraculous food as they really needed and not to store it for future use. When they disobeyed this commandment, **the meat began to rot** — and this is how they harmed, not Allah, but themselves.

*A reflection of my own:* there is a fittingness in that penalty. A person unsure that tomorrow's provision will come reaches for more of today's, and watches it turn in his hands.

Sin never reaches Allah. It only ever circles back.

## A comparison Ibn Kathir insists on

Ibn Kathir pauses here to point out the virtue of the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ over the companions of all other prophets — their firmness in the religion, their patience, and their lack of arrogance, may Allah be pleased with them.

Although they accompanied the Prophet ﷺ in his travels and battles, such as at Tabuk, in intense heat and hardship, **they did not ask for a miracle**, though this was easy for the Prophet ﷺ by Allah's leave. When they became hungry, they merely asked the Prophet ﷺ to invoke Allah for an increase in the amount of food; they collected whatever food they had and brought it to him, he asked Allah to bless it, told each of them to take some, and they filled every pot they had. When they needed rain, the Prophet ﷺ asked Allah to send down rain, and a rain cloud came — they drank, gave water to their camels and filled their water skins, and when they looked around they found the cloud had only rained on their camp. Ibn Kathir calls this the best example of those willing to accept Allah's decision and follow the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Set the two side by side. One community was given clouds, manna and quail, and rebelled. Another asked only for a little more of what they already had, and were given a cloud and its rain.

*A reflection of my own:* the difference between them is not in what came down.

## Living it

- **Beware the moving condition.** The seventy heard the words of Allah with their own ears and immediately raised a new objection. When we tell ourselves *if I just saw one clear sign, I would commit* — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's account is worth sitting with. The condition was met, and another appeared in its place.
- **Do not tie faith to the messenger's likeability.** Their words were "we will never believe *in you*," and their question was "should we believe this statement because you said it?" Truth is not disproved by a dislike of the one who carries it.
- **Witnessing does not lift responsibility.** They died and were raised, and still refused the Book. Al-Qurtubi's position is that no such experience relieves a responsible adult of the commandments.
- **Take today's rizq without hoarding it.** The manna and the quail spoiled when stored beyond the day. The mercy came fresh each dawn.
- **The word for the food was "gift."** *Mann* signifies a gift or favour. Shade they did not build, food they did not plant, clothes that did not wear out — and the reason given in ayah 56 is *laʿallakum tashkurūn*: that you might be grateful. Gratitude is not an afterthought owed once the favour has landed. It is the purpose the favour was sent for.

passages.title: The town, the twelve springs, and craving lesser food
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat gather three of Allah's favours upon the Children of Israel — a town they were told to enter and eat from freely, water brought out of a rock in twelve springs, and the manna and quails provided to them — and record, alongside each favour, how it was met. A command to enter bowed and to ask for pardon was answered with mockery. Water was drawn from a stone, and the same ayah had to warn them not to spread corruption in the land. Food that came, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "without any effort or hardship," was met with *"We cannot endure one kind of food."* Ibn Kathir's own heading over the first episode is blunt: **"The Jews were Rebellious instead of Appreciative when They gained Victory."**

## The setting: a people in the wilderness

Ibn Kathir places this in the aftermath of the coming out of Egypt. When Banu Isra'il came from Egypt with Musa, they were commanded to enter the holy land and to fight the disbelieving 'Amaliq (Canaanites) who dwelt there — and they did not want to fight, because they were weak and exhausted. Allah punished them by causing them to become lost, and to continue wandering. Musa's call is recorded elsewhere in the Qur'an: *"O people! Enter the holy land which Allah has assigned to you and turn not back (in flight)"* (5:21).

What was "the holy land"? Ibn Kathir considers the correct opinion to be Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) — the view of As-Suddi, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas, Qatadah, Abu Muslim al-Asfahani and others. Some scholars said it was Jericho (Ariha'), an opinion mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd.

The wandering ended forty years later. In the company of Yusha' (Joshua) bin Nun, Allah allowed them to conquer the holy land on the eve of a Friday — and Ibn Kathir mentions that on that day the sun was kept from setting for a little more time, until victory was achieved. It is at that moment of triumph that the command of ayah 58 arrives.

**When did this happen?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes two views. Shah 'Abd al-Qadir held that when the Israelites grew weary of eating the same *mann* and *salwa* (manna and quails) every day and prayed for the kind of food they were used to — the request in ayah 61 — they were commanded to go to a certain city where they could get what they wished for; the command in ayah 58 then lays down the etiquette of action and speech for entering that city. The other view is that the command pertains to the city they had been ordered to fight for, entered only after their long wanderings, the command reaching them through Yusha' (peace be upon him), who was the prophet among them at the time.

Maʿārif adds something worth pausing on: the Qur'an does not tell stories for the sake of telling stories, the usual purpose of which is entertainment. The real intention is to draw conclusions and illustrate spiritual principles, and in view of a particular effect sought in a particular context, episodes may be arranged to serve the pattern of meaning intended rather than strict chronology. This is a quite usual literary method — in any piece of writing or speech, it is the intention that governs the ordering of the material. So a question about sequence here should not unsettle the reader.

## "Enter the gate in prostration"

Having been given victory, they were commanded to enter the gate *sujjadan* — in appreciation to Allah for making them victorious and triumphant, returning them to their land, and saving them from being lost and wandering.

The scholars explored what this bodily posture meant in practice:

- **Bowing.** Al-'Awfi said that Ibn 'Abbas said *sujjadan* means "while bowing."
- **A small door.** Ibn Jarir reported Ibn 'Abbas saying it means "through a small door while bowing." Al-Hakim also narrated it; Ibn Abi Hatim added, "And they went through the door backwards!"
- **Face to the ground.** Al-Hasan al-Basri said they were ordered to prostrate on their faces when they entered the city, though Ar-Razi discounted this explanation.
- **Inward submissiveness.** It was also said that the *sujud* mentioned here means submissiveness, since actually entering while prostrating is not possible.

On the gate itself: Khasif said that 'Ikrimah said that Ibn 'Abbas said the door mentioned here was facing the Qiblah — and Ar-Razi likewise reported that some said it was a door in the direction of the Qiblah. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, As-Suddi, Qatadah and Ad-Dahhak said the door is the door of Hittah in Iylya', which is Jerusalem.

Notice the timing of the command. It comes at the height of their strength, at the moment of conquest — and what it asks for is that they come in stooped and small. Ibn Kathir draws the parallel directly to Surat an-Nasr: *"When there comes the help of Allah and the conquest… So glorify the praises of your Lord, and ask His forgiveness. Verily, He is the One Who accepts the repentance"* (110). **Victory is an occasion for istighfar, not for swagger.**

## "Hittah" — the one word

Alongside the posture came a word: *"and say: Hittah."* Ibn 'Abbas commented, "Seek Allah's forgiveness." Al-Hasan and Qatadah said it means, "Say: 'Relieve us from our errors.'" Maʿārif describes the word as one that indicates repentance for one's sin and the request for pardon. Every rendering points the same way: an admission of wrongdoing and a plea that it be lifted. One word, and it holds the whole posture of a servant.

The promise attached is generous: *"We shall forgive you your sins and shall increase (reward) for the good-doers."* Ibn Kathir reads it as: if you implement what We commanded you, We will forgive your sins and multiply your good deeds. In summary, he says, upon achieving victory they were commanded to submit to Allah in tongue and deed, to admit their sins and seek forgiveness for them, to be grateful for the blessings He gave them, hastening to the deeds Allah loves.

Maʿārif notes that the promise of pardon was general — extending to everyone ready to obey the new command, including (on the first of the two views above) their rejection of the mann and salwa, a demand it calls really insolent — while a special reward was promised to those who devoted themselves to good deeds sincerely and wholeheartedly.

**What is ihsan?** Maʿārif points out that "sincerity" and "wholeheartedness" are a very weak English rendering of the quality behind *muhsinun*. *Ihsan* signifies "doing a thing beautifully — that is, in the manner that is proper to it." Beside this lexical meaning, it carries a technical meaning defined in a famous hadith of the Prophet ﷺ: *"Offer your prayers as if you can see Him, and if you do not see Him, He is seeing you (in any case)."*

## What they did instead

As-Suddi reported, from Abu Sa'id Al-Azdy, from Abu Al-Kanud, from 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud, that they were commanded to *"enter the gate in prostration (or bowing with humility)"* — but instead, they entered while their heads were raised in defiance. (Khasif also reported, from 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, that they entered the door sideways.)

And al-Bukhari recorded Abu Hurayrah saying that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "The Children of Israel were commanded to enter the door while bowing and to say 'Hittah'. Yet, they entered the door on their behinds, distorting the words. They said: 'Habbah (seed), in Sha'rah (a hair).'"

Ibn Kathir notes that An-Nasa'i recorded part of this from Abu Hurayrah, with a chain from the Prophet ﷺ, explaining *Hittah* — "So they deviated and said 'Habbah'"; that 'Abdur-Razzaq narrated similarly, his route also collected by al-Bukhari; and that Muslim and At-Tirmidhi narrated similar versions, At-Tirmidhi saying, "Hasan Sahih." Maʿārif gives the mocking substitution as *Habbatun fi sha'irah* (grain in the midst of barley), or *Hintatun* (wheat).

Ibn Kathir's summary of what the scholars have said: they distorted Allah's command to submit to Him in tongue and deed — commanded to enter bowing down, they entered sliding on their rear ends and raising their heads; commanded to say *Hittah*, meaning "Relieve us from our errors and sins," they mocked the command and said "Hintah (grain seed) in Sha'irah (barley)." This, he says, demonstrates the worst type of rebellion and disobedience, and it is why Allah released His anger and punishment upon them.

Ayah 59 is precise about who was struck: *"those who did wrong."* Not everyone — the wrongdoers, "because of their rebellion" (*fisq*).

## "Rijz from the sky"

Ad-Dahhak said that Ibn 'Abbas said, "Every word in Allah's Book that says *Rijz* means 'a punishment.'" Mujahid, Abu Malik, As-Suddi, al-Hasan and Qatadah were reported to have said that *Rijz* means "torment." Maʿārif, citing Qurtubi, says the punishment that descended was plague, which wiped out seventy thousand men.

Ibn Kathir connects the word to the Sunnah. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated that Sa'd bin Malik, Usamah bin Zayd and Khuzaymah bin Thabit said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"The plague is a Rijz, a punishment with which Allah punished those before you."* This is also how An-Nasa'i recorded it, and the basis of the hadith was collected in the Two Sahihs — where we also find: *"If you hear of the plague in a land, then do not enter it."* Ibn Jarir recorded Usamah bin Zayd saying that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"This calamity and sickness is a Rijz, a punishment with which some nations who were before you were punished"* — the basis of this hadith likewise collected in the Two Sahihs. Maʿārif also recalls a report that plague is a punishment for the disobedient and a blessing for the obedient.

## Why changing one word mattered so much

Maʿārif turns ayah 59 into a serious point of law. The Israelites were punished for having changed a word ordained by Allah and substituting a phrase of their own invention, thus distorting the meaning itself. **According to the consensus of the fuqaha', a change in the words of the Holy Qur'an, or of a hadith, or of a divine commandment, which invents or distorts the actual meaning, is impermissible.**

But what about changing wording in such a way that the meaning remains intact? Imam al-Qurtubi's answer, as Maʿārif relays it: in certain texts and certain kinds of speech, the *words themselves* are as much a part of the intention as the meanings — and there, changing the words is not permitted. The adhan must use the words laid down for it. So must the recitations of salah — *Subhanaka Allahumma*, *at-Tahiyyat*, *Qunut*, and the glorifications of Allah in ruku' and sujud — all exactly in the reported words, even if the meaning would not change.

This is why a translation, however accurate, is not the Qur'an. Maʿārif notes the reported merit of reciting the Qur'an — for every letter one recites, the reward of ten good deeds — and then says plainly: read a very accurate translation, or even an Arabic version with the original words replaced without injuring the sense, and the Shari'ah will not accept it as recitation of the Qur'an. It is not the meanings alone that constitute the Qur'an; "Qur'an" is the name of meanings *inherent in the words* Allah revealed to the Prophet ﷺ, so that the two are inseparable.

Where meaning alone is intended, the scholars differed:

- **Reporting by meaning is allowed.** Al-Qurtubi cites Imam Abu Hanifah, Imam Malik and Imam Shafi'i as holding that reporting a hadith by its meaning is quite permissible, provided the one reporting has perfect knowledge of Arabic and is familiar with the situation the hadith pertains to, so that he neither misinterprets the text nor distorts the sense.
- **Only the exact words.** Muhammad ibn Sirin and Qasim ibn Muhammad held that a hadith must be reported exactly in the words in which it was received — some insisting that even a reporter's lexical mistake be passed on as heard, only indicating what the correct word is likely to be. Their evidence includes the Prophet's ﷺ instruction to a man who, in a bedtime supplication, said *Rasul* where the prescribed word was *Nabiyy*: he was told not to make a change, but to say *Nabiyy*. They also cite the supplication, *"May Allah make the man flourish who heard my speech, and then conveyed it exactly as he had heard."*

Most jurists and hadith scholars, however, hold the middle position: it is better to report the exact words without intentional change, but where one cannot recall them, reporting the meaning in one's own words is permitted — and the very words "conveyed it exactly as he had heard" may mean conveying the *meaning* exactly and without alteration. Al-Qurtubi observes that this very hadith has itself come down in different wordings in different versions. As for the *Nabiyy*/*Rasul* case, he offers two explanations: *Nabiyy* carries the sense of sublimity far more than *Rasul*, since the latter is used for any messenger whatsoever while the former is reserved for those specially chosen by Allah to be addressed directly through revelation; and in supplication, the words appointed by Allah or His Messenger ﷺ have a much greater efficacy than any other words. Hence those who prescribe supplications are careful to keep to the authentically reported words without the slightest change.

**Living it:** guard the wording of what you have received. Say the du'a as it was taught. Do not improve on revelation.

## Twelve springs from one rock (ayah 60)

The scene shifts to the wilderness. Parched with thirst, the people requested Musa to pray to Allah for water. Allah commanded him to strike a rock with his staff, and twelve streams gushed forth — one for each of the twelve tribes, *"each (group of) people knew its own place for water."*

Ibn Kathir renders the favour in Allah's own voice: remember My favour when I answered the supplication of your Prophet Musa and made water gush out for you through a stone, a designated spring for each of your tribes; you eat from the manna and the quails and drink from the water I provided, without any effort or hardship — so worship the One Who did this for you.

Ibn 'Abbas described a square stone that Musa was commanded to strike with his staff; twelve springs burst out of it, three on each side. Each tribe was designated a certain spring and used to drink from it. **And the provision travelled with them:** "They never had to travel from their area, they would find the same bounty in the same manner they had in the first area." Ibn Kathir notes this narration is part of the long hadith about the trials recorded by An-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim.

Why twelve? Maʿārif explains: Ya'qub (peace be upon him) had twelve sons, each with a large family of his own; the families were considered tribes, each with its own administrative organisation and its own head. Hence the number twelve — and hence a spring apportioned to each.

Ibn Kathir compares this with the parallel in Surat al-A'raf, revealed in Makkah, where Allah used the third person in mentioning the Children of Israel, while here in al-Baqarah, revealed in Madinah, He directed His speech at them. He also observes a difference of wording: 7:160 describes what first occurred as the water begins to gush out, while the Ayah in al-Baqarah describes what happened later on, when the water burst out in full force. And Allah knows best.

**On miracles.** Maʿārif quotes al-Qadi al-Baydawi: it is a great error — even a great error in logic — to deny miracles. When Allah has given a certain stone the unusual property of drawing iron to itself, it cannot be logically or rationally impossible that He should give another stone the property of absorbing water from the earth and releasing it again. And even that explanation is meant for those who take a superficial view of things; it is in no way impossible that Allah should produce water within the stone itself. Those who call it impossible, Baydawi says, do not actually understand the technical meaning of the term "impossible."

**Praying for rain.** Maʿārif draws a fiqh point from the ayah: Musa (peace be upon him) simply prayed for water, and Allah made a miraculous provision — which shows that the essential thing in beseeching Allah for rain is the prayer itself. In the Shari'ah of Musa a mere prayer was considered sufficient, and according to Imam Abu Hanifah this principle holds good for the Islamic Shari'ah too. The Prophet ﷺ acted differently on different occasions: an authentic hadith reports that he once went out to the open prayer-ground, offered formal prayers, delivered a khutbah, and then prayed to Allah for rain; and al-Bukhari and Muslim record from Anas that he once prayed for rain while delivering the Friday khutbah, and Allah sent down rain. Whatever form the prayer takes, Maʿārif adds, all the scholars agree it cannot be effective unless accompanied by repentance for one's sins, confession of one's powerlessness, a sincere expression of humility, and an affirmation of servitude to Allah. So long as one persists in sin and transgression, one has no right to hope for an answer — though if Allah in His mercy grants it anyway, that is His will, and He is All-Powerful.

The ayah closes with a warning: *"and do not act corruptly, making mischief on the earth"* — which Ibn Kathir reads as, "Do not return the favour by committing acts of disobedience that cause favours to disappear." Maʿārif glosses the "disorder" here as disobedience to Allah and transgression of His commandments.

## "We cannot endure one kind of food" (ayah 61)

Now the ingratitude becomes explicit. The mann and salwa were, as Ibn Kathir describes them, a good, pure, beneficial, easily acquired food — and they asked Musa to exchange this for an inferior type consisting of vegetation and so forth: herbs, cucumbers, *fum*, lentils and onions. Al-Hasan al-Basri said of them: "They were bored and impatient with the type of food they were provided. They also remembered the life they used to live, when their diet consisted of lentils, onions, garlic and herbs."

**"One kind of food"** means the manna and quails, because they ate the same food day after day.

**What is *fum*?** The other items are known types of food; this one the scholars discussed. Ibn Mas'ud read it *Thum* — garlic. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan that Ibn 'Abbas said *fum* means garlic. It was also said that the expression *fumu lana* meant "bake for us" in the languages of old; Ibn Jarir commented that if this is true, then *fum* is one of the words whose pronunciation was altered, the letter *fa'* replacing *tha'*, since the two are similar in sound. And Allah knows best. Others said *fum* is wheat, the kind used for bread. Al-Bukhari said, "Some of them said that Fum includes all grains or seeds that are eaten."

Musa's reply is one of the great questions of the Qur'an: *"Would you exchange that which is better for that which is lower?"* Ibn Kathir reads it as a criticism: they asked for inferior foods although they were living an easy life, eating tasty, beneficial and pure food.

**"Go down to any Misr."** Ibn 'Abbas said *misr* here means "any city." Ibn Jarir also reported that Abu al-'Aliyah and Ar-Rabi' bin Anas said the Ayah refers to Misr, the Egypt of Fir'awn — but Ibn Kathir concludes the truth is that it means any city, as Ibn 'Abbas and other scholars stated. The sense then becomes: what you are asking for is easy, available in abundance in any city you might enter; so I will not ask Allah to provide us with it, especially when it is an inferior type of food. Since their request was the result of boredom and arrogance, and since fulfilling it was unnecessary, their request was denied. Allah knows best. Maʿārif's rendering is that they were commanded through Musa (peace be upon him) to go to a certain town lying somewhere in the wilderness, to till the land there, and to grow whatever they liked to eat.

**This is the passage's sharpest mirror.** Their fault was not wanting vegetables. Ibn Kathir names the diagnosis plainly: boredom and arrogance. Al-Hasan al-Basri fills it in: bored and impatient with what they were given, and looking backwards to the diet of the life they used to live. To be given "a good, pure, beneficial, easily acquired food" every day and find it unbearable *because* it came every day — that is the ingratitude the ayah is exposing. Maʿārif's word for it is that they were being ungrateful and impertinent.

## Humiliation, wrath, and their causes

The ayah ends heavily: *"And they were covered with humiliation and misery, and they drew on themselves the wrath of Allah."*

Ibn Kathir reads the humiliation as enduring — it will never cease, and they will continue to suffer it at the hands of those who interact with them, along with the disgrace they feel inwardly. Al-Hasan commented, "Allah humiliated them, and they shall have no protector." Abu al-'Aliyah, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas and As-Suddi said "misery" here means poverty; 'Atiyah al-'Awfi said it means paying the tilth. On *"they drew on themselves the wrath of Allah,"* Ad-Dahhak said, "They deserved Allah's anger," and Ibn Jarir explained the verb as "They went back with the wrath" — comparing the same construction in 5:29, *"Verily, I intend to let you draw my sin on yourself as well as yours"* — so: they went back carrying Allah's anger, having earned it.

Maʿārif adds that verse 3:112 helps elucidate this one: *"And disgrace has been stamped over them wherever they are found, unless (saved) through a rope from Allah and through a rope from men."* The "rope from Allah" refers to those whom Allah Himself has, by His own commandment, saved from this disgrace — for example children, women, and those totally devoted to prayer and worship who never go to war against Muslims. The "rope from men" refers to a treaty of peace, or permission to live under protection among others.

Crucially, the Qur'an gives the reasons rather than leaving it as blank condemnation: *"That was because they used to disbelieve in the Ayat of Allah and killed the Prophets wrongfully. That was because they disobeyed and used to transgress the bounds."* Ibn Kathir: Allah's anger that descended on them was part of the humiliation they earned, because of their defiance of the truth, disbelief in Allah's Ayat, and belittling of the carriers of Allah's law — the Prophets and their followers. They rejected the Messengers and even killed them; and surely there is no form of disbelief worse than disbelieving in Allah's Ayat and murdering the Prophets of Allah. He distinguishes the last two terms: **disobedience** is to do what is prohibited; **transgression** is overstepping the set limits of what is allowed and what is prohibited. Allah knows best.

Two hadith are cited here. In a hadith recorded in the Two Sahihs, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Kibr is refusing the truth and degrading people"* — precisely the two things this passage has been narrating. And Imam Ahmad recorded 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud saying that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that the people who will receive the most torment on the Day of Resurrection are a man who was killed by a Prophet or who killed a Prophet, an unjust ruler, and one who mutilates the dead.

## Carrying it

The passage is placed in front of a Muslim audience for a reason. Read as a mirror, it asks four concrete things:

1. **Enter your victories bowed.** Ibn Kathir's link to Surat an-Nasr makes this explicit: when the help of Allah and the conquest come, the response is praise and istighfar.
2. **Say "Hittah" and mean it.** Admit the sin in plain words — "Relieve us from our errors" — instead of managing it with clever ones.
3. **Do not edit what was revealed.** The adhan, the recitations of salah, the transmitted du'as — keep the words. They turned an ordained word of repentance into mockery, and the punishment followed.
4. **Do not trade down.** Boredom and impatience with a gift are not grounds to ask for something lesser. Ask instead for *ihsan* — to do what is in front of you beautifully, praying as though you see Him, knowing that He sees you in any case.

passages.title: Faith and righteous deeds are what count
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

Ayah 62 is a single verse, but it carries a whole doctrine. Allah names four groups — the believers, the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabians — and then, instead of assigning each a verdict, opens a single door for all of them: *"whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous good deeds shall have their reward with their Lord, on them shall be no fear, nor shall they grieve."* What saves a person is not the label of a community but **faith in Allah and the Last Day, joined to righteous deeds**.

Before turning to the commentaries, notice the shape of the sentence itself: the list of communities comes first, the condition comes last, and the condition is laid on all of them alike.

## Where it sits in the surah

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** makes the connection explicit. The previous verse spoke of how the Israelites drew upon themselves the wrath of Allah through their habitual insolence and disobedience. That account, it notes, may lead the listeners — or the Jews themselves — to suppose that in view of such transgression, their *Taubah* (repentance), even if they agreed to offer it, would no longer be acceptable to Allah. The present verse exists to dispel exactly that misgiving. It lays down a general principle: **no matter how a man has been behaving earlier, so long as he submits himself fully to the commandments of Allah — in his beliefs and in his deeds both — he is acceptable to Allah and will get his reward.**

**Ibn Kathir** reads the placement the same way. After Allah described the condition and the punishment of those who defy His commands, fall into His prohibitions, and transgress the limits He set, He stated that the earlier nations who were righteous and obedient received the rewards for their good deeds — and that this shall be the case until the Day of Judgment. The rebuke of the preceding verse was never a closing of the file. It was a warning issued alongside an open invitation.

## "Whoever" — the pivot of the verse

Notice what the verse does *not* do. It does not say "the believers will be rewarded, and the others will not." It gathers four communities into one sentence and then hangs the promise on a single relative pronoun: *whoever*. Reward attaches to a quality, not to a name.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the force of this with a striking comparison. It is as if a king should say that his laws are impartially applicable to all his subjects, and that whoever obeys them shall receive his reward for obedience — *irrespective of whether he has earlier been a friend or a foe*. Obviously the friend has always been loyal and obedient; the warning and the promise are really addressed to the foe. But the suggestion contained in such a formulation is this: **the favours of the king do not proceed from any personal attachment to his friends, but depend on the quality of obedience and loyalty.** And hence the foes too will become worthy of his favours if they acquire the necessary quality.

This, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is the reason the Muslims are mentioned at all. One might reasonably ask why the verse mentions the Muslims — for if it is an invitation to Islam, there is no need to extend an invitation to those who have already accepted it. But keeping in mind the richly concentrated style of the Holy Qur'an, and looking beyond the literal sense of the words into the implications the verse carries, the inclusion of the Muslims adds a new dimension to the meaning. And it should never be taken to imply that salvation can be attained without accepting Islam.

## What the verse does not mean

Both commentaries in this bundle are emphatic on this point, and it needs stating plainly because the verse is often read in the opposite direction.

**Ibn Kathir** transmits that ʿAli bin Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, about this verse, that Allah revealed the following ayah afterwards:

> *"And whoever seeks religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted of him, and in the Hereafter he will be one of the losers."* (3:85)

Ibn Kathir explains what Ibn ʿAbbas's statement indicates: **Allah does not accept any deed or work from anyone unless it conforms to the Law of Muhammad ﷺ — that is, after Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ.** Before that, every person who followed the guidance of his own Prophet was on the correct path, following the correct guidance, and was saved.

Putting those two halves together — this is a summary of Ibn Kathir's logic rather than a sentence of his own — the picture is not of several parallel roads that all arrive, but of one road across time. Before the final Messenger, whoever followed the guidance of the Prophet sent to him was saved; after him, no deed is accepted unless it conforms to his Law. That is why Ibn Kathir states the verse's upshot as: *whoever follows the unlettered Messenger and Prophet ﷺ shall acquire eternal happiness.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same thing more directly, and warns against reading the verse as opening the way to salvation for every "man of good will" irrespective of the creed he follows. Read in its proper context and along with other relevant verses of the Holy Qur'an, the verse in fact **promises salvation in the other world only to those who accept Islam**. Its tone is not one of indifference but of welcome: it is an *invitation* to Islam extended to the Jews, the Christians, the Sabeans — and, as a matter of fact, to the followers of all possible religions, and even to non-believers. The specific names, Maʿārif notes, serve only as examples. And the invitation carries a generous guarantee: once a man has accepted Islam, all his former transgressions, whether in the matter of beliefs or in that of deeds, will be forgiven, and he will become worthy of receiving the rewards of the other world.

## Why only two articles of faith?

A careful reader will notice that the verse names just two items of creed — faith in Allah and faith in the Day of Judgment — and may conclude that these two alone suffice for salvation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses this head-on: the Holy Qur'an repeatedly declares that he who does not believe in the prophets, in the angels, and in the Books of Allah is not a Muslim.

**Faith in Allah is the first article in the Islamic creed; faith in the Day of Judgment is the last.** By mentioning only these two, the verse intends to say, in a succinct manner, that it is necessary to have faith in all the articles of the creed, from the first to the last.

There is also a logical dependency, and it is worth sitting with. It is through the prophets and the Books of Allah alone that a man can acquire any knowledge of the essence and the attributes of Allah, or of what is to happen on the Day of Judgment — and the Books of Allah are revealed to the prophets through an angel. So **it is not possible to have faith in Allah and the Day of Judgment until and unless one has faith in the angels, in the Books of Allah, and in the prophets.** The two named articles are the two ends of a chain; you cannot hold both ends without holding what lies between.

## The names of the communities

Ibn Kathir pauses on each name, and the etymologies are quietly illuminating.

**Yahud (the Jews)** — the followers of Prophet Musa, who used to refer to the Tawrah for judgment. Ibn Kathir explains that *Yahud* is a word meaning **"repenting,"** just as Musa said, *"Certainly we have* Hudna *to You"* — meaning, *we repent to You*. This indicates that they were called Yahud because they repented and because they were kind to each other. It was also said that they were called Yahud in reference to **Yahuda (Judah)**, the eldest son of Prophet Yaʿqub. Abu ʿAmr bin al-ʿAlaʾ said they were called Yahud because **they swayed when they read the Tawrah**.

**Nasara (the Christians)** — when ʿIsa was sent, the Children of Israel were required to follow and obey him. The followers of ʿIsa and his companions are called *An-Nasara* because **they gave aid and support to each other**. They are also called *Ansar* (helpers), as ʿIsa said, *"Who will be my helpers in Allah's cause?"* and al-Hawariyyun said, *"We are the helpers of Allah"* (61:14). It was also said that they were called Nasara because they inhabited a land called **An-Nasirah (Nazareth)**, as Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn ʿAbbas were reported to have said; *Allah knows best*. *Nasara* is certainly the plural of *Nasran*.

**Muʾminun (the believers)** — when Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ as the Last and Final Prophet and Messenger to all of the Children of Adam, mankind was required to believe in him, obey him, and refrain from what he prohibited them; those who do this are true believers. Ibn Kathir notes that the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ was called *Muʾminin* **because of the depth of their faith and certainty, and because they believe in all of the previous Prophets and matters of the Unseen.** It is a name earned by breadth of belief, not narrowness.

## The Sabians

Here the scholars genuinely differed, and Ibn Kathir reports the disagreement rather than resolving it by force.

- Sufyan ath-Thawri said that Layth bin Abu Sulaym said that **Mujahid** said: *"The Sabians are between the Majus, the Jews and the Christians. They do not have a specific religion."* Similar is reported from Ibn Abi Najih, and similar statements were attributed to **ʿAtaʾ** and **Saʿid bin Jubayr**.
- Others say the Sabians are a sect among the People of the Book who used to read the **Zabur (Psalms)**.
- Others say they are a people who **worshipped the angels or the stars**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that nothing is definitely known as to the beliefs and practices of the Sabeans and that different opinions have been expressed, adding that most probably they used to worship the stars.

Ibn Kathir's own judgement — *and Allah knows best* — is that the closest opinion to the truth is Mujahid's statement, and that of those who agree with him like Wahb bin Munabbih: **the Sabians are neither Jews nor Christians nor Majus nor polytheists.** Rather, they did not have a specific religion that they followed and enforced, because they remained living according to their **Fitrah** — the instinctual, original nature Allah placed in every human being. Ibn Kathir offers a telling piece of evidence: this is why the idolators used to call whoever embraced Islam a *Sabiʾ*, meaning that he had **abandoned all religions that existed on the earth**. Some scholars stated that the Sabians are those who never received a message by any Prophet. *And Allah knows best.*

## "No fear, nor shall they grieve"

The closing promise deserves to be felt, not skimmed. Ibn Kathir unpacks it with precision: such a person **shall neither fear what will happen in the future nor become sad for what has been lost in the past**. Fear looks forward; sorrow looks back. Between them they cover the whole span of a human being's anxiety — and the verse cancels both.

Ibn Kathir places this alongside two other passages. Allah says:

> *"No doubt! Verily, the Awliyaʾ of Allah, no fear shall come upon them nor shall they grieve."* (10:62)

The word left in Arabic there, *Awliyaʾ*, is the plural of *wali* — one who is close to Allah, His ally and friend.

And Ibn Kathir notes that the angels will proclaim the same words to the dying believers, at the very moment they are needed most:

> *"Verily, those who say: 'Our Lord is Allah (alone),' and then they stand firm, on them the angels will descend (at the time of their death) (saying): 'Fear not, nor grieve! But receive the glad tidings of Paradise which you have been promised!'"* (41:30)

Note the shape of that verse: a statement of faith — *our Lord is Allah* — **and then they stand firm**. Belief, then steadfastness. It is the same pairing ayah 62 makes when it joins faith in Allah and the Last Day to *righteous good deeds*.

## Living it

Three things this passage asks of a reader.

**First, do not rest on a label.** The verse lists four communities and then makes every one of them wait on the same condition. Belonging to the right group is not the currency; belief and deeds are. Maʿārif's king does not reward friendship — he rewards obedience.

**Second, never assume the door has closed.** The verse was revealed precisely to dispel the fear that a record of transgression makes repentance pointless. No matter how a man has been behaving earlier, full submission to Allah's commandments — in beliefs and in deeds both — is accepted and rewarded.

**Third, hold the whole creed and let it show in action.** Faith in Allah and faith in the Day of Judgment are the first and last links; the prophets, the Books, and the angels lie between and cannot be dropped. And the verse never lets faith stand alone — it is *believes* **and** *does righteous good deeds*. The reward is *"with their Lord."* Not paid out here, not measured by anyone else, but held with Him.

passages.title: The covenant under the mountain and the Sabbath-breakers
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These four ayat set two scenes from Israelite history side by side: a covenant sworn under a mountain suspended over their heads (63–64), and a coastal town that lost its humanity for cheating its way around a divine command (65–66). What holds them together is a single argument. In ayah 63 a solemn pledge is taken; in ayah 64 it is broken, and yet no destruction falls — only Allah's grace holds it back. Then ayah 65 shows what happens when that grace is *not* extended: another group of transgressors, and sudden, dreadful punishment. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, "In order to emphasize what the present verse has said, the next verse tells the story of another group of earlier transgressors and of the dreadful punishment which overtook them all of a sudden."

So the passage is a reminder addressed to the Children of Israel — and through them to anyone who has taken on a covenant with Allah: *you know exactly what you promised, you know exactly what happened to those who played games with what they promised, and you are still here only because Allah is merciful.*

## The mountain over their heads: what actually happened

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān tells the story that sits behind ayah 63. Sayyidnā Mūsā (peace be upon him) came down from Mount Ṭūr with the Torah and recited it to the Israelites. The commandments in it were rigorous — and, Maʿārif notes, "their conduct and habits of mind really called for such strict discipline."

Their first response was to demand verification: they would not obey until Allah Himself told them the Book was His. Seventy men were selected to go to Mount Ṭūr and hear Allah attest to the Torah's authenticity. They came back and bore witness that it was indeed a Book of Allah — but they added something of their own to what Allah had actually said. They told the people that Allah had allowed them to act on the injunctions only as much as they could, and had promised to forgive them for what they could not accomplish.

That fabricated concession became a pretext. The people, already inclined to rebellion, now flatly refused: it was beyond their endurance, they said, to act on such harsh regulations. And in response, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, "Allah commanded the angels to raise Mount Ṭūr and let it hang in the air above their heads as a threat that if they did not fulfill their covenant with Allah, it would fall on them and crush them. The Israelites, then, had no choice but to submit."

Ibn Kathir brings the parallel ayah that fills in the sensation of the moment — Sūrat al-Aʿrāf 7:171: *"And when We raised the mountain over them as if it had been a canopy, and they thought that it was going to fall on them."* A canopy. Not a distant peak — a roof of rock, and the thought in every heart that it was coming down. Ibn Kathir also records that in the hadith about the trials, Ibn ʿAbbās said: "When they refused to obey, Allah raised the mountain above their heads so that they would listen."

**Why "aṭ-Ṭūr" and not simply "the mountain"?** Ibn Kathir reports that the mount here is aṭ-Ṭūr, just as it was explained in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf, and this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas and others; Ibn Kathir calls this "more obvious." He also preserves a second report from Ibn ʿAbbās about the word itself: "The Ṭūr is a type of mountain that vegetation grows on; if no vegetation grows on it, it is not called Ṭūr." So the name itself carries the sense of a mountain that bears growth — and it is the same Mount Ṭūr from which, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates, Mūsā (peace be upon him) had brought the Torah down, and to which the seventy had gone to hear Allah attest to it.

## "Hold fast to what We have given you"

The command in ayah 63 is *khudhū mā ātaynākum bi-quwwah* — "hold fast to that which We have given you."

Ibn Kathir gathers the early explanations. Al-Ḥasan said that "that which We have given you" means the Torah. Mujāhid said the ayah commanded: "Strictly adhere to it." And on *wa-dhkurū mā fīh* — "and remember that which is therein" — Abū al-ʿĀliyah and ar-Rabīʿ said it means: "Read the Torah and implement it."

Notice the two-part shape of the command. *Take it with strength* — grip, resolve, seriousness, not a casual holding. And *remember what is in it* — which these early authorities did not read as mental recall alone but as recitation followed by implementation. Remembering, in this idiom, is doing. The stated purpose seals it: *laʿallakum tattaqūn* — so that you may acquire taqwā, the God-consciousness that makes a person careful about the limits Allah has set. Ibn Kathir's rendering of the parallel phrase in 7:171 is "so that you may fear Allah and obey Him." The mountain was raised, in Ibn Kathir's words, so that they would affirm the pledge they gave Allah "and abide by it with sincerity and seriousness" — and that is exactly the quality the passage will show them abandoning.

## Was this force in religion?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the objection directly: the Qur'an says elsewhere that force should not be used to make a man change his religion, yet here force appears to be used.

The answer given is that no one was being forced to change religion. These people had *already* accepted Sayyidnā Mūsā (peace be upon him) as a prophet of Allah, and had willingly made a covenant with Allah that they would act upon the Book of Allah if one was given to them. Having sworn that and then refused, "they now stand as rebels, and are being threatened with dire punishment for persisting in their rebellion."

Maʿārif draws the analogy: this is exactly how even a secular state deals with rebels, adopting towards them an attitude quite different from that towards aliens or enemies, leaving the rebel only two ways open — to submit, or to lose his life. "That is why it is only an apostate (Murtadd) who is, according to the Islamic Sharīʿah, condemned to capital punishment, and not an outright disbeliever." And the Israelites, Maʿārif adds, were being threatened as criminals and offenders against a law which they themselves acknowledged to be the divine law, but which they refused to obey.

## Ayah 64: "Then you turned away"

*Thumma tawallaytum min baʿdi dhālik.* Ibn Kathir renders the sense plainly: "Yet, after the firm pledge that you gave, you still deviated and broke your pledge."

The pledge was made under a suspended mountain. The terror could not have been more vivid — and still it did not hold.

**"Had it not been for the grace and mercy of Allah upon you."** Ibn Kathir explains this as Allah "forgiving you and by sending the Prophets and Messengers to you" — and *lakuntum mina'l-khāsirīn*, "indeed you would have been among the losers," he glosses as loss "in this life and the Hereafter due to their breach of the covenant."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the mercy in two directions. The sin was so grave that one could have expected utter destruction and ruin to descend on them; Allah in His mercy spared them so far as physical life is concerned, though they will have to pay for their treason in the other world. And Allah's mercy, Maʿārif explains, is of two kinds: one general, extending to believers and disbelievers alike, seen in the shape of worldly well-being and prosperity; the other special, pertaining to believers alone, manifesting particularly in the other world in the shape of salvation and closeness to Allah.

Maʿārif also observes that the last phrase of this ayah appears to be addressed to the Jews who were the contemporaries of the Prophet ﷺ. Since having faith in him is also part of the Covenant, they too are included among those guilty of infringement — and Allah asks them to realise that it is by His mercy alone that He has not, in spite of their treason, sent down on them the kind of catastrophic worldly punishment that used to descend on those who went before.

Maʿārif adds a further point: since a number of authentic ahadith declare that it is by the barakah of the Prophet ﷺ that catastrophic punishments no longer descend on any people, some commentators have identified this particular grace and mercy of Allah with the sending down of Muhammad ﷺ as a Prophet and Messenger of Allah.

## Ayah 65: the town that fished on the Sabbath

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places this episode in the time of Sayyidnā Dāwūd (peace be upon him). Allah had appointed Saturday as the *Sabt* — the sacred day for the Israelites, specially set apart for prayers and worship — and fishing was therefore prohibited on it. But these people lived on the seashore, and were very fond of fish.

Ibn Kathir describes the mechanics of the evasion: they placed nets, ropes and artificial pools of water for the purpose of fishing before the Sabbath. When the fish came in abundance on Saturday as usual, they were caught in the ropes and nets for the rest of Saturday; during the night, once the Sabbath had ended, the fish were collected. Maʿārif gives another version of the same device: on Saturday they would tie one end of a cord to the tail of a fish and the other end to something on the shore, leaving the fish in the water, and on Sunday they would take it out and eat it.

Ibn Kathir's verdict on this is the heart of the passage: "Their evil deeds and deceit appeared lawful on the surface, but they were in reality wicked." The letter of the law was technically untouched; its purpose was destroyed. And Allah had made this precisely the test — Ibn Kathir cites 7:163, where the fish came to them openly on the Sabbath day and did not come on the day they had no Sabbath: *"Thus We made a trial of them, for they used to rebel."* The temptation was engineered. It was the exam, not an accident.

Maʿārif, citing al-Qurṭubī, adds that the Israelites at first invented all sorts of clever pretences for catching fish on Saturday and gradually started doing so openly — and that the town divided over it. Some scholars and pious men tried to dissuade the transgressors; when they paid no heed, these others broke away altogether and began to live in a separate part of the town. One day they felt that no sound was coming from the other part. Growing curious, they went there and found that all the transgressors had been changed into apes.

## What the transformation was

Ibn Kathir notes that Allah changed them from humans into monkeys — "the animals having the form closest to humans" — and that "this is why their punishment was compatible with their crime." Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that Allah changed their bodies into those of monkeys and swine: the young people turned into monkeys while the old people turned into swine. Shaybān an-Naḥwī reported that Qatādah commented on this ayah: "These people were turned into howling monkeys with tails, after being men and women." Maʿārif likewise reports from Qatādah that the young ones had become apes and the old ones swine, and adds the detail that the apes could recognise their relatives and friends, and would approach them weeping out of remorse, seeking their sympathy and help. Then all of them died after three days.

**Did they leave descendants?** Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said those who violated the sanctity of the Sabbath were turned into monkeys, then perished without offspring. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said that Ibn ʿAbbās said: they only lived on the earth for three days, "for no transformed person ever lives more than three days"; they did not eat, drink or have offspring. And Ibn ʿAbbās added the essential creedal frame: "He does what He wills, with whom He wills and He changes the shape of whomever He wills" — while, on the other hand, Allah created the monkeys, swine and the rest of the creation in the six days that He mentioned in His Book.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports a hadith on this from Imam Muslim, narrated from the blessed Companion ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him): some people asked the Prophet ﷺ whether the apes and the swine were the descendants of those who had been transformed. He reminded them that apes and swine existed in the world even before, and said that when Allah sends down this particular kind of punishment on a people, the race comes to an end with this, and there is no further breeding.

Maʿārif also rejects the reading that treats the transformation as merely psychological — a change of character rather than of body. To say such a thing, it argues, is to deny an explicit statement of the Qur'an, and it also denies the power of Allah by putting limitations on it. And it is flimsy even as literary exegesis: even before the punishment fell on them, these people had been displaying the moral and psychological traits of beasts — "the greed of swine and the craftiness of apes." Where, then, is the change that the Qur'an declares to be a punishment for the offenders and a warning for others?

## Ayah 66: made into an example

*Fa-jaʿalnāhā nakālan.* Ibn Kathir explains *nakāl* as an exemplary punishment — Allah made the people of this village an example by the way they were punished, just as He said of Pharaoh in 79:25: *"So Allah seized him with punishing example for his last and first transgression."*

On *li-mā bayna yadayhā wa-mā khalfahā* — "for those in front of it and those behind it" — Ibn Kathir explains it as meaning the other villages, and reports Ibn ʿAbbās: "We made this village an example for the villages around it by the manner in which We punished its people." He compares 46:27, on towns destroyed round about. Ibn Kathir then draws both dimensions together: Allah made them an example for those who lived during their time as well as a reminder for those to come, "by preserving their story."
