And *mawʿiẓatan lil-muttaqīn* — "and a lesson for al-muttaqīn, the pious" — Ibn Kathir explains simply as a reminder, and spells out what it should produce: the torment came as a result of indulging in Allah's prohibitions and of their deceit, "hence, those who have Taqwa should be aware of their evil behavior, so that what occurred to this village does not befall them as well."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distinguishes the two audiences among those who witnessed the event or heard of it. For the disobedient it served as a deterrent, an example and a warning, which persuaded them to repent of their disobedience. For the obedient it was a lesson and a reminder that they should be steadfast in their obedience. "It serves these two purposes even now."

## Living it: the lowest kinds of deceit

Ibn Kathir closes with a report from Imam Abū ʿAbdullāh bin Baṭṭah, that Abū Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Do not commit what the Jews committed, breaching what Allah has forbidden, by resorting to the lowest types of deceit."* Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith has a good (jayyid) chain of narration, and adds, "Allah knows best."

That is the passage aimed straight at us. The Sabbath-breakers did not stand up and declare Allah's law abolished. They kept the form and gutted the substance — the fish was caught on the Sabbath, but nobody *lifted* it on the Sabbath. Their sin was self-deception dressed as compliance.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful, though, to stop a wrong conclusion. It distinguishes *ḥīlah* in its literal Arabic sense — "a trick, a stratagem" — from *ḥīlah* as a technical term in fiqh (Islamic jurisprudence), where it signifies a device for giving legitimacy to an action in a contingency by making the necessary modifications to bring it into consonance with the Sharīʿah. That, Maʿārif says, "is not a way of by-passing the Shariʿah, but of helping people to conform to it even in a situation where necessity or human weakness would compel them to go against it." The Sabbath-breakers' tricks were the opposite: they "necessarily involved the negation of the divine commandment," and were in fact a mockery of it — which is why the punishment was so severe.

Maʿārif gives an example of the legitimate kind, one it says was suggested by the Prophet ﷺ himself. Bartering a kilo of good dates for two kilos of bad dates is, according to the Sharīʿah, a kind of usury (ribā). Where such a transaction becomes necessary, the lawful route is to use the exchange value of money instead of bartering one commodity for another: first sell the two kilos of bad dates for money, and then with that money buy the kilo of good dates. Here nothing in the Sharīʿah is negated; the intention is to conform to it, not to by-pass it.

The line between the two runs through the intention. One device exists so that a person can actually obey; the other exists so that a person can disobey while appearing to obey. The test the passage leaves us with is not whether an arrangement can be defended on paper, but whether we would be content for Allah — who sees the cord tied to the fish's tail — to judge it exactly as it is.

passages.title: The cow: evasive questions and the murder revealed
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

A man among the Children of Israel is murdered, the community falls into mutual accusation, and Allah commands them — through Musa (peace be upon him) — to slaughter a cow. Instead of obeying, they interrogate the command question by question until the description narrows to a single animal; and when they finally obey, a piece of that cow is struck against the corpse, the dead man rises, names his killer, and dies again.

What holds ayat 67–73 together is not really the cow. It is a single unified demonstration: Allah exposes what people bury — a hidden crime, and a hidden disposition to disobey — and He does it by an act that is itself the proof of the Resurrection.

## The story behind the command

The Qur'an does not narrate the murder until ayah 72, but the commentators supply the background at ayah 67 so the command makes sense.

Ibn Kathir records, from Ibn Abi Hatim, the account of ʿUbaydah as-Salmani: there was a man among the Children of Israel who was impotent. He had substantial wealth, and only a nephew who stood to inherit from him. The nephew killed him, moved the body at night, and left it at the doorstep of a certain man. In the morning the nephew was the first to cry out for revenge. The people took up their weapons and very nearly fought each other. Then the wise men among them said: *"Why would you kill each other, while the Messenger of Allah is still among you?"* So they went to Musa, and Musa said what ayah 67 records — that Allah commands them to slaughter a cow.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān mentions a different report of the backstory, citing Mirqat (a commentary on Mishkat): a man wanted to marry a girl, her father refused, and the enraged suitor killed the father and disappeared. Maʿārif also notes, from Maʿālim al-Tanzīl on the authority of Kalbi, that Allah had not yet revealed any injunction concerning man-slaughter — which, if so, would place the incident before the Torah was revealed. The reports differ on the details; what they agree on is the shape of the crime: a killing, and then a cover-up that dragged innocent people toward bloodshed.

Hold on to that opening image. A whole nation with weapons drawn over a killing none of them committed — and the killer standing among them, shouting loudest for justice.

## "Do you make fun of us?"

Their first response to a prophet's command (ayah 67) is not *how* or *when* but an accusation of mockery. To them, "slaughter a cow" sounded absurdly unconnected to "find the murderer." They could not see the link, so they assumed there was none.

Musa's reply is not an argument. It is a refuge: *"I seek Allah's refuge from being among al-jāhilīn"* — the ignorant, or the foolish. Ibn Kathir's rendering carries both senses. A prophet does not toy with revelation; making sport of Allah's command is exactly what an ignorant man does, and Musa distances himself from it entirely. Notice, too, that he does not soften the command or explain the wisdom behind it. He simply repeats it.

## How the command tightened around them

This is the heart of ayat 68–71, and it is the passage's central lesson.

Ibn Kathir states it plainly: **had they slaughtered a cow — any cow — it would have been sufficient for them.** He reports this from Ibn ʿAbbas and from ʿUbaydah. The command in ayah 67 is unrestricted: *a cow*. No age, no colour, no working history. Any animal in any field in Israel would have discharged it.

But they did not obey; they questioned. And Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion: *they made the matter difficult, and this is why Allah made it even more difficult for them.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that a teaching of the Prophet ﷺ conveys the same point — that had they obeyed without raising so many doubts and unnecessary questions, no such strict conditions would have been imposed, and the sacrifice of any cow whatsoever would have been accepted. (Maʿārif reports this as hadith without naming the collection, so we take the teaching without attributing it to a named book.)

Watch the noose close, question by question:

**First question (ayah 68) — what kind?** The answer: *lā fāriḍ wa lā bikr* — neither too old nor too young. Ibn Kathir explains this as neither aged out nor below the age of breeding, and lists a striking consensus for it: Abu al-ʿAliyah, as-Suddi, Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, ʿAtiyah al-ʿAwfi, ʿAta' al-Khurasani, Wahb bin Munabbih, ad-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn ʿAbbas. The word *ʿawān* — "between the two" — is glossed by Ibn ʿAbbas, in a report transmitted by ad-Dahhak, as the age when the cow is strongest and fittest. Musa closes with *"so do what you are commanded"*: the door is still open, obey now.

**Second question (ayah 69) — what colour?** The answer: yellow, *fāqiʿ lawnuhā*, brilliant in its colour, *pleasing the beholders*. Al-ʿAwfi reports from Ibn ʿAbbas that this means a deep yellowish white. As-Suddi explains *tasurru al-nāẓirīn* as: it delights whoever looks at it — the same understanding is reported from Abu al-ʿAliyah, Qatadah and ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas. Wahb bin Munabbih gives the most vivid image: if you looked at that cow's hide, you would think the sun's rays were shining out through it. Ibn Kathir adds a note of textual criticism here: the present version of the Tawrah says the cow was red, and he judges that an error — though he allows that the yellow may have been so intense that it read as darker or reddish. Then, as he does whenever certainty runs out, he stops: *Allah knows best.*

**Third question (ayah 70) — what is it, exactly?** Their excuse: *"to us all cows are alike."* Ibn Kathir reads this as: cows are plentiful, so describe this one further. And they add the words *"if Allah wills, we will be guided"* — meaning, as Ibn Kathir puts it, *if you describe it to us further*, then we will find it. Even their *in shā' Allāh* is conditional on getting more information first.

**The final answer (ayah 71):** a cow not broken to labour — *lā dhalūl* — neither tilling the soil nor watering the fields; Ibn Kathir explains that it was not used for farming or irrigation at all, but was honourable and fair-looking. *Musallamah* — sound: ʿAbdur-Razzaq records, from Maʿmar, from Qatadah, that it means the cow suffers from no defect; the same from Abu al-ʿAliyah, ar-Rabiʿ and Mujahid, while ʿAta' al-Khurasani specifies that its legs and body are free of physical defect. And *lā shiyata fīhā* — no blemish in it.

Only now do they say: *"Now you have brought the truth."*

## "And they were near to not doing it"

The closing clause of ayah 71 is the verdict on the whole exchange. Ibn ʿAbbas, in a report transmitted by ad-Dahhak, explains *"they slaughtered it, though they were near to not doing it"* with brutal economy: **"They did not want to slaughter it."**

Ibn Kathir spells out what that means. After every question was answered and every doubt removed, they still almost refused — because the questions had never been about clarity. Their aim was obstruction. That is why the Qur'an censures them here: the whole interrogation was stubbornness dressed as inquiry.

The cost of that stubbornness is part of the story. In the report Ibn Kathir carries, the one animal matching the description belonged to a man who owned only that cow, and he said: *"By Allah, I will only sell it for its skin's fill of gold."* And they paid it — the cow's hide filled with gold. That they bought the cow for a large amount of money is also reported from ʿUbaydah, Mujahid, Wahb bin Munabbih, Abu al-ʿAliyah and ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam, though Ibn Kathir notes there is a difference of opinion on the point.

**What this asks of us.** There is a kind of questioning that seeks understanding, and a kind that seeks a way out. The second is what is condemned here. When the command is clear, the safest and easiest path is the one that was open on day one: obey it as it came, in its plainest form, and do not go looking for specifications Allah did not impose. Difficulty in religion is very often something we manufacture ourselves.

## The murder revealed (ayat 72–73)

*"And when you killed a soul and disputed over it."* Al-Bukhari glossed *fa-ddāra'tum fīhā* as "disputed," and that is also the tafsir of Mujahid; ʿAta' al-Khurasani and ad-Dahhak say "disputed about this matter." Ibn Jurayj — and likewise ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam — pictures the scene concretely: some of them said, *"You killed him,"* and the others said, *"No, you killed him."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the murderer had supporters who wanted to hide his crime, and so began accusing different people.

Against all that noise stands the clause that towers over the passage: **"And Allah was going to bring out what you were concealing."** Mujahid's gloss on *taktumūn* is simply: "what you were hiding." Every voice in that crowd was managing the truth. Allah brought it out anyway.

Then ayah 73: *"Strike him with a part of it."* Ibn Kathir's comment here is a model of restraint. Any part of the cow would have produced the miracle. Which part they used was not disclosed to us — because knowing it benefits us in neither our worldly life nor our religion. Had it mattered, Allah would have made it clear. **Allah left it unspecified, so we leave it unspecified.** That is a discipline worth carrying into every story of the past that the Qur'an tells in outline.

*"Thus Allah brings the dead to life."* Ibn Kathir explains: they struck him with it, and he came back to life. Maʿārif fills in the moment — the dead man came back to life, announced the name of his murderer, and died again. In ʿUbaydah's report, asked *"Who killed you?"*, he said, *"That man,"* and pointed at his nephew.

Two consequences followed. The nephew was denied the inheritance he had killed for; and thereafter, whoever committed murder in order to gain an inheritance was not allowed to inherit. The crime cost him the very thing it was committed to obtain.

## An important legal caution

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to fence this off so it is not misread as a precedent. The statement of the murdered man was accepted as evidence for condemning the murderer **because Allah had informed Sayyidna Musa (peace be upon him) through revelation that the man would, on coming back to life, speak the truth.** Outside such a case, no one may be declared guilty of murder without proper evidence, the rules of which have been laid down by the Shariʿah.

## Why a cow at all? Why raise him at all?

Maʿārif raises the honest question a thoughtful reader will ask: Allah had the power to bring the man back to life without any such means, and the name of the murderer could have been revealed even otherwise. Why this route?

Its answer is a piece of sound creed, not a piece of speculation. Allah is omnipotent and does not act under any kind of compulsion; all His actions proceed from His all-embracing wisdom; and He alone knows, and can know, the reason behind what He does. The Shariʿah does not oblige us to discover the reason behind each and every divine act, nor is it necessary — or possible — that we should comprehend it in every case. The best way in such a case, Maʿārif says, is to accept what Allah or the Holy Prophet ﷺ has said, and to keep quiet.

## The greater sign inside the smaller one

Ibn Kathir identifies what the miracle was really for. This ayah demonstrates Allah's ability to bring the dead back to life; beyond settling one murder, Allah made this incident a proof against the deniers that **the Resurrection shall occur** — and with it, their disputing and stubbornness over the dead man came to an end.

He then points out a pattern running through this very surah: Allah mentions His bringing the dead back to life in five places in Surat al-Baqarah — beginning with *"Then We raised you up after your death,"* then this story of the cow, then those who escaped death in their land though they numbered in the thousands, then the prophet who passed by a village that had been destroyed, then Ibrahim and the four birds, and the land that comes back to life after it has died. All of these, he says, alert us to one fact: bodies will become whole again after they have rotted. And he brings the same argument from elsewhere in the Qur'an: *"And a sign for them is the dead land. We give it life, and We bring forth from it grains, so that they eat thereof…"* (36:33–35).

This is why ayah 73 ends *"so that you may understand"* — or as Maʿārif puts it, this precedent should induce people to make use of their reason, and see that what has happened in a past instance can as easily happen in a future instance.

## A last word on the order

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes with an observation about sequence that is easy to miss. Ayah 72 — the murder and the mutual accusations — is chronologically the *beginning* of the story, yet it is placed after the account of the cow in ayat 67–71. The chronological order has not been preserved; it has been inverted, and that re-arrangement has a subtle significance.

The reason: this long section of the surah is dealing with the transgressions of the Israelites, and the Qur'an does not narrate stories for their own sake here. This episode is meant to show two misdeeds — first, committing a murder and then trying to hide it; second, raising uncalled-for objections to divine commandments. Had the chronological order been kept, readers would have supposed that only the first was really intended, and that the second was added merely to complete the story. The present arrangement shows that both misdeeds are equally emphasized.

That is the passage's quiet sting. We instinctively rank the murder as the grave sin and the endless questioning as a minor irritation. The arrangement of these ayat says otherwise: the heart that hides a crime and the heart that argues with a clear command are being addressed together.

passages.title: Hardened hearts and the distortion of Scripture
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat trace what happens to a community when its heart goes hard: first the hardening itself (74), then what hardened people do with revelation — bend it, hide it, invent it, and sell it (75–79). The thread holding the passage together is a single movement from an inner state to an outward crime, and from the crime of the learned down to the confusion of the unlearned and back up again to the learned who caused it.

## The moment the heart set

Ayah 74 opens with "Even then" — Ibn Kathir renders it, **"Then after that your hearts were hardened."** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān sets the scene: the sūrah has been recounting one incident after another showing that the Israelites were prone to disobedience and rebellion and had to be punished again and again. That experience should have taught them humility and obedience. Instead their hearts grew all the more hardened against divine guidance, and that insensibility led them into further misdeeds and transgressions.

Ibn Kathir points to the specific miracle just described. Al-ʿAwfī reported in his Tafsīr that Ibn ʿAbbās said: when the slain man was struck with a part of the cow, he stood up and became more alive than he had ever been. He was asked, "Who killed you?" He said, "My nephews killed me." Then he died again. And after Allah took his life away, those same nephews said, "By Allah! We did not kill him" — denying the truth while they knew it. It was of that moment, Ibn ʿAbbās said, that Allah declared **"and became as stones or even worse in hardness."**

Sit with that. A dead man speaks, names his killers, and dies again in front of them — and they deny it, knowing the truth. This is why Ibn Kathir says their hearts were like stones that never become soft: by the passage of time they were unlikely to accept any admonishment at all, even after the miracles and signs they had witnessed, with no hope of ever softening.

**And this is not a museum piece.** Ibn Kathir immediately notes that this is why Allah forbade the believers from imitating them, citing: *"Has not the time come for the hearts of those who believe to be affected by Allah's Reminder and that which has been revealed of the truth, lest they become as those who received the Scripture before, and the term was prolonged for them and so their hearts were hardened?"* (57:16). The verse names the danger precisely: the term was prolonged, and the hearts hardened. Long exposure to revelation is not by itself the same thing as being softened by it.

## "Or harder" — what the grammarians saw

The Arabic says *fa-hiya ka-l-ḥijārati aw ashaddu qaswah* — "so they are like stones, or harder still." Ibn Kathir records that the scholars of the Arabic language disagreed over the meaning of this phrase **after agreeing on one thing**: that the word *aw* ("or") here is not being used to reflect doubt. They then differed on what it does express:

- **"Or" meaning "and"** — as hard as stones *and* harder. They compared it to *"And obey not a sinner or a disbeliever among them"* (76:24) and *"To cut off all excuses or to warn"* (77:6).
- **"Or" meaning "rather"** — as hard as stones; *rather*, harder. Compare *"A section of them fear men as they fear Allah or even more"* (4:77), *"And We sent him to a hundred thousand or even more"* (37:147), and *"And was at a distance of two bows' length or even nearer"* (53:9).
- **"Or" dividing them into two kinds** — their hearts are only of two types: some as hard as stone, some harder than stone. Ibn Jarīr commented that this is the sense of it, and said he favoured this last interpretation, though he held the others plausible.

Ibn Kathir gives his own view: the last reading resembles the way Allah gives one parable — *"Their likeness is as the likeness of one who kindled a fire"* (2:17) — and then a second, *"Or like a rainstorm from the sky"* (2:19); and again *"their deeds are like a mirage in a desert"* (24:39) followed by *"Or like the darkness in a vast deep sea"* (24:40). Some of them are like the first example, and some like the second. And he closes, as the scholars do, with **"Allah knows best."** Where they genuinely differed, we hold the difference rather than flatten it.

## Even the stones are softer than that

Having made the comparison, the ayah then dismantles it — because stones come off better. Ibn Kathir explains: sometimes springs and rivers burst out of stones; sometimes stones split and water comes out of them, even if there are no springs or rivers around them; and sometimes stones fall down from mountaintops out of their fear of Allah. Muhammad bin Isḥāq narrated that Ibn ʿAbbās explained the meaning: *"Some stones are softer than your hearts — they acknowledge the truth that you are being called to."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws out why the three states are listed in that order, and the order is deliberate. Placed highest are the stones whose responsiveness is so strong that rivers gush from them and provide sustenance to beasts and men — against which the hearts of these people are so hard that they are incapable of feeling any sympathy for a fellow human being even in suffering and pain. In the second degree come stones that do serve Allah's creatures, but to a lesser extent. Their hearts are harder than even those. To the lowest degree belong stones that benefit no one at all — but can at least *feel* the fear of Allah. And they are devoid of even that minimum.

**Does a stone really feel?** Some claimed the humility of stones is mentioned only as a metaphor. Ibn Kathir records that Ar-Rāzī, Al-Qurṭubī and other Imams said there is no need for that explanation, because Allah creates this characteristic in stones. He lines up the evidence: *"We did offer the trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they declined to bear it and were afraid of it"* (33:72); *"The seven heavens and the earth and all that is therein glorify Him"* (17:44); *"And the stars and the trees both prostrate themselves"* (55:6); *"Have they not observed things that Allah has created — how their shadows incline"* (16:48); *"They both said: We come willingly"* (41:11); *"Had We sent down this Qurʾan on a mountain…"* (59:21); and *"And they will say to their skins, Why do you testify against us? They will say: Allah has caused us to speak"* (41:21).

From the Sunnah, Ibn Kathir cites what is recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ, that the Prophet ﷺ said of Mount Uḥud: **"This is a mount that loves us and that we love."** He mentions likewise the compassion of the stump of the palm tree for the Prophet ﷺ, as confirmed in authentic narrations. And in **Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim** it is recorded that the Prophet ﷺ said: **"I know a stone in Makkah that used to greet me with the salām before I was sent. I recognise this stone now."** He also said of the Black Stone that on the Day of Resurrection it will testify for those who kiss it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān meets the objection on its own ground: the ability to feel fear does not always require reason — after all, animals feel fear without possessing reason. Sensibility is necessary, but there is no rational argument that denies sensibility to minerals, since sensibility depends on life and minerals may possibly possess a kind of subtle life man is not aware of. It adds that scientists have recently found signs of life and sensibility in minerals too. But its decisive point is the right one for a believer: **an explicit statement in the Qurʾan carries a validity and an authority no physical science or rational argument can dispute.** It also cautions against overreach — the Qurʾan itself says this cause operates only in the case of *some* stones; other stones may fall for causes that are purely physical.

## From hard hearts to handled scripture (75)

Ayah 75 turns to the Muslims and asks: **"Do you covet that they will believe in your religion?"** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān explains the setting — the Muslims used to take great pains in trying to make the Jews accept Islam. After so many accounts of their perversity, the Qurʾan points out to the Muslims that they cannot expect such a people to be sensible, and asks them not to worry much about them: men so enslaved to their desires and so shameless in their pursuit of evil cannot be expected to listen to anyone.

Note the careful wording Allah uses: **"a party of them"** — *farīq*. Ibn Kathir identifies them as the deviant sect whose fathers witnessed the clear signs but whose hearts became hard afterwards. The charge is precise, not blanket.

Their crime is *taḥrīf*: they "used to hear the Word of Allah, then they used to change it" — which Ibn Kathir glosses as distorting its meaning — **"after they understood it"**, and **"knowingly."** They understood well, yet they used to defy the truth, being fully aware of their erroneous interpretations and corruption. He connects it to *"because of their violation of their covenant, We cursed them and made their hearts grow hard. They change the words from their places"* (5:13) — the same two-step: hardness, then handling scripture.

Qatādah commented that these were the Jews who used to hear Allah's Words and then alter them after they had understood and comprehended them. Mujāhid was blunter: *"Those who used to alter it and conceal its truths; they were their scholars."*

Ibn Wahb reported from Ibn Zayd a picture of how it worked in practice. They altered the Tawrāh that Allah revealed to them, making it say that the lawful is unlawful and the prohibited is allowed, that what is right is false and what is false is right. **So when a person seeking the truth came to them with a bribe, they judged his case by the Book of Allah; when a person came seeking to do evil with a bribe, they took out the other, distorted book, in which it was stated that he was in the right; and when someone came who was neither seeking what is right nor offering a bribe, they enjoined righteousness on him.** Which is exactly why, Ibn Zayd said, Allah addressed them: *"Do you enjoin righteousness on the people and forget yourselves, while you recite the Scripture? Have you then no sense?"* (2:44).

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes two views on which "Word of Allah" is meant: the Tawrāh, which they had heard from the prophets — and the distortion then covers changes made in the words themselves, or in the sense, or in both — or the words of Allah heard directly by the seventy men at Mount Ṭūr, who had gone to seek divine confirmation of what Sayyidnā Mūsā (peace be upon him) had been telling them, and who then declared before their people that Allah had promised to forgive them if they could not act upon certain commandments. It also answers an obvious objection: the Jews who were contemporaries of the Prophet ﷺ may not themselves have been involved in some of these transgressions, but since they did not abhor the misdeeds of their forefathers, they are to be considered their counterparts.

## Two faces, one Knower (76–77)

Ayah 76 catches them mid-conversation. Muhammad bin Isḥāq reported that Ibn ʿAbbās commented: they would tell the Muslims they believed Muhammad ﷺ is the Messenger of Allah — *"but he was only sent for you Arabs."* Then when they met each other: *"Do not convey the news about this Prophet to the Arabs, because you used to ask Allah to grant you victory over them when he came, but he was sent to them, not to you."*

Al-Ḥasan Al-Baṣrī described the same scene: when they met the believers they used to say "We believe"; when they met each other, some of them would say, *"Do not talk to the companions of Muhammad about what Allah has foretold in your Book, so that the news does not become a proof for them against you with your Lord — and thus you will win the dispute."*

Ibn Kathir spells out the reasoning behind it: *if you admit to them that he is a Prophet, knowing that Allah took the covenant from you to follow him, they will know that Muhammad is the Prophet we were waiting for and whose coming we find foretold in our Book. Therefore, do not believe in him, and deny him.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān adds the political texture: seeing the growing power of the Muslims in Madinah and around it, some of them pretended to have accepted Islam, and in order to assure the Muslims of their sincerity and win their favour they would now and then disclose that the Torah itself had given the good tidings of the coming of the Prophet ﷺ and mentioned the Qurʾan. But when they met other Jews who openly declared their adherence to Judaism, they would admit they were only trying to deceive the Muslims — and would be reprimanded for revealing what the others were trying to keep concealed, since a knowledge of those verses could be very useful to the Muslims in defeating them in argument.

Then ayah 77 lands: **"Do they not know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal?"** Abū Al-ʿĀliyah — and this is also Qatādah's reading — said what they *conceal* is their secret denial and rejection of Muhammad ﷺ, although they find his coming recorded in their Book. Al-Ḥasan said the concealment refers to when they were alone with each other, away from the Companions, forbidding one another from passing on the news. What they *reveal*, said Abū Al-ʿĀliyah, Ar-Rabīʿ and Qatādah, is the words "We believe."

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws the practical conclusion: it would make no difference at all whether the hypocrites tried to conceal their infidelity from the Muslims, or the other group tried not to disclose the verses of the Torah that speak of the Prophet ﷺ — because Allah Himself has, on different occasions, informed the Muslims in the Qurʾan both of the hypocrisy and of the testimony. **You cannot manage information in front of the One who knows the concealed and the open alike.**

## The unlettered and their wishes (78)

Ayah 78 shifts down to the crowd. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān maps the structure: ayah 77 deals with the educated ones among them, ayah 78 speaks of those who were unlettered, and ayah 79 turns back to the scholars.

*Ummiyyūn* is the plural of *ummī* — a person who does not write, as Abū Al-ʿĀliyah, Ar-Rabīʿ, Qatādah, Ibrāhīm An-Nakhaʿī and others said; Ibn Kathir notes that this meaning is clarified by the phrase "who know not the Book." The word is not itself a slur: *ummī* was one of the descriptions of the Prophet ﷺ, since he was unlettered — *"Neither did you read any book before it, nor did you write any book with your right hand; in that case, indeed, the followers of falsehood might have doubted"* (29:48) — and Allah says *"He it is Who sent among the ummiyyīn a Messenger from among themselves"* (62:2). The Prophet ﷺ said, "We are an *ummī* nation, neither writing nor calculating. The month is like this, this and this" (thirty or twenty-nine days), which Ibn Kathir explains to mean that Muslims do not need to rely on books or calculations to decide the timings of their acts of worship.

What is condemned is not their illiteracy but what filled the vacuum: **amānī**. Ad-Ḍaḥḥāk reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said this means "a false statement they utter with their tongues." It was also said that *amānī* means wishes and hopes. Mujāhid commented that Allah described them as not understanding any of the Book He sent down to Mūsā, yet they create lies and falsehood — so the word here refers to lying and falsehood. On "and they but guess," Mujāhid said: "They lie"; Qatādah, Abū Al-ʿĀliyah and Ar-Rabīʿ said: "They have evil, false ideas about Allah." Maʿārif ul Qurʾān names the cause: their own scholars did not give them correct or proper information about their religion, so no wonder their minds were stuffed with baseless superstitions which they found very pleasant and flattering.

**A clarification worth having.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān pauses on *ẓann*, the word rendered "guess," because people misuse this verse — ignoring the context and concluding that no view or injunction resting on *ẓann* may be followed at all. The Qurʾan uses *ẓann* in three ways: perfect certitude — *"Those who are certain that they are going to meet their Lord"* (2:46); the greatest likelihood — *"And he said to him whom he thought was the more likely of the two to be released from the prison"* (12:42); and mere fanciful supposition, as here. Only the third is what the Qurʾan prohibits us to follow: a fanciful opinion unsupported by a respectable argument, or one that goes against a valid one. It is necessary to follow the first two. When certain ahadith, or arguments and conclusions in the Sharīʿah, are described as resting on *ẓann*, that is the second signification — the kind one cannot avoid in any sphere of life and which the Sharīʿah requires us to accept and follow. To apply this verse's condemnation to every case, and use such verses to reject the legitimate arguments and injunctions of the Sharīʿah, says Maʿārif ul Qurʾān, is to betray one's ignorance of the Qurʾan.

## Woe to the pen for hire (79)

Ayah 79 comes back up to the top and strikes: **"Then woe to those who write the book with their own hands and then say, 'This is from Allah,' to purchase with it a little price!"** Ibn Kathir explains *waylun* — a well-known word in the Arabic language, carrying the meanings of destruction and perishing. This, he says, is another category of people among them: those who called to misguidance with falsehood and lies about Allah, thriving on unjustly amassing people's property.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān is unsparing about why this verse turns to the scholars. Since the dishonesty of their scholars was the real cause of the people's superstitiousness, **the crime of the former was greater than that of the latter.** Greedy and self-seeking, and in order to please the people so as to receive money and respect from them, they used to misrepresent divine injunctions — going so far as to change the words of the Torah or distort the sense, pretending all the while that this was just what Allah had said or meant. And the ayah announces a grievous punishment for *two* distinct sins — distorting the Word of Allah, and earning money by doing so — which is why "woe" is repeated. Ibn Kathir renders it: woe to them because of what they have written with their own hands, the lies, falsehood and alterations; and woe to them because of the property they unjustly acquired. Ad-Ḍaḥḥāk reported Ibn ʿAbbās commenting that the torment will be theirs because of the lies they wrote with their own hands, and because of what they unjustly acquired from people, "be they commoners or otherwise."

What is the "little price"? Al-Ḥasan Al-Baṣrī answered: **"The little amount here means this life and all that it contains."**

Az-Zuhrī said that ʿUbaydullāh bin ʿAbdullāh narrated that Ibn ʿAbbās said — and Ibn Kathir notes this was also collected by **Al-Bukhārī**: "O Muslims! How could you ask the People of the Book about anything, while the Book of Allah that He revealed to His Prophet ﷺ is the most recent Book from Him and you still read it fresh and young? Allah told you that the People of the Book altered the Book of Allah, changed it and wrote another book with their own hands. They then said, 'This book is from Allah,' so that they acquired a small profit by it. Hasn't the knowledge that came to you prohibited you from asking them? By Allah! We have not seen any of them asking you about what was revealed to you."

## What the passage asks of us

Read as one unit, these ayat are a warning delivered to a Muslim audience about a pattern, not a museum label on someone else's history:

- **Guard the heart against hardening.** Ibn Kathir made this the first lesson, through 57:16: the believers are forbidden to imitate them. And if some stones split for water and fall from mountaintops out of fear of Allah, then Ibn ʿAbbās's verdict stands as the measure — some stones are softer than a heart that will not acknowledge the truth it is called to.
- **Never handle revelation to fit a customer.** Ibn Zayd's portrait — one ruling for the truth-seeker who pays, another for the wrongdoer who pays, and fine advice for whoever brings no money — is the exact shape of religious knowledge corrupted by interest.
- **Do not practise two faces.** Saying "we believe" in one room and something else in the next is answered not by argument but by ayah 77: Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal.
- **Scholars carry the heavier weight.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān is explicit that the crime of the learned was the greater one, because the superstition of the unlearned traced back to them.
- **And do not sell it.** Whatever the fee, Al-Ḥasan Al-Baṣrī has already priced it: this life and all that it contains is the "little price."

passages.title: "The Fire will only touch us a few days"
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat take a comforting religious slogan and dismantle it. Some among the Jews were saying that the Fire could only touch them for a short, countable stretch of days — a brief inconvenience, then out. Ayah 80 quotes the claim and answers it with a question that has no safe answer; ayat 81 and 82 then replace wishful thinking with the actual law by which Allah settles every case, stated in two clean halves: one for the person whose sin has closed over him, one for the person who believes and acts on it.

What holds the passage together is a single move — from **what people hope** to **what Allah has decreed**. Read ayah 82 as the second half of a sentence that begins in ayah 81; they are one ruling with two sides.

## "Only a few numbered days"

The wording the Qur'an quotes is precise: not "a while", but *ayyāman maʿdūdah* — **days that are numbered**, a small, finite tally. That is the whole appeal of the claim. It concedes punishment in principle while emptying it of weight.

How many days? Al-'Awfi reported that Ibn 'Abbas said of this ayah: "The Jews said, 'The Fire will only touch us for forty days.'" Ibn Kathir adds that others said this was the period during which they had worshipped the calf. So the claim was not random; it was a piece of theology. A specific sin, a specific sentence, then release.

### The argument behind the slogan

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reconstructs the reasoning, and it is worth following carefully, because it is more sophisticated than a mere boast.

It begins from a principle it describes as common to all the revealed Sharīʿahs: a **believer** who commits sins may receive punishment in Hell for a time, in accordance with the degree and nature of his sins — but because he possesses *īmān* (faith), he is not assigned to Hell forever, and is released once his term is served.

The Jews making this claim applied that principle to themselves. Their premise was that the Sharīʿah of Sayyidnā Mūsā (peace be upon him) had not, in their view, been abrogated. If that were so, they reasoned, then they were still *muʼmins* — true believers — and denying the prophethood of Sayyidnā ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) and of Sayyidnā Muhammad ﷺ had not turned them into disbelievers. Believers who sin get a limited term. Therefore: a few days, then out.

Notice where Maʿārif ul Qurʼān aims its reply. It does not dispute the first step; it goes after the premise about perpetuity. As it puts it, this false assertion is based on another false assertion. The Torah never declares that the Sharīʿah of Mūsā (peace be upon him) is meant to last forever; to claim perpetuity for it is unfounded. Once that premise falls, the conclusion falls with it — and on this commentary's reading, those who made such a claim while denying the two prophets who came after Mūsā must on account of that denial be held to be disbelievers. And no Book of Allah holds out to disbelievers the promise that they will be released from Hell after a while. That promise is precisely what the ayah calls a **pledge** — a covenant — from Allah; since Allah never made it, the claim has nothing under it.

## The question with no safe answer (ayah 80)

Notice how Allah instructs His Prophet ﷺ to reply. Not with a counter-assertion, but with **"Say: Have you taken a covenant from Allah, so that Allah will not break His covenant?"**

Ibn Kathir unfolds the force of it. In effect: *if you had a promise from Allah for that, then Allah will never break His promise* — the argument concedes without hesitation that a covenant from Allah is absolutely secure. That is not the weak point. The weak point is that, as Ibn Kathir says, such a promise never existed. And so the ayah closes the second door: **"Or is it that you say of Allah what you know not?"** What you say about Allah, you have no knowledge of, and you thus utter a lie about Him.

Two exits, both sealed. Either produce the covenant, or admit you are speaking about your Lord without knowledge. The passage treats confident religious claims about the unseen as a serious matter: a comforting slogan about the Hereafter, if it has no basis in revelation, is not optimism — it is speech about Allah without knowledge.

### The Prophet ﷺ puts the claim to them face to face

Ibn Kathir cites a report that Al-Hāfiz Abu Bakr bin Marduwyah recorded from Abu Hurayrah, noting that Imam Ahmad, Al-Bukhari and An-Nasa'i recorded similarly. When Khaybar was conquered, a roasted poisoned sheep was presented to the Prophet ﷺ as a gift. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered, "Assemble before me all the Jews who were here." When they were summoned he ﷺ asked, "Who is your father?" They replied, "So-and-so." He said, "You have lied; your father is so-and-so." They said, "You have uttered the truth." He then asked, "Will you now tell me the truth, if I ask you about something?" They replied, "Yes, O Abul-Qasim; and if we should tell a lie, you will know our lie as you have about our fathers."

Then came the question that touches our passage: **"Who are the people of the Fire?"** They said, "We shall remain in the Fire for a short period, and after that you will replace us in it." The Prophet ﷺ said, "May you be cursed and humiliated in it! By Allah, we shall never replace you in it." He then asked whether they had poisoned the sheep. They said, "Yes." Asked what made them do so, they said they wanted to know if he was a liar, in which case they would get rid of him — and that if he were a Prophet, the poison would not harm him.

The report is illuminating precisely because the claim of ayah 80 is not reported second-hand there. It is spoken to the Prophet ﷺ directly, by people who had just conceded that he could see through their lies.

## "But no!" — the law replaces the wish (ayah 81)

Ayah 81 opens with *balā*, rendered here as **"But no!"** — a word of rebuttal. Ibn Kathir's paraphrase is exactly this: *the matter is not as you have wished and hoped it to be.*

Then the actual criterion: **"Whosoever earns evil and his sin has surrounded him."** The image is one of encirclement — the sin has closed around the person on every side. Ibn Kathir explains the case as one who does an evil deed and *abides purposefully in his error*, coming on the Day of Resurrection with no good deeds, only evil deeds; then he will be among the people of the Fire. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same idea as evil taking hold of a man so completely that no trace of goodness is left.

### What "his sin has surrounded him" means — the early scholars differ

Ibn Kathir gathers several early readings of this phrase, and they are worth keeping distinct:

- **Shirk.** Abu Hurayrah, Abu Wa'il, ʿAtā' and Al-Hasan said it means his *shirk* — associating partners with Allah — has surrounded him.
- **Dying unrepentant.** Al-A'mash reported from Abu Razin that Ar-Rabīʿ bin Khuthaym said it means "whoever dies before repenting from his wrongs." As-Suddi and Abu Razin said similarly.
- **Major sins.** Abu Al-ʿĀliyah, Mujāhid, Al-Hasan, Qatādah and Ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas said it refers to major sins.

Ibn Kathir does not set these against one another. He comments that all of these statements carry similar meanings — **and Allah knows best.** So the phrase is not left as an unresolved puzzle: the reports are treated as describing one reality from different angles.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the piece that keeps this ayah from crushing a sinful believer. How can evil take hold of a man so completely that no trace of goodness is left? That, it says, happens only in the case of disbelief, and not to Muslims even when they are sinners. No good deed of a disbeliever is acceptable to Allah on account of his disbelief, so on the Day of Judgment he has nothing but evil to show. The believer's situation is structurally different: he has, to begin with, the greatest and highest good deed to his credit — *īmān* itself — and his other good deeds are recorded in his account alongside it. Such a person cannot be devoid of all goodness, and evil cannot be said to have taken hold of him completely.

### From the Sunnah: how small sins accumulate

Under this ayah Ibn Kathir mentions a hadith that Imam Ahmad recorded, in which 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"Beware of the belittled sins, because they gather on a person until they destroy him."**

He ﷺ then gave them an example: people who set up camp on a flat land, and then their servants came. One of them collected some wood and another man collected some wood until they collected a great deal. They then started a fire and cooked what they put on it.

That is the mechanism of the ayah made visible. No single stick is a fire. Every stick is dismissed as nothing much. And the blaze that eventually rises is made of nothing but the things that were dismissed. Sin "surrounds" a person the way that woodpile grew: one negligible piece at a time.

## The other half of the law (ayah 82)

**"And those who believe and do righteous good deeds, they are dwellers of Paradise."** Ibn Kathir glosses it: they believe in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and perform the good deeds that conform with the Islamic Law — they shall be among the people of Paradise.

Note the pairing the ayah insists on: belief *and* deeds. Not a claim of identity on its own; not activity without faith. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point in its own terms — faith in Allah and in the Holy Prophet ﷺ, whose Sharīʿah has now abrogated all the earlier Sharīʿahs, together with good deeds done in conformity with it.

Ibn Kathir places beside this the passage at 4:123–124, which states the whole principle in one breath: *It will not be in accordance with your desires (Muslims), nor those of the People of the Scripture; whosoever works evil will have the recompense thereof, and he will not find any protector or helper besides Allah. And whoever does righteous good deeds, male or female, and is a true believer — such will enter Paradise, and not the least injustice, even the size of a naqīr* (the speck on the back of a date stone), *will be done to them.*

That cross-reference is doing something important. The correction in ayah 81 was aimed at a claim made by others, but 4:123 addresses the Muslims first — *not in accordance with your desires*. Nobody inherits the Hereafter through group membership. Muhammad bin Ishaq reported that Ibn 'Abbas said of ayah 82: whoever believes in what you (Jews) did not believe in, and implements what you refrained from implementing of Muhammad's religion ﷺ, shall acquire Paradise for eternity — and Ibn 'Abbas draws out the symmetry, that Allah stated that the recompense for good or evil works shall remain with its people for eternity.

## Living it

**Do not carry a claim you cannot produce a covenant for.** The question of ayah 80 is worth asking of any comfortable assumption we hold about our own end: *is there a covenant from Allah behind this, or am I saying about Him what I do not know?* Hope grounded in revelation is faith; hope invented to soothe ourselves is exactly what ayah 80 names.

**Take the small ones seriously.** The hadith of Ibn Mas'ud attaches directly to the image of encirclement. The sins we have trained ourselves to call belittled are the very material out of which the surrounding is built.

**Reach for repentance while there is life.** On the reading reported from Ar-Rabīʿ bin Khuthaym, the phrase "his sin has surrounded him" describes "whoever dies before repenting from his wrongs" — so on that reading, repentance is the thing to hurry toward while the door is still open.

**Faith is your largest good deed — guard it, then build on it.** The consolation in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is real and should be received as such: a believer is not devoid of all goodness, because *īmān* stands at the head of his record. But receive it as encouragement to add to that record — not as a new version of the very slogan ayah 80 came to demolish.

passages.title: The covenant on worship, kin, and bloodshed broken
passages.tafsir:
This passage sets a covenant beside its breach. In ayah 83 Allah recalls the pledge He took from the Children of Israel — worship Him alone, be dutiful to parents and kin, care for orphans and the poor, speak good to people, perform the prayer and give Zakah. Ayah 84 recalls further articles of that same pledge: do not shed one another's blood, do not drive one another from your homes. Then ayat 85–86 hold up the mirror: this is exactly what you are doing, in Madinah, now. The unity of the passage is the distance between a promise made and a life lived.

## The covenant of ayah 83: rights in their proper order

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 83 as a list arranged by rank. First comes worship of Allah alone with no partner — "this is the highest and most important right," he says, and it is why Allah created His creatures at all. He gathers other verses to show it was never a command peculiar to Israel: no Messenger was sent before the Prophet ﷺ except that it was revealed to him that there is no deity but Allah, so worship Me (21:25), and in every community a Messenger was raised proclaiming: worship Allah alone, and avoid all false objects of worship (16:36).

"After that comes the right of the creatures" — and among those, first, the parents. Ibn Kathir notes a habit of the Qur'an: Allah usually mentions the rights of parents alongside His own. "Give thanks to Me and to your parents" (31:14); "your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be dutiful to your parents" (17:23), running on to "give to the kinsman his due and to the poor and to the wayfarer" (17:26) — the same descending order this ayah follows.

The Two Sahihs record that Ibn Masʿud said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah! What is the best deed?' He said, 'Performing the prayer on time.' I said, 'Then what?' He said, 'Being kind to one's parents.' I said, 'Then what?' He said, 'Jihad in the cause of Allah.'"

Ibn Kathir then defines two of the categories. The orphans are "the young who have no fathers to fend for them." *Al-Masakin*, the poor, is the plural of *Miskin*, "the one who does not find what he needs to spend on himself and his family" — poverty defined not abstractly but as a shortfall in a household.

Maʿarif ul Qurʼan draws out the wider point: this one verse brings out the basic elements common to Islam and all the earlier revealed law — *Tauhid* (the doctrine of Allah's oneness), service to parents, relations, orphans and the needy, gentleness in speaking to all human beings, Salah and Zakah. Nothing here is fresh legislation peculiar to Israel; it is the permanent shape of a life owed to Allah.

## "And speak good to people"

Ibn Kathir explains this as "say good words to them and be lenient with them," and adds that this includes commanding good and forbidding evil. He cites al-Hasan al-Basri: "The good saying means commanding good and forbidding evil, and being patient and forgiving. The good words to people, as Allah commanded, also includes every good type of behaviour that Allah is pleased with."

Notice what al-Hasan does. Gentleness of speech is not softness about truth; commanding good and forbidding evil is itself part of good speech — provided it is carried with patience and forgiveness.

Ibn Kathir sees an order in the sequence: Allah commands the servants to say good words to people after commanding them to be kind to them, "thereby mentioning two categories of manners: good speech and good actions." And he cites a hadith Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Dharr, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not belittle any form of righteousness, and even if you did not find any good deed except meeting your brother with a smiling face, then do so." Ibn Kathir notes it was also collected by Muslim in his *Sahih* and by at-Tirmidhi, who graded it *Sahih*. The smallest unit of good conduct is a face that does not shut people out.

**Who is included in "people"?** Maʿarif ul Qurʼan is emphatic: the verse asks us to adopt a gentle tone and an open-hearted manner in speaking to others, whether they are "good or evil, pious or impious, orthodox or aberrant," followers of the Sunnah or adherents of innovations. But it draws the line where al-Hasan drew it: in religious matters one should not try to hide the truth for the sake of pleasing people or winning their approval. Gentle manner, undiluted message.

Its proof: when Allah sent Musa and Harun (peace be upon them) to Pharaoh, He instructed them to use gentle and soft words (20:42). Maʿarif puts the argument directly: none of us who addresses another today can be superior to Musa (peace be upon him), nor can the man addressed be viler than Pharaoh.

It follows this with an account from Talha ibn ʿUmar, who said to ʿAtaʾ — a great master of the sciences of exegesis and hadith — "One can see around you people who are not quite orthodox in their beliefs. As for me, I am rather short-tempered. If such people come to me, I deal with them harshly." ʿAtaʾ replied, "Do not behave like this," and, reciting this very verse, added: Allah has commanded us to speak to people politely; when Jews and Christians are all to be treated like this, would this commandment not apply to a Muslim, no matter what kind of a man he is? (Maʿarif cites this from Qurtubi.)

The ayah closes with the two pillars that bind worship to society — perform As-Salah and give Zakah — and then the verdict: "then you slid back, except a few of you." Ibn Kathir stresses that they abandoned these orders "knowingly and intentionally." Maʿarif identifies the faithful few as those who acted on the Shariʿah of Musa (peace be upon him) as long as it was in force, and who followed the Shariʿah of Muhammad ﷺ once it came.

Ibn Kathir adds that Allah ordered this Ummah similarly in Surat an-Nisaʾ (4:36), in a fuller list that includes the neighbour who is near of kin, the neighbour who is a stranger, the companion by your side, the wayfarer, and those whom your right hands possess — and comments that of these orders "this Ummah has practised what no other nation before it has, and all praise is due to Allah."

## Ayah 84: "your own blood, your own homes"

The second set of articles is phrased with a striking pronoun: shed not the blood of **your** people, nor turn out **your own** people from their dwellings. Ibn Kathir explains the meaning as: "Do not kill each other, nor expel one another from their homes, nor participate in fighting against them." And he draws attention to the wording itself — Allah "mentioned the word 'your own' here," just as He did in 2:54 — "because the followers of one religion are just like one soul."

He then quotes the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "The example of the believers in their kindness, mercy and sympathy to each other is the example of one body — when an organ of it falls ill, the rest of the body rushes to its aid in fever and sleeplessness." A community is not a set of individuals holding a truce; killing a fellow believer is self-harm.

Ayah 84 ends: "then you ratified it, and you bore witness." Ibn Kathir: "You testified that you know of the covenant and that you were witnesses to it." Maʿarif ul Qurʼan sharpens the legal texture: sometimes a person does not express willingness in so many words, but the manner of his speech suggests it — their agreement was not of that order, but "as clear and explicit as the statement of a witness usually is." They could not plead that they never understood the terms.

## What was actually happening in Madinah

This is the passage's key: it is not ancient history but current affairs. Ibn Kathir reports, through Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Yasar, that Ibn ʿAbbas commented on these ayat and said that "the behaviour of the Jews regarding the Aws and Khazraj was the reason behind revealing these Ayat."

The Aws and Khazraj were two tribes of Madinah, idol-worshippers before Islam, locked in recurring war. Around them lived Jewish tribes bound to them by alliance — in Ibn Kathir's account, Banu Qaynuqaʿ and Banu an-Nadir allied to the Khazraj, and Banu Qurayzah to the Aws. When war erupted, each Jewish tribe fought alongside its Arab allies. So a Jew would fight beside polytheists against Jews of the other camp, shedding the blood of his own brethren — though they had the Tawrah with them and knew their rights and dues — driving each other from their homes and looting whatever furniture and money they could. Meanwhile, as Ibn ʿAbbas notes, the Aws and Khazraj themselves "did not know about Paradise, the Fire, Resurrection, Divine Books the lawful and prohibited." The people who had the Book were slaughtering each other for the sake of people who had none.

Then the war would end — and the same men would scrupulously ransom the Jewish prisoners taken by the other side, "according to the rulings of the Tawrah," and ask for blood money too. Maʿarif ul Qurʼan (which names Banu Qurayzah as friendly with the Aws and Banu Nadir with the Khazraj) lays out three special injunctions binding on them: they should not kill one another in internecine war; they should not force their own people into exile; and if they found one of their own a prisoner of war, they should pay a ransom and get him released. "The Israelites disregarded the first two injunctions, and acted upon the third alone which they supposed easier to be carried out."

Maʿarif also records their two-sided justification. Asked why they showed such solicitude for the prisoners, they would say that it was obligatory for them to get prisoners released. When someone objected to their helping non-Jews slaughter Jews in the first place, they replied that it would be a real disgrace if they did not go to the aid of their friends, even if those friends were not Jews. Religion where it cost little, tribal loyalty where it counted.

## "Do you believe in a part of the Book and reject the rest?" (85)

That question is the heart of ayah 85, and it is asked of people who could not claim ignorance. Ibn Kathir paraphrases it: "Do you ransom them according to the rulings of the Tawrah, yet kill them while the Tawrah forbade you from killing them and from expelling them from their homes? The Tawrah also commanded that you should not aid the polytheists and those who associate with Allah in the worship against your brethren. You do all this to acquire the life of this world."

Maʿarif ul Qurʼan notes that the Qur'an indicts their behaviour as "sin and aggression," and reads that pairing as naming two distinct violations: they were infringing the right of Allah, by disobeying Him, and the right of His creatures, by inflicting pain and loss on them. Both ledgers were being run up at once.

Ibn Kathir adds that a people who implemented the Tawrah sometimes and defied it at other times — knowing all the while that what they were doing was wrong — should not be trusted to preserve or convey it. Nor, he says, should they be believed regarding what the earlier Prophets had told them about the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, his coming, his expulsion from his land and his Hijrah: all of which they hid among themselves.

## Was this disbelief?

Ayah 85 speaks of these people, on the face of it believers in a Book, as rejecting part of it. Maʿarif ul Qurʼan handles this carefully and offers two readings.

It first notes a prior fact: the Jews referred to here had already become disbelievers by refusing to accept and affirm the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ. Yet the verse sets that aside and points to another aspect.

Taken literally, the verse means they had become disbelievers by not having faith in some parts of the Tawrah — "for a Divine Book has to be accepted as a whole; to reject a part is to reject the whole," and that amounts to disbelief.

Read the second way, the verse reprimands them not for rejecting rulings in principle but for failing to act upon them. This raises a real question, since a believer is not judged an unbeliever so long as he accepts, at least in principle, the lawful and the unlawful exactly as the Shariʿah lays them down. Maʿarif's answer is that when a sin is very grave, "the idiom of the Shariʿah sometimes delineates it as Kufr (infidelity) in order to emphasize its gravity and its moral nature" — the same idiom, it says, in the hadith wording it cites, that whoever gave up the Salah wilfully became an infidel. Maʿarif is careful to add that this second interpretation does not attenuate or modify the disbelief the Jews had already been guilty of by denying the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ.

**The recompense.** Disgrace in the life of this world, and on the Day of Resurrection consignment to the most grievous torment — "because they defied Allah's Law and commandments," says Ibn Kathir, and "as punishment for defying the Book of Allah that they had." The worldly half was not left abstract: Maʿarif notes it came to pass in the Prophet's ﷺ own lifetime, when the Jews of Banu Qurayzah lost their lives or underwent imprisonment, and those of Banu Nadir were expelled for having broken the pact they had earlier made with the Muslims.

**A doctrinal note.** One may very well ask why the direst punishment should be named here, when these people at least believed in Allah, unlike outright atheists. Maʿarif ul Qurʼan reports the answer of a famous commentator in his *Ruh al-Maʿani*: every punishment meted out to the disbelievers will be "the direst" in the sense that it will have no end or limit. So the verse does not imply that their punishment will exceed that of every other disbeliever; it places them in the category of punishment that does not stop — implying that the punishment of the disbelievers is more severe than that of Muslim sinners. And if there are going to be different degrees of punishment among different kinds of disbelievers, that does not go against what this verse implies. (Maʿarif cites this from *Bayan al-Qurʼan*.)

And then the clause that closes ayah 85: **"And Allah is not unaware of what you do."** Every calculation in this story assumed that no one was keeping the full account. Someone was.

## Ayah 86: the bargain itself

Ayah 86 names the transaction underneath everything: "Those are they who have bought the life of this world at the price of the Hereafter." Ibn Kathir's gloss is stark — "they prefer this life to the Hereafter." The alliances, the plunder, the standing among the tribes: all of it purchased, and the currency was their own eternity.

Two consequences follow. "Their torment shall not be lightened" — Ibn Kathir: "not even for an hour." "Nor shall they be helped" — they "shall find no helper who will save them from the eternal torment they will suffer, nor shall they find any to grant them refuge from it." Maʿarif adds that their sin being so great, Allah will not reduce or mollify their punishment, nor will He allow anyone to intercede on their behalf.

## What this asks of us

Ibn Kathir points out that Allah ordered this Ummah similarly in 4:36 — so ayah 83 is our covenant too.

**Keep the order.** Allah's right first, then parents, then kin, then orphans and the poor, then good words to everyone, then prayer and Zakah. Ibn Kathir's whole reading of ayah 83 is that this sequence is not accidental.

**Do not split the Book.** The failure indicted in ayah 85 is not disbelief in the abstract but selective obedience — keeping the commands that cost little and setting aside the ones that cost. Maʿarif's summary is exact: they acted upon the third injunction alone, "which they supposed easier to be carried out." Anyone who has kept an easy act of worship while shelving a hard obligation knows that temptation.

**Guard the blood and the homes of your own.** The Qur'an calls the victims "your own." What lets a community turn on itself is an outside loyalty that has quietly outgrown the inside one — as in Madinah, where standing by a war-band outweighed a covenant with Allah. What protects against it is what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ described: a single body, in which no limb can fall ill without the rest of it losing sleep.

passages.title: Rejecting messengers out of arrogance and envy
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These five ayat begin with a gift, not an accusation. Allah recounts the chain of guidance He sent to the Children of Israel — the Torah through Musa (peace be upon him), a succession of prophets after him, and finally 'Isa son of Maryam (peace be upon him) with clear signs — and then asks why every messenger who came with something their desires did not want was met with arrogance, denial, or the sword.

Ibn Kathir heads this section "The Arrogance of the Jews who denied and killed Their Prophets," and opens by saying that Allah described their insolence, their rebelliousness, defiance and arrogance towards the prophets, "following their lusts and desires." Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān opens on the other side of the same ayah: here the Qur'an is "again reminding the Israelites how Allah in His mercy forgave them their transgressions again and again, and provided them with all the means of guidance." Both comments describe the same verse — one traces what was given, the other what was done with it.

The remaining ayat move step by step, and the commentators themselves supply the links. Ayah 88 records their reply, "our hearts are ghulf" — which Ma'ārif reads as a piece of self-congratulation that the Qur'an turns into a verdict. Ayah 89 records their rejection of a Book they had themselves been praying for; Abu al-'Aliyah says they knew he was the Messenger of Allah and rejected him out of envy of the Arabs. Ma'ārif then notes that "the next verse attributes the infidelity of the Jews to their malice" — and ayah 90 indeed names their grudging that Allah gives His grace to whom He wills. Ma'ārif again points forward: the next verse "reports what the Jews used to say with regard to the Holy Qur'an, which clearly shows their envy and malice as well as their infidelity" — and ayah 91 gives us their last line of defence, "we believe in what was sent down to us," which the passage then dismantles.

---

## Ayah 87: a chain of mercy, met with a chain of refusal

Allah begins with the gift. He gave Musa **the Book** — the Torah — and, as Ibn Kathir notes, the Jews then "changed, distorted, and defied its commands, as well as altered its meanings." Yet the giving did not stop. Allah sent messengers and prophets after Musa who followed his law, as He says elsewhere: "Verily, We did reveal the Tawrah, therein was guidance and light, by which the Prophets, who submitted themselves to Allah's will, judged for the Jews" (5:44).

**The word *qaffaynā*.** The phrase in ayah 87 is *wa qaffaynā min baʿdihi bi'r-rusul*. As-Suddi reports from Abu Malik that *qaffaynā* means "succeeded" — one after another; others said it means "followed." Ibn Kathir says both meanings are plausible, and points to Allah's words, "Then We sent Our Messengers in succession" (23:44). The image is of prophets arriving one behind another. Guidance was not a single event these people happened to miss; it was a steady stream.

**And then 'Isa.** Ibn Kathir says Allah then sent the last prophet among the Children of Israel, 'Isa son of Maryam, who came with some laws that differed from some in the Torah — and this, Ibn Kathir explains, is why Allah also sent miracles to support him: bringing the dead back to life, forming the shape of birds from clay and blowing into them so that they became living birds by Allah's leave, healing the sick, and foretelling the unseen, as Ibn 'Abbas stated. All of these signs testified to his truthfulness and to what he was sent with. 'Isa himself said, "And to make lawful to you part of what was forbidden to you, and I have come to you with a proof from your Lord" (3:50). Yet, in Ibn Kathir's words, "the Children of Israel became more defiant and envious of him."

## "Ruh al-Qudus" — who is meant?

Allah says He supported 'Isa *bi rūḥ al-qudus*, the Holy Spirit. Ibn Kathir states that this refers to **Jibril**, citing the statement of Ibn Mas'ud in explanation of this very ayah, and the same view from Ibn 'Abbas, Muhammad bin Ka'b, Isma'il bin Khalid, As-Suddi, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas, 'Atiyah al-'Awfi and Qatadah. He supports it with Allah's words, "Which the trustworthy Ruh has brought down. Upon your heart, that you may be one of the warners" (26:193–194).

Two narrations in Ibn Kathir strengthen the identification. **Al-Bukhari** recorded from 'A'ishah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ erected a minbar in the mosque on which Hassan bin Thabit, the renowned poet, used to defend the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with his poems, and the Prophet ﷺ said: *"O Allah! Aid Hassan with Ruh al-Qudus, for he defended Your Prophet."* Ibn Kathir notes that Abu Dawud recorded this hadith in his *Sunan*, as did At-Tirmidhi, who graded it *hasan sahih*. And **Ibn Hibban recorded in his *Sahih*** that Ibn Mas'ud said that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"Ruh al-Qudus informed me that no soul shall die until it finishes its set provisions and term limit. Therefore, have taqwa of Allah and seek your sustenance in the most suitable way."*

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān adds that Jibril (peace be upon him) is often called "Ruh al-Qudus" in the Qur'an and the Hadith — as in "Say: the Holy Spirit has brought it down" (16:102) — and cites a couplet of the poet and Companion Hassan ibn Thabit, may Allah be pleased with him, reported in the Hadith: "Jibra'il, the messenger of Allah, comes to us; he is the Holy Spirit, the incomparable." Ma'ārif lists four ways Allah supported 'Isa (peace be upon him) through Jibril: 'Isa was conceived through the breath of the Archangel; Jibril protected him from being touched by Satan at the time of his birth; the Archangel always accompanied him to defend him against the hostility of the Jews; and it was through him that 'Isa was raised to the heavens.

## The question at the heart of ayah 87

Then comes the reproach: *"Is it that whenever there came to you a Messenger with what you yourselves desired not, you grew arrogant? Some you disbelieved and some you killed."*

Notice the criterion being exposed. Their test for a messenger was not *is he truthful?* but *does he bring what I already want?* Ibn Kathir spells out the mechanism: the prophets used to command them with "what differed from their desires and opinions," and they upheld the rulings of the Torah that the Jews had changed — "and this is why it was difficult for them to believe in these Prophets." Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān puts it starkly: they were "so stubborn in the worship of their desires" that whenever the prophets brought divine injunctions which did not please them, they would deny the prophets — they denied even 'Isa (peace be upon him) — "or would kill them outright," as they did with Zakariyya and Yahya (peace be upon them).

**A grammatical detail worth pausing on.** The ayah says "some you disbelieved" in the past tense, but "some you *kill*" — in the present. Az-Zamakhshari commented that Allah did not say "killed" here "because the Jews would still try to kill the Prophet in the future, using poison and magic." Ibn Kathir then cites the words of the Prophet ﷺ during the illness that preceded his death: *"I kept feeling the effect of what I ate (from the poisoned sheep) during the day of Khaybar, until now, when it is the time that the aorta will be cut off"* — a hadith Ibn Kathir says was collected by al-Bukhari and others. The tense is not a slip; it holds the pattern open into the Prophet's ﷺ own lifetime.

---

## Ayah 88: the excuse that condemns itself

*"And they say: 'Our hearts are ghulf.'"* The early authorities read this in two directions.

**Reading one — a plea of incapacity.** Muhammad bin Ishaq reported that Ibn 'Abbas said it means "our hearts are screened." Mujahid: "they are covered." 'Ikrimah: "there is a stamp on them." Abu al-'Aliyah: "they do not comprehend." On this reading they are saying: *we cannot take in what you bring; something seals us off.* Ibn Kathir links the statement to another verse where deniers say, "Our hearts are under coverings from that to which you invite us" (41:5).

**Reading two — a boast of sufficiency.** Mujahid and Qatadah said that Ibn 'Abbas read the ayah in a way that means: "Our hearts contain every type of knowledge and do not need the knowledge that you, O Muhammad, have." Ibn Kathir adds that this is the opinion of 'Ata' and Ibn 'Abbas. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān sharpens it: they used to say it *sarcastically* — their hearts were so well protected against Islam that it could never touch them, "their way of congratulating themselves on being staunch in their belief."

Either way, the Qur'an's answer is the same and it is devastating: **"Nay — Allah has cursed them for their disbelief."** Ibn Kathir explains the curse as meaning "Allah expelled them and deprived them of every type of righteousness," and adds: it is not as they claim; "rather, their hearts are cursed and stamped." The parallel in Surat an-Nisa' makes the reversal explicit: "And of their saying: 'Our hearts are wrapped' — nay, Allah has set a seal upon their hearts because of their disbelief, so they believe not but a little" (4:155). What they offered as an excuse, or paraded as a virtue, is in fact a judgment already passed on them. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān: "this is not the firmness of faith, but a damnation."

**"So little is that which they believe."** Ibn Kathir records a genuine difference here. Qatadah read it as "only a few of them believe." Some scholars said the ayat indicate that a few of them would believe, or that their faith is minute — because they believed in the Resurrection and in Allah's reward and punishment which Musa had foretold, "yet this faith will not benefit them since it is overshadowed by their disbelief in what Muhammad ﷺ brought them." Other scholars said they did not actually believe in anything at all, and that "so little is that which they believe" means *they do not believe* — comparable to the Arabic expression "hardly have I seen anything like this," meaning "I have never seen anything like this."

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān adds a precise and important qualification. The "little faith" they had pertained to doctrines common to Islam and Judaism — belief in Allah, belief in the Day of Judgment — but they did not accept Muhammad ﷺ as a prophet nor the Qur'an as the Word of Allah, so their faith was not complete. And when the verse calls that fragment *īmān*, it does so "only in the lexical sense," for *īmān* signifies total certitude even if it pertains to certain things and not to others. **From the point of view of the Sharī'ah, such a partial faith cannot be described as *īmān* at all**: the Sharī'ah accepts as valid only the *īmān* which affirms with certitude each and everything one is required to affirm.

---

## Ayah 89: waiting for a prophet, then rejecting him

This is the passage's most concrete moment, and the sources give us the scene.

Before the Prophet ﷺ was sent, the Jews *used to pray for his coming*. Ibn Kathir explains *yastaftihūn*: before this Messenger came to them, they used to ask Allah to aid them by his arrival, against their polytheistic enemies in war. They used to say to the polytheists, "A Prophet shall be sent just before the end of this world and we, along with him, shall exterminate you, just as the nations of 'Ad and Iram were exterminated."

Then Muhammad bin Ishaq narrated from Ibn 'Abbas the moment the prayer was answered — and refused. The Jews had invoked Allah for the coming of the Prophet ﷺ in order to gain victory over the Aws and Khazraj; when Allah sent him to the Arabs, they rejected him and denied what they used to say about him. So **Mu'adh bin Jabal and Bishr bin al-Bara' bin Ma'rur**, of Bani Salamah, said to them: *"O Jews! Fear Allah and embrace Islam. You used to invoke Allah for the coming of Muhammad ﷺ when we were still disbelievers, and you used to tell us that he would come and describe him to us."* **Salam bin Mushkim** of Bani an-Nadir replied: *"He did not bring anything that we recognize. He is not the Prophet we told you about."* Ibn 'Abbas said Allah then revealed this ayah about their statement.

Sit with the collision. The men quoting the prophecy back are the ones who had been disbelievers. The men denying it are the ones who had taught it to them. Abu al-'Aliyah names the reason: they used to ask Allah to send Muhammad ﷺ so that they would gain victory over the Arab disbelievers, but when Allah sent him "and they saw that he was not one of them, they rejected him and envied the Arabs, **even though they knew that he was the Messenger of Allah**." The ayah's own phrasing carries this: *"then when there came to them that which they had recognised, they disbelieved in it."* Not something strange — something *recognised*.

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān notes that the Torah had in several places foretold the coming of the Prophet ﷺ, and that the Jews themselves used to tell the Arabs that a new prophet and a new Divine Book was soon to come; but when the Qur'an came down, and even when they had recognised its authenticity, they denied it out of sheer spite. Ma'ārif then presses the logic of the Qur'an "confirming what is with them": the Qur'an is itself concrete evidence of the truth of the Torah's prophecies about the coming of the Prophet ﷺ and of this Book. So "one who believes in the Torah cannot justifiably deny the Holy Qur'an and the Holy Prophet ﷺ, for such a denial would involve a denial of the Torah itself."

## Knowledge is not faith

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān raises the obvious objection here and answers it, and this is one of the most useful things in the whole passage. If they *recognised* the truth as truth, why does the Qur'an call them disbelievers?

Because *īmān* does not merely mean "knowing the truth"; it really signifies **"accepting the truth and affirming it deed-wise."** Otherwise, Ma'ārif points out, Satan too would have to be called a believer, "for he knows fully well what the truth is."
