In fact, that knowledge "intensifies the gravity of his kufr all the more." Recognition without surrender is not a lesser faith — it is an aggravated rejection.

---

## Ayah 90: the price, and the envy underneath

*"How bad is that for which they have sold their own selves."* Mujahid said: "The Jews sold the truth for falsehood and hid the truth about Muhammad." As-Suddi said it means "the Jews sold themselves" — that is, Ibn Kathir explains, what they chose for themselves was disbelief in what Allah revealed to Muhammad ﷺ "instead of believing, aiding and supporting him." A soul is the one thing a person cannot buy back, and this is what they traded away.

Ibn Kathir says this behaviour of theirs "is the result of their injustice, envy and hatred" — and the ayah then names the object of that envy without softening it: **"grudging that Allah should reveal of His grace unto whom He wills of His servants."** Ibn Kathir's comment is one line: **"There is no envy worse than this."** Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān states the principle they had trampled: prophethood cannot be earned through one's own efforts or one's own merit; it is a special grace which Allah bestows on whomsoever He likes. In begrudging it, "they were questioning the will of Allah Himself."

**"So they have drawn on themselves wrath upon wrath."** Ibn Kathir explains *bā'ū* as meaning that they deserved and acquired *multiplied* anger. Ibn 'Abbas commented that Allah became angry with them because they ignored some of the Torah and disbelieved in the Prophet He sent to them. Abu al-'Aliyah — and similarly 'Ikrimah and Qatadah — said Allah became angry with them because of their disbelief in the Injīl and 'Isa, and became angry with them again because they disbelieved in Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān counts the two wraths differently: one for denying a true prophet, and one for their envy and malice.

**"And for the disbelievers there is a disgracing torment."** Ibn Kathir draws the punishment tightly to the crime: since their disbelief was the result of their transgression and envy, which was caused by *arrogance*, they were punished with disgrace and humiliation in this world and the Hereafter — as Allah said, "Verily, those who scorn My worship, they will surely enter Hell in humiliation" (40:60). Imam Ahmad narrated that 'Amr bin Shu'ayb said that his father said that his grandfather said that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"The arrogant people will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in the size of ants, but in the shape of men. Everything shall be above them, because of the humiliation placed on them, until they enter a prison in Jahannam called 'Bawlas' where the fire will surround them from above. They shall drink from the pus of the people of the Fire."* The one who made himself large is made small; the one who looked down is stepped over.

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān draws out a mercy hidden in this. The added element of *disgrace and abasement* is what marks this out as the punishment peculiar to the disbelievers, "and is not meant for a true Muslim at all, for a Muslim, no matter how great his sins are, will be punished for the purpose of being purified, not for being disgraced."

---

## Ayah 91: the last excuse, dismantled

Told "Believe in what Allah has sent down" — that is, Ibn Kathir explains, believe in what was sent down to Muhammad ﷺ and follow him — they answer: *"We believe in what was sent down to us."* Ibn Kathir paraphrases the attitude: it is enough for us to believe in what was revealed to us in the Torah and the Injīl, and this is the path that we choose. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān exposes what the sentence really implies: they denied the other Books *just because* they had not been sent down to them — and "such an argument betrays their envy and malice."

The ayah answers with the phrase *"while it is the truth confirming what is with them."* Ibn Kathir: since what was sent to Muhammad ﷺ conforms to what was revealed to the People of the Book, that very fact "constitutes a proof against them" — as Allah says, "Those to whom We gave the Scripture recognize him as they recognize their sons" (2:146).

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān sets out three refutations of their claim:
1. The truth and authenticity of the other Books has been established on the basis of irrefutable arguments. Had they any doubts about those arguments, they could well have voiced the doubt and satisfied themselves — so why this *flat* refusal?
2. Those other Books, the Qur'an among them, confirm the Torah. To deny them is at the same time to deny the Torah itself.
3. According to all the Divine Books, to slay a prophet is tantamount to disbelief. The prophets the Jews killed were themselves Israelites, and their teachings were based on the injunctions of the Torah — and they not only killed these prophets but "also accepted the killers as their chiefs." That is a direct denial of the Torah, and it falsifies their claim to believe in it.

That third point is exactly where the Qur'an itself lands: *"Say: 'Why then have you killed the Prophets of Allah aforetime, if you indeed have been believers?'"* Ibn Kathir unpacks it: if your claim to believe in what was revealed to you is true, then why did you kill the prophets who came to you affirming the Torah's law, although you knew they were true prophets? "You killed them simply out of transgression, stubbornness and injustice with Allah's Messengers. Therefore, you only follow your lusts, opinions and desires." As-Suddi noted that in this ayah Allah chastised the People of the Book with that very question. Ibn Kathir then places beside it the ayah we began with: *"Is it that whenever there came to you a Messenger with what you yourselves desired not, you grew arrogant?"* — ayah 91 is answered by ayah 87, and the passage closes on the charge it opened with.

---

## Living it

The passage is a mirror, not a museum exhibit. Read honestly, it puts a few questions to any believer:

- **What is my actual test for truth?** Ayah 87 condemns a people for whom, as Ibn Kathir says, the prophets commanded "what differed from their desires and opinions" — and that was reason enough to refuse. The alternative is to receive Allah's command *especially* when it cuts against what I want; that is precisely where submission is proved.
- **Do I dress up my resistance as a fact about myself?** "Our hearts are ghulf" is the excuse of a heart that has decided in advance. When we say *this just isn't for me*, we should ask whether that is a description or a refusal.
- **Is my faith whole, or selective?** Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān's point is unsparing: a faith that affirms some of what Allah requires and withholds on the rest is *īmān* only in the lexical sense, not in the reckoning of the Sharī'ah.
- **Knowing is not believing.** By Ma'ārif's argument from Satan's own knowledge, information about the truth saves no one; accepting it and affirming it deed-wise is what *īmān* means. Knowledge that does not bend the will only raises the stakes.
- **Guard against envy of Allah's gifts to others.** Ibn Kathir says of their grudging Allah's grace to whom He wills: "There is no envy worse than this." And as Ma'ārif reminds us, prophethood was never something that could be earned by merit in the first place — it is a grace Allah bestows on whomsoever He likes. To begrudge the gift is to quarrel with the Giver.

passages.title: "Wish for death if the Hereafter is yours alone"
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat put a claim on trial. A community said, in effect, that it already believed — and this passage tests that claim twice: once against its own record (ayat 92–93), and once against a challenge so simple it needed nothing but a sentence said out loud (ayat 94–96). Both tests return the same verdict. One question runs the length of the passage and holds it together: *if your faith is what you say it is, why does your history — and your fear — say otherwise?*

Ibn Kathir sets the scene in his commentary here. When the Jews and the People of the Book were told, "Believe in what Allah has sent down" — that is, believe in what came to Muhammad ﷺ and follow him — they answered that it was enough for them to believe in what had been revealed to them, and that this was the path they chose. But, Ibn Kathir notes, they were rejecting what came afterwards *while it is the truth confirming what is with them*: the very agreement between the new revelation and their own scripture was a proof standing against them, not for them, since those given the Scripture "recognize him as they recognize their sons" (2:146). Allah then turns their claim back on them — *Why then have you killed the Prophets of Allah aforetime, if you indeed have been believers?* Ibn Kathir presses the force of it: if you truly believed in what was revealed to you, why did you kill prophets who came affirming the Torah's own law, knowing them to be true prophets? His answer is blunt — out of transgression, stubbornness and injustice, following desires and opinions rather than evidence. As-Suddi is quoted saying that in this ayah Allah chastised the People of the Book.

That is the claim on trial. Everything that follows is the cross-examination.

## First test: a record that answers back

*And indeed Musa came to you with clear proofs, yet you worshipped the calf after he left, and you were Zalimun.*

Notice the compression. The ayah puts the proofs and the calf side by side, joined by nothing but "then." Ibn Kathir lists what those clear proofs were — the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the staff and the hand, and beyond those the parting of the sea, the cloud that shaded them, the manna and quails, the stone that gushed with water. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that signs of this kind came *before* the Torah was given, and were meant to establish two things at once: the Oneness of Allah and His omnipotence, and the prophethood of Sayyidnā Mūsā (peace be upon him).

That is precisely what makes the calf so damning. Ibn Kathir explains *after he left* to mean after Mūsā went to Mount Ṭūr to speak to Allah — the proofs were behind them, not forgotten. And when Allah closes the ayah with *and you were Zalimun* — wrongdoers — Ibn Kathir reads it exactly: you were unjust in this behaviour of worshipping the calf, *although you knew* that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah. This was not ignorance. It was knowledge overridden.

The next ayah keeps the same thread running rather than starting a new topic. *And (remember) when We took your covenant and We raised above you the Mount (saying), "Hold firmly to what We have given you and hear (Our Word)."* Ibn Kathir reads this as a reminder of their errors — breaking the covenant, transgression, defiance: the mountain was raised above them so that they would believe and agree to the terms, and yet they broke it soon afterwards. Their reply, *"We have heard and disobeyed,"* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains with real psychological care: out of sheer fright they said with their tongues that they had heard — that is, accepted — the Command of Allah, but there was no real consent in their hearts, and their whole posture and attitude was as if they were saying that they would not, or could not, obey. Words of submission over a will that had not submitted.

So the same shape appears twice. Proofs, then the calf. A covenant taken under a raised mountain, then defiance. The argument of these two ayat is not two anecdotes; it is one pattern, produced as evidence against a claim.

## How a calf gets inside a heart

Then comes the phrase that gives this stretch of the passage its strange power: *and their hearts absorbed (the worship of) the calf because of their disbelief.* ʿAbdur-Razzāq said that Maʿmar narrated that Qatādah explained it: *they absorbed its love, until its love resided in their hearts* — and Ibn Kathir notes that this is also the opinion of Abū al-ʿĀliyah and ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas. The image is of something drunk in and soaked up rather than merely done: an idol that moved from the hands into the bloodstream.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces how it got there, and this is the most searching passage in the commentary on these ayat. After the Israelites escaped from Egypt with Allah's help and crossed the sea, they came upon a people who used to worship idols. They found the cult so attractive that they asked Sayyidnā Mūsā (peace be upon him) to fabricate a visible, concrete god for them too. He reprimanded them; they realised their error and offered repentance. But — and this is the hinge — *repentance has many degrees*. Since theirs was not of a very high order, the darkness of their error did not altogether leave their hearts. It stayed, it continued to grow, and finally it manifested itself in the worship of the golden calf. In penance some of them had to be slain; others, as some commentators report, were forgiven and not slain — and possibly their repentance too was of a low order. As for those who had not indulged in the worship of the calf at all: they did not hate the action of the worshippers as much as they should have, so their hearts too carried a trace of the sin of association. Whether through the feebleness of their repentance or through a want of proper hatred for disbelief, their hearts became *indolent in religious matters* — sluggish, slow to move — so much so that when Allah asked them to pledge themselves to the injunctions of the Torah steadfastly, Mount Ṭūr had to be suspended over their heads to threaten them.

Read that alongside ayah 92 and the passage tightens rather than wanders: the calf of ayah 92 and the raised mountain of ayah 93 are not two separate failures but one story with a cause. A sin half-repented does not stay where you left it.

Which is why the first test closes with a verdict rather than a description: *Say: "Worst indeed is that which your faith enjoins on you if you are believers."* Ibn Kathir explains this as covering both past and present — their behaviour then and now, disbelieving in Allah's signs, defying the prophets, and worst of all disbelieving in Muhammad ﷺ, the Final Messenger and master of all Prophets, sent to all mankind: how can you claim to believe while breaking Allah's covenant, rejecting His signs, and worshipping the calf instead of Allah? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the logic in a single question — could a true faith ever inspire men to such deeds? If this is what their brand of "faith" produces, it cannot be a true faith; so the claim to be true believers is evidently false.

The record has answered. Now the passage turns from the past to the present tense, and asks them to stake the claim.

## Second test: one sentence, spoken aloud

*Say to (them): "If the abode of the Hereafter with Allah is indeed for you especially and not for others of mankind, then long for death if you are truthful."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān first sets out the claim being answered. The Jews used to claim that the blessings of the other world were specially reserved for them and not meant for any other people; the Qur'an records versions of this elsewhere — "the fire will not touch us but for a few days" (2:80), "No one will enter Paradise except he who is a Jew or Christian" (2:111), "We are the sons of Allah and His close friends" (5:18). And here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a fair and important concession: the use of improper expressions like "sons of Allah" notwithstanding, claims of this kind are *in themselves quite correct*, provided they pertain to people who follow a true and valid faith. Confidence in Allah's promise is not the error. The error was that the faith they were still following had been abrogated and was thus no longer valid — a fact which nullified the claim.

So why this particular test rather than a debate? Because, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, the habitual method of settling a dispute is discussion, with both parties presenting their arguments — and since the Jews knew they could not win that way, they fought shy of it. The Qur'an therefore proposed an abnormal method, one calling for no learning and no cleverness, but only, in its memorable phrase, "a little strain on the tongue." If the blessings of the next world are exclusively yours, declare that you wish to die. That declaration would establish you as genuine; refusal would show you were liars. And the Qur'an went further still: it predicted in advance that they would never have the courage to go through with it.

What does "wish for death" actually mean here? Muhammad bin Isḥāq narrated that Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as: invoke Allah to bring death to the lying camp among the two — Muslims or Jews — and that the Jews declined this offer by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. This is *mubāhalah*, which Ibn Kathir defines as an invocation to Allah to destroy the liars: two disputing parties calling down Allah's judgement on whichever side is false. Ad-Ḍaḥḥāk said that Ibn ʿAbbās said that "then long for death" means "invoke Allah for death." ʿAbdur-Razzāq narrated that ʿIkrimah said that Ibn ʿAbbās commented: had they invoked Allah for death, they would have perished. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded Saʿīd bin Jubayr saying that Ibn ʿAbbās said: had they asked for death, one of them would have choked on his own saliva. Ibn Kathir states that these statements have authentic chains of narration up to Ibn ʿAbbās. Ibn Jarīr also said in his Tafsīr — introducing it only with "we were told," without a chain — that the Prophet ﷺ said that had the Jews wished for death they would have died and seen their seats in the Fire, and that those who invoked such a curse against Allah's Messenger would have found no families and no property had they returned to their homes.

Ibn Kathir also explains *why* such an invocation is described as a "wish": every just person wishes that Allah destroy the unjust opponent who is disputing with him, especially when the just person holds a clear, apparent proof for the truth he calls to. And it targets *death* specifically because to disbelievers life is the biggest prize of all — above all when they know the evil destination they will meet on the other side of it. That last observation is the seam that joins this test to the two ayat that follow: the reason they cannot make the wish is already the reason they cling to living.

Ibn Kathir places two further scenes beside this one, both showing the same instinct. Allah addresses the identical challenge to them in Sūrat al-Jumuʿah — "If you pretend that you are friends of Allah, to the exclusion of all other mankind, then long for death if you are truthful… Verily, the death from which you flee will surely meet you" (62:6–8). And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called a delegation of Najrān's Christians to curse, after he had refuted them in a debate in which they showed stubbornness and defiance — the ayah of mutual invocation, "Come, let us call our sons and your sons… then we pray and invoke the curse of Allah upon those who lie" (3:61). When they heard it, some of them said to each other: "By Allah! If you do such with this Prophet, none of you will have an eye that blinks." They resorted to peace and gave the jizyah in disgrace; the Prophet ﷺ accepted it and sent Abū ʿUbaydah bin al-Jarrāḥ with them as a trustee. In every case: people who claimed certainty were offered the chance to stake it, and quietly withdrew.

## The verdict the silence delivered

*But they will never long for it because of what their hands have sent before them. And Allah is Aware of the Zalimin.*

Ibn Kathir gives the reason in a line: *since they know that they recognise you, and yet disbelieve in you*. He adds that had they wished for death that day, no Jew would have remained alive on the face of the earth. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same thing from the inside: given their hostility to the Prophet ﷺ, one could have expected them to seize so simple a challenge zealously — but they knew very well in their heart of hearts that the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims stood for the truth while they themselves were the champions of falsehood, and so they refused, struck with awe, fearing that the moment they expressed the wish to die, death would come over them and they would be sent to Hell. Their refusal was itself evidence of the truth of Islam.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then closes two loopholes, and both are worth keeping. Could they have wished for death silently, in their hearts? No: the Qur'an itself predicted they never would, and in any case if they could have wished it inwardly they would have declared it aloud, since their victory lay in exactly that declaration — it was a very easy way of refuting the Prophet ﷺ, and they did not avail themselves of it. Could they have declared it and history simply failed to record it? Also no: the opponents of Islam have always outnumbered its adherents, and had such a thing happened they would have trumpeted it aloud to show the world that the Jews had passed the test the Qur'an itself proposed. And note the limit Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explicitly draws: this trial was proposed not for all the Jews of all the ages, but specially for the contemporaries of the Prophet ﷺ who denied him out of sheer envy and malice *in spite of* having recognised that he was a genuine prophet.

The passage does not stop at the refusal; it names the appetite underneath it. *And verily, you will find them the greediest of mankind for life and (even greedier) than those who ascribe partners to Allah. One of them wishes that he could be given a life of a thousand years. But the grant of such life will not save him even a little from (due) punishment.* Ibn Kathir explains the greed as greed to live longer, because they know their evil end and that the only reward awaiting them with Allah is total loss. He captures the whole inversion in one sentence: this life is a prison for the believer and Paradise for the disbeliever. So the People of the Book wish they could delay the Hereafter as much as possible — yet they shall certainly meet the very thing they are trying to avoid.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why the comparison with the idolaters lands so hard. Such an inclination should not surprise anyone on the part of the Arab polytheists — after all, they did not believe in the other world, and physical life was the be-all and end-all for them. But the Jews acknowledged the other world, and even had the illusion that they alone deserved its joys, and yet it was they who, above all others, wished to live in this world as long as possible. That very desire shows how baseless the pretension was, and how they themselves knew what awaited them — physical life serving, as long as it lasted, as a kind of protection against their final fate. The refusal in ayah 94 and the greed in ayah 96 are one and the same fact seen from two sides.

Muhammad bin Isḥāq narrated Ibn ʿAbbās's comment on *the grant of such life will not save him even a little from punishment*: long life shall not save them from torment. And ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam gave the comparison that seals it — living for a thousand years would not save them from torment, just as Iblīs's long life did not benefit him, due to his being a disbeliever. Duration is not mercy. More time without faith is only more of the same.

And the passage closes on the One before whom all of it happened: *And Allah is Seer of what they do* — which Ibn Kathir explains as Allah knowing what His servants are doing, whether good or evil, and compensating each of them accordingly. We affirm that Allah sees, as He has described Himself, without likening His seeing to ours and without explaining it away. The silence in ayah 94 was never silence to Him.

## Living it

The argument is aimed at a specific claim made by a specific community at a specific moment, and the sources are careful to keep it there — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says so in as many words. But its logic travels.

**Test the claim, not the label.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's question is one any believer can turn on himself: could a true faith ever inspire such deeds? If what I call my faith is not shaping what I actually do, then the label is not doing the work I think it is.

**Repent properly the first time.** The most sobering thing in this passage is not the calf; it is the account of how the calf became possible — an inclination repented at too low a degree, a wrong not sufficiently hated, hearts growing indolent in religious matters, until a mountain had to be suspended overhead to get their attention.

**Watch what your fear tells you.** The close of the passage diagnoses a claim not by what people argue but by what they cannot bring themselves to say. A person genuinely confident of what is with Allah does not organise his whole life around postponing it. That is a mirror worth standing in front of, long after the historical dispute has closed.

passages.title: Enmity to Gabriel and the covenants thrown aside
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is doing

These five ayat answer an objection and then strip it bare. The Jews said they could not accept the Qur'an because the angel who brought it — Jibrīl (Gabriel) — was their enemy. Allah answers that Jibrīl did not act on his own, that hostility to him is hostility to Allah Himself, and then turns the argument around: the problem was never the messenger. It was a settled habit of throwing aside what they already knew to be true — the clear signs (ayah 99), the covenants they had given (ayah 100), and finally the Book of Allah itself (ayah 101). Read the five together and you watch an excuse dismantled and a diagnosis put in its place.

## The objection, and where it came from

Imam Abu Ja'far bin Jarir At-Tabari said that "the scholars of Tafsir agree that this Ayah (2:97-98) was revealed in response to the Jews who claimed that Jibril (Gabriel) is an enemy of the Jews and that Mika'il (Michael) is their friend."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in their reasoning. When they learnt that it was Jibrīl (peace be upon him) who brought the Qur'an to the Prophet ﷺ, they said he was their enemy, because it was through him that the rigorous commandments and the catastrophic punishments had always descended upon them — and for that reason they would not accept a Book revealed through him. They added that they could have accepted the Qur'an had Mīkāʾīl (peace be upon him) brought it down, since he is connected with rain and with divine mercy.

Read that slowly, because it is a recognisable human move. They had sorted the angels of Allah into a friendly one and a hostile one, according to whether the news each brought was pleasant. Then they used their own sorting as grounds for refusing revelation.

## The moment it was said out loud

Al-Bukhari recorded, from Anas bin Mālik, an episode that Ibn Kathir places directly under this ayah.

When 'Abdullah bin Salām heard of the arrival of the Prophet ﷺ in Al-Madinah, he was working on his land. He came and said: "I am going to ask you about three things which nobody knows except a Prophet. What will be the first portent of the Hour? What will be the first meal taken by the people of Paradise? Why does a child resemble its father, and why does it resemble its maternal uncle?"

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Jibrīl has just told me the answers."

At that, 'Abdullah said: "He — Jibrīl — among all the angels, is the enemy of the Jews." And the Prophet ﷺ recited this very ayah: *"Whoever is an enemy to Jibrīl … for indeed he has brought it down to your heart."*

He ﷺ then gave the three answers: the first portent of the Hour will be a fire that brings the people together from the east to the west; the first meal of the people of Paradise will be the caudate lobe of the liver of fish; and as for resemblance, if the man's discharge comes first the child will resemble the father, and if the woman's comes first the child will resemble her side of the family.

'Abdullah bin Salām said: "I testify that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah and you are the Messenger of Allah." Then he asked the Prophet ﷺ to question the Jews about him before they learned of his Islam, warning that they would lie about him. When they came, 'Abdullah went inside the house, and the Prophet ﷺ asked what kind of man 'Abdullah bin Salām was. They answered: "He is the best among us, the son of the best among us, our master and the son of our master." He ﷺ asked: "What do you think if he would embrace Islam?" They said, "May Allah save him from it." Then 'Abdullah came out before them and gave his testimony of faith — and at once they said, "He is the evilest among us, and the son of the evilest among us," and kept talking badly about him. He said: "This is what I feared, O Messenger of Allah."

Ibn Kathir notes that only Al-Bukhari recorded this hadith with that chain of narration, and that Al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded it from Anas using another chain.

The scene explains the passage better than any argument could. The same man is "our master" one minute and "the evilest among us" the next — the verdict has nothing to do with him and everything to do with what they need to be true. That is exactly the logic the closing ayat of this passage expose.

## The answer: Jibrīl is a messenger, not a principal

Ibn Kathir explains the ayah's core: whoever becomes an enemy of Jibrīl should know that he is Rūḥ al-Qudus, who brought down the Glorious Dhikr — the Qur'an — to the Prophet's ﷺ heart from Allah, by His leave. He is therefore a messenger from Allah. And "whoever takes a messenger as an enemy, will have taken all the messengers as enemies. Further, whoever believes in one messenger, is required to believe in all of the messengers. Whoever rejects one messenger, he has rejected all of the messengers." He cites Allah's ruling on those who "make distinction between Allah and His Messengers … saying, 'We believe in some but reject others'" (4:150) — Allah decreed that they are disbelievers, because they believe in some Prophets and reject others.

Jibrīl chose no mission of his own; he acted by the command of his Lord. Ibn Kathir cites the angels' own words, *"And we descend not except by the command of your Lord"* (19:64), and *"Which the trustworthy Rūḥ has brought down. Upon your heart, that you may be one of the warners"* (26:192-194).

**Two little words carry the weight: *bi-idhnillāh*, "by Allah's permission."** Once you see them, the objection collapses. To be angry at the courier for the contents of the letter is to be angry at the one who wrote and sent it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the same point as a question: Jibrīl is only a messenger, and brought the Qur'an down under a divine command — so why should they be so particular about the messenger, and not look at the Book itself?

**And look at the Book itself, says the ayah.** It is *muṣaddiqan limā bayna yadayh* — confirming what came before it, meaning, Ibn Kathir says, the previous Books; and it is *hudan wa bushrā lil-muʾminīn* — guidance and glad tidings for the believers, "as guidance to their hearts and bringer of the good news of Paradise, which is exclusively for the believers." He connects this to *"Say: it is for those who believe, a guide and a healing"* (41:44) and *"And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy to those who believe"* (17:82). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion: confirming the earlier Books, guiding people, giving good tidings to the believers — this is precisely what the Divine Books are meant for. The Qur'an is evidently enough a Divine Book, and must as such be obeyed. To deny it out of hostility to Jibrīl is, in that tafsir's blunt words, sheer stupidity or outright perversity.

## The names themselves

Al-Bukhari transmitted from 'Ikrimah: "Jibr, Mīk and Isrāf all mean *worshipper*, while *īl* means *Allah*." On that explanation, these names are compounds — and the angel they were declaring their enemy is named "worshipper of Allah."

Ibn Kathir then records a second account, introducing it as what *some people say*: that *īl* means worshipper, while whatever word is added to it becomes a Name of Allah, since *īl* is the constant element in such a compound. He compares this to the names ʿAbdullāh, ʿAbdur-Raḥmān, ʿAbdul-Malik, ʿAbdul-Quddūs, ʿAbdus-Salām, ʿAbdul-Kāfī, ʿAbdul-Jalīl — in these, *ʿAbd* is the constant while the remainder differs from name to name; and the same case applies to Jibrīl, Mīkāʾīl, ʿAzrāʾīl, Isrāfīl.

The two reports assign the halves of the compound in opposite directions, and Ibn Kathir does not settle between them. He closes with the scholar's honesty: *Allah knows best.* What is not in dispute is that a name of this kind is built out of servanthood and the divine Name — which is a quiet rebuke to anyone treating such a bearer as an enemy.

## "Brought down upon your heart" — a warning worth heeding

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that Maulānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānavī, in *Bayān al-Qurʼān*, warned against a very grave error people might draw from the statement in ayah 97 that Jibrīl brought the Book down *upon the heart* of the Prophet ﷺ: the conclusion that Allah revealed only the meanings of the Qur'an and not its words. That supposition is quite baseless, he says, because many ayat of the Qur'an itself mention the Arabic language as the vehicle of revelation in the case of this particular Book of Allah.

He adds two further points. First, the heart perceives words as much as it perceives meanings — in fact the perceiving agent is the heart, while the ears and the rest are only its instruments; and in the state of revelation the external organs of the senses become dormant, so the heart receives even the words directly, without the intervention of the ears. Second, as a mundane analogy only — for we cannot understand the nature of revelation properly — while dreaming in sleep we do hear words and remember them afterwards, though our outward hearing was suspended. So the revelation of meanings to the heart in no way precludes the revelation of the words. And he concludes that it is a sin, and an intellectual dishonesty, to rely on one's own conjectures in defiance of a clear and definite statement in the Qur'an.

## The answer is then widened, deliberately

They named one angel. The passage answers with a list: *"Whoever is an enemy to Allah, His Angels, His Messengers, Jibrīl and Mīkāʾīl — then verily, Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers."*

Ibn Kathir notes that Allah's messengers include angels and men, citing *"Allah chooses Messengers from angels and from men"* (22:75). So why single out Jibrīl and Mīkāʾīl when both are already included among the angels who were messengers? Because, he says, this ayah was meant to support Jibrīl, the emissary between Allah and His Prophets — and Mīkāʾīl is mentioned because the Jews claimed that Jibrīl was their enemy and Mīkāʾīl their friend. Allah informs them that whoever is an enemy of either one is an enemy of the other, as well as of Allah.

Ibn Kathir adds that Mīkāʾīl sometimes descended to some of Allah's Prophets, though to a lesser extent than Jibrīl, since that was primarily Jibrīl's task; and that Isrāfīl is entrusted with blowing the Trumpet for the commencement of the Resurrection. It is recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ that whenever the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would wake up at night, he would supplicate: *"O Allah, Lord of Jibrīl, Mīkāʾīl and Isrāfīl, Creator of the heavens and earth and Knower of the seen and the unseen! You judge between Your servants regarding what they differ in, so direct me to the truth which they differ on, by Your leave. Verily, You guide whom You will to the straight path."* Notice how the Prophet ﷺ names all three together under one Lord — the opposite of picking favourites among them.

**Then the terrifying line.** Ibn Kathir cites what Al-Bukhari reported from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah the Exalted has said: *"Whoever takes a friend of Mine as an enemy, will have started a war with Me."* Ibn Kathir comments that whoever takes a friend of Allah as an enemy has taken Allah as an enemy, and whoever treats Allah as an enemy shall be Allah's enemy — and whoever is an enemy of Allah will lose in this life and the Hereafter.

Note the exact wording of the ayah's close. They said, "Jibrīl is *our* enemy." Allah does not reply "then Allah is their enemy"; He replies *"Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers."* The label lands before the sentence ends. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the ayah the same way: it puts down the enemies of angels and prophets as *kāfirīn*, infidels, in saying that Allah is the enemy of the infidels — and those who deny or oppose the angels and the prophets will have their due punishment in the other world.

## What was really being thrown aside

Having answered the excuse, the passage names the habit underneath it. Three things are thrown aside in succession — the signs, the covenants, and the Book — and each throw is heavier than the last.

**First, the signs.** *"And indeed We have sent down to you manifest Ayat, and none disbelieve in them but the fāsiqūn"* — those who rebel against Allah's command. Imam Abu Ja'far bin Jarir explains these as clear signs testifying to the Prophet's ﷺ prophethood: the Qur'an narrates the secrets of the knowledge the Jews possessed and hid, and the stories of their earlier generations; it mentions texts in their own Books known only to their rabbis and scholars, and the sections where they altered and distorted the rulings of the Tawrāh. Since Allah mentioned all of this in the Book revealed to His Prophet ﷺ, this fact alone should be evidence enough for those who are truthful with themselves and who wish to avoid destroying themselves through envy and transgression — and beyond that, he says, human instinct itself testifies to the truth Muhammad ﷺ was sent with and to the clear signs he brought, which he did not learn or acquire from mankind.

Ad-Ḍaḥḥāk reported from Ibn ʿAbbās a sharper version of the same point: *"You recite and convey this Book to them day and night, although you are ummī (unlettered) who never read a book. Yet you inform them of what they have in their own Books."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets this against their complaint that no clear evidence or sign of his prophethood had been revealed such as they could recognise and accept. In reply, it says, Allah has revealed a number of very clear signs which even they know and understand very well. So the denial "is not based on a lack of recognition or knowledge, but on their habitual disobedience" — as a general rule, no one denies evidence like this except those who are wilful and stubborn in their disobedience. That is the hinge of the whole passage: the diagnosis moves from the head to the will.

**Second, the covenants.** Ibn Kathir gives the occasion. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent and Allah reminded them of the covenant they had with Him, especially concerning Muhammad ﷺ, Mālik bin aṣ-Ṣayf said: "By Allah! Allah never made a covenant with us about Muhammad, nor did He take a pledge from us at all." Then Allah revealed: *"Is it not the case that every time they make a covenant, some party among them throw it aside?"* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Torah itself reports the pledge that they would have faith in the Prophet ﷺ when he appeared — and on being reminded of it, they flatly denied ever having taken such a pledge.

The ayah does not say they forgot the covenant or failed at it. It says they threw it aside — and it says *every time*, so this is not one lapse but a pattern. Al-Ḥasan Al-Baṣrī glossed *"Nay, most of them believe not"* with: "There is not a promise that they make, but they break it and abandon it. They make a promise today and break it tomorrow." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a distinction here that is worth carrying: going against a pledge is only a sin and a transgression, but having no faith in the pledge one gives to Allah in the first place is outright infidelity. The ayah's *"most of them believe not"* is telling us that behind the serial breaking lay an absence of belief in the compacts themselves.

**And a note of fairness the Qur'an itself insists on.** The ayah says *farīq* — *a party* among them — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points this out explicitly: the Qur'an speaks of one group or another breaking the pledge, and not of all the Jews, for there were some among them who did fulfil their pledges — so much so that many Jews finally accepted Sayyidnā Muhammad ﷺ as a true prophet and joined the ranks of the Muslims. The Qur'an is indicting a documented behaviour, not a bloodline.

**Third, the Book.** *"And when there came to them a Messenger from Allah confirming what was with them, a party of those who were given the Scripture threw away the Book of Allah behind their backs, as if they did not know."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this the latest instance of the habit just described, and the most relevant to the context. The Torah had already given them the good tidings of the coming of the Prophet ﷺ. When he actually came with all the signs the Torah had indicated, thus confirming their own Sacred Book, a large number of them refused to accept him. In doing so they were in fact denying the Torah itself, behaving as if they knew nothing of the prophecy, or even of the Torah being a Book of Allah — and so they were guilty of disbelief in terms of the Torah itself.

The image is precise: to throw something *behind your back* is to put it where you cannot see it, so that you can go on as if it were not there. And *"as if they did not know"* — Qatādah's comment lands hard: "They knew the truth but abandoned it, hid it and denied the fact that they even had it." The ayah does not say they were ignorant; it says they acted the part.

As-Suddi describes the same manoeuvre from the inside. When Muhammad ﷺ came to them, they wanted to contradict and dispute with him using the Tawrāh — but the Tawrāh and the Qur'an affirmed each other, so there was no leverage there. So they gave up on using the Tawrāh. A Book they had been given was quietly set down the moment it stopped serving the argument they wanted to win.

## Living it

**Never judge a message by who carries it.** The whole passage turns on this. It asks them to look past the courier to the letter — does it confirm the earlier Books, does it guide, does it bring good news to the believers? Rejecting truth because of the one who delivers it, or because of what it costs us to accept it, is the exact error named here.

**Do not sort Allah's servants into ones you like and ones you resent.** They wanted the angel connected with rain and mercy and refused the angel through whom hard commands had come. Faith takes the whole of what Allah sends — the warnings as well as the glad tidings, the messengers as a body and not by preference. Ibn Kathir's point stands: believing in one and rejecting another is rejecting all.

**Treat enmity toward the friends of Allah as a danger to yourself.** The Prophet ﷺ conveyed Allah's own words that whoever takes a friend of Allah as an enemy has begun a war with Him. It is worth pausing over the next time contempt for a righteous person rises in the heart.

**Keep your covenants — and believe you are bound by them.** Ayah 100 exposes not just broken promises but a heart that never regarded the promise as binding. Every commitment we make before Allah — a vow, a repentance, an oath, a trust taken on — is measured by that.

**Do not put knowledge behind your back.** Ayah 101 is not a portrait of ignorant people; it is a portrait of informed people acting as if they were not. Knowing, and then arranging your life so as not to have to look at what you know, is a distinct sin, and this ayah names it.
